Part 2 — Corrected report (Parts 0–12, corrections applied in place)

Every section and all detail from the original report are preserved; only what the audit changed has changed. “Verify” and “Unavailable” appear only on items that remain genuinely unresolved. Every fact keeps the source link the checker attached to it. The original report's Run 1 gaps section and Run 2 cover are not reproduced as separate text: each gap in them is either resolved in the audit above or carried into the still-unverified list, and the combined research notes' Part 11/12 follow-up lists are preserved in full in that list. No personal phone number or personal email address of any individual licence holder is reproduced anywhere in this file; names are kept with a link to the official source only.

Last audited: 1 November 2026. Research cut-off: 1 November 2026. No 3 November 2026 election result is included. "Retail" = adult-use. "Medical" = medical marijuana. MED = Marijuana Enforcement Division, Colorado Department of Revenue. DOR = Colorado Department of Revenue. CDPHE = Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment. CDA = Colorado Department of Agriculture. OEDIT = Office of Economic Development and International Trade. AMR = Average Market Rate.

Federal baseline — fixed context, not re-researched. Split scheduling: state-licensed medical marijuana and FDA-approved products moved to Schedule III effective 28 April 2026 (91 FR 22714). All adult-use marijuana remains Schedule I. The broader 2024 rescheduling proposal is not final. IRS §280E is generally lifted for Schedule III medical activity; adult-use remains fully subject to §280E. Hemp: PL 119-37 §781 takes effect 12 November 2026, but PL 119-103 §2019 limits it until 11 December 2026 to only the provisions excluding cannabinoids that are not naturally produced or are synthesised; after 11 December 2026 the full total-THC hemp definition and the 0.4 mg total THC per container cap apply. USDA enforcement of DEA-registered laboratory hemp testing is delayed to 31 December 2026. The federal medical-marijuana appropriations rider runs through 11 December 2026. There is no federal cannabis banking law. Colorado application — do not blur this. Colorado licenses medical and retail marijuana separately under one consolidated code, Title 44, Article 10, and many businesses hold both licences. Schedule III and the §280E change therefore apply, on the baseline as given, to the medical licence activity only. A dual holder must split its activity: medical sales, inventory, books and tax treatment on one side; retail on the other. All retail activity remains Schedule I and fully subject to §280E, even from the same premises or company. No Colorado guidance document prescribing the exact federal accounting split for dual holders was located — that mechanic is Verify against IRS and MED guidance before any filing position. If any tribe operates a medical programme, whether it counts as "state-licensed" for Schedule III is Verify — no tribal medical programme source was located (see Part 10 follow-up). Sourcing rule: official government sources were prioritised. Where a fact rests only on a secondary source, search extract, or a reproduction (Justia / Cornell / FindLaw / vLex) rather than the official page itself, that is stated. Anything uncertain, conflicting or unavailable is marked Verify or Unavailable. No proposed bill is presented as current law. Personal phone numbers and emails of individuals are not reproduced.

PART 0 — HEADLINES

0.1 A mature market still shrinking, more slowly. 2025 total sales (medical + retail): $1,315,678,364 — DOR Marijuana Sales Reports (https://cdor.colorado.gov/data-and-reports/marijuana-data/marijuana-sales-reports). 2024 was $1,397,131,978, so 2025 was about 5.8% down year-on-year. Peak vs now: 2021 peak $2,228,994,553 → 2025 $1,315,678,364, down $913,316,189 (−41.0%, calculated). 2025 was the fourth consecutive annual decline. Jan–July 2026: $740,950,923, down 4.4% on Jan–July 2025 ($774,660,013). July 2026 alone $111,212,979, up 5.3% on June 2026 but 3.9% below July 2025. Cumulative sales through July 2026: $18,959,563,281 (DOR figures, 15 Oct 2026 release). Price collapse is the driver, measured by the Average Market Rate (the DOR wholesale benchmark, §2.3): retail bud AMR was $1,721/lb in Q1 2021 and $648/lb in Q1 2026 (announced 10 Dec 2025, effective 1 Jan–31 Mar 2026 — https://tax.colorado.gov/average-market-rate), then $574/lb in Q3 2026 and $601/lb in Q4 2026. [CORRECTED: the original text mislabelled $648 as "December 2025 median wholesale"; $648 is the Q1 2026 AMR. The $648→$601 movement is a quarter-to-quarter AMR movement, not a contradiction.] Conflict flagged, not mixed: Headset's POS-sample report puts the 2021 peak at $1.8bn and a 35% decline since peak. DOR totals govern; Headset reflects its retailer sample only. 0.2 Licence counts and closures. End of 2025 (MED 2025 Regulatory & Enforcement report, as reported secondarily — Verify against the MED report PDF itself): 2,106 approved business licences, including 687 retail stores, 478 retail cultivations, 210 retail product manufacturers and 14 hospitality establishments; 25,401 employee licences; 1,331 owner licences; 207 owner entity licences (also secondary-reported). Cultivation is the collapse: retail cultivation licences fell from a June 2022 peak of 817 to 478 at end 2025 (−41.5%, calculated) — Verify. [CORRECTED: the "488 active cultivations at end 2025" claim is deleted. 488 retail + 183 medical stores reported sales in June 2026 — licensed ≠ reporting ≠ operating.] A separate DOR-derived claim of a "48% reduction 2021–2025" does not reconcile exactly with 817→478 and is Verify. Stores stabilised: retail stores 644 (Sep 2021) → 665 (Sep 2022) → 685 (Sep 2023) → 687 (end 2025) — Verify. Stores reporting sales in June 2026 were fewer (488 retail + 183 medical). Named closures (secondary, examples only — no official total closure count exists, so none is given): Green Dragon / Eaze ceased Colorado operations autumn 2025 (17 dispensaries at the time); Native Roots Denver cultivation shut with last work day 2 Oct 2026 (WARN, 141 workers); PharmaCann Denver cultivation/processing closed 20 May 2026 (132 workers). All Verify vs WARN/MED sources. 0.3 Tax changes — the local share is now gone. Before 1 July 2025 local governments got 10% of the 15% retail sales tax. SB 25-268 (signed 3 June 2025 — https://leg.colorado.gov/bills/sb25-268) cut it to 3.5% from 1 July 2025. HB 26-1409 (signed 4 June 2026, effective 1 July 2026 — https://leg.colorado.gov/bills/hb26-1409) eliminates the local share (0%) and reallocates the gross 15% retail sales tax as 73.17% Marijuana Tax Cash Fund, 11.33% State Public School Fund, 1.5% Marijuana Cash Fund, 14% General Fund — confirmed by the enacted summary and DOR (https://tax.colorado.gov/marijuana-tax-information-for-local-governments). From 1 July 2026 a city/county gets marijuana revenue only from taxes it levies itself, plus competitive grants such as BEST — not from a state sales share. [Verify: whether 0% is permanent or FY 2026-27 only — a reengrossed-text excerpt suggests the 3.5% paragraph may reappear on and after 1 July 2027; confirm in signed-act §39-28.8-203 before advising beyond FY 2026-27.] HB 26-1409 also directs the Treasurer to transfer from the Marijuana Tax Cash Fund to the State Public School Fund on 30 June 2027 and each 30 June thereafter an amount equal to the difference between the fund balance and (15% of that fiscal year's appropriations from the fund + any emergency-reserve designation). Legislative Council Staff September 2026 forecast (secondary-reported): state marijuana tax revenue $220.1m in FY 2025-26, $218.1m in FY 2026-27 — Verify in the LCS forecast itself. 0.4 Social equity and accelerator. Programme created by HB 20-1424 (2020). Denver reserves store, transporter, cultivation, manufacturing and hospitality licences for social equity applicants until 1 July 2027, with no cap for social equity applicants; only social equity applicants may deliver in Denver (https://denvergov.org/Government/Agencies-Departments-Offices/Agencies-Departments-Offices-Directory/Business-Licensing/Business-licenses/Marijuana-licenses/FAQ). Social-equity licences must remain at least 51% social-equity-owned until 1 July 2027. Denver DLCP published a social-equity report 1 July 2026; since the 2021 rollout Denver had issued 79 marijuana business licences to social equity applicants. What did NOT become law: HB 24-1061 (independent delivery licences, accelerator deliverer/hospitality/transporter licences, $50,000 accelerator-host tax credit, 1 Apr 2025 eligibility reform) was postponed indefinitely 21 Mar 2024, House Business Affairs & Labor. Secondary summaries that list those items without "failed" are wrong. OEDIT grant round reported closed since October 2024 (secondary — Verify against OEDIT). 0.5 Delivery and hospitality — small rollout. [CORRECTED dates:] Medical delivery permits from 1 January 2020; retail delivery from 1 January 2021 — in each case only where the locality opts in, to private residences only. Hospitality: two licences from HB 19-1230 (consumption-only, which may be mobile; and hospitality-and-sales, not mobile) — 14 hospitality establishments at end 2025 (MED report via secondary, Verify vs PDF) but only 10 businesses held a hospitality licence in February 2026 per the HB 26-1117 fiscal note (Arvada, Aurora, Denver); use the dated figures, do not average them. Failed 2026: HB 26-1117 (temporary hospitality permits) — postponed indefinitely Senate Finance 7 May 2026 [CORRECTED: the "after passing the House 6 May 2026" date is deleted; exact House third-reading date Verify on the bill page]. HB 25-1331 (hotel / special-event delivery, Denver hotels only, social-equity holders only) — postponed indefinitely House Business Affairs & Labor 16 Apr 2025. Neither is law. 0.6 Intoxicating hemp — Colorado's low-dose regime meets the federal 0.4 mg cap. Current Colorado rule (SB 23-271): hemp products sold outside a licensed dispensary must have no more than 1.75 mg THC per serving and a CBD:THC ratio of at least 15:1. Products with a ratio less than 20:1 and more than 1.25 mg THC cannot be sold to anyone under 21 [CORRECTED conjunction: bill-summary "and"; CDOT's "or" wording is broader — exact enrolled-text wording Verify]. Delta-8 and other chemically synthesised cannabinoids are strictly prohibited outside the marijuana system. Federal collision, stated by CDOT itself: "A new federal law set to take effect in November 2026 caps hemp products at 0.4 mg of THC per container. This will effectively ban almost all intoxicating hemp products currently legal in the Colorado market." On the fixed baseline the operative date for the full cap is after 11 December 2026; CDOT's "November" wording predates/simplifies the PL 119-103 §2019 delay (12 Nov–11 Dec 2026 limited to non-naturally-produced/synthesised cannabinoid exclusions) — the December date governs for planning, and the CDOT page should be re-checked after December (Verify). A typical Colorado-compliant 1.75 mg can exceeds the federal 0.4 mg per-container cap by more than 4×. After 11 Dec 2026 such a product would be federally non-hemp even if Colorado-compliant as a hemp product, unless Congress acts again or the product moves into the MED marijuana system (MED licence + dispensary sale, not liquor-store sale). Colorado's attempted loosening failed: SB 26-164 (up to 10 mg THC per 12-oz hemp beverage serving; 3 mg in grocery/convenience) was postponed indefinitely Senate Finance 28 Apr 2026. Not law. No Colorado statute, order or guidance responding specifically to PL 119-37 / PL 119-103 was located in this run — Unavailable / Verify after 11 Dec 2026. 0.7 Major bills enacted 2025–2026 (headline; full table in §1.9). HB 25-1209 Marijuana Regulation Streamline — digital occupational licences, name-based employee checks, relaxed R&D sampling — Enacted, signed 3 June 2025; most provisions eff. 5 Jan 2026. SB 25-268 Local share 10% → 3.5% from 1 July 2025 — Enacted, signed 3 June 2025. HB 26-1077 Separate AMRs for fresh-frozen indoor / outdoor unprocessed retail marijuana; DOR rules by 1 July 2027 — Enacted, signed 3 June 2026; eff. 1 July 2026. HB 26-1409 Local share 3.5% → 0% from 1 July 2026 — Enacted, signed 4 June 2026; eff. 1 July 2026. SB 26-007 Medical marijuana use in health facilities for terminally ill registered patients (opt-in facilities, no smoking/vaping; facility need not handle marijuana; CDPHE may not condition facility licensure on compliance) — Enacted, signed 30 Mar 2026; eff. 12 Aug 2026. SB 26-031 Prescription products containing Schedule I substances (FDA-approved + DEA-designated/rescheduled products exempt from state Schedule I; controlled in Colorado as DEA controls them) — Enacted, signed 20 Apr 2026 [CORRECTED: signed date added]; eff. 12 Aug 2026. SB 26-161 Would have replaced 15% excise with $1/lb and 15% sales tax with potency tax; moved testing to CDPHE — Dead, postponed indefinitely Senate Finance 28 Apr 2026, 8–0. SB 26-164 Hemp beverages up to 10 mg / 3 mg — Dead, postponed indefinitely 28 Apr 2026. HB 26-1117 Temporary hospitality permits — Dead, postponed indefinitely Senate Finance 7 May 2026. 0.8 Key numbers at a glance. 2025 total sales $1,315,678,364 (DOR). 2021 peak sales ~$2.23bn (DOR). Jan–July 2026 sales $740,950,923 (−4.4% YoY) (DOR 15 Oct 2026 release). Cumulative sales to July 2026 $18,959,563,281 (DOR). Cumulative tax + fees since Feb 2014 $3,262,200,388 (DOR). 2025 tax + fee revenue $236,449,405 (DOR Tax Reports). Bud AMR, Q1 2021 $1,721/lb; Q1 2026 $648/lb; Q3 2026 $574/lb; Q4 2026 $601/lb (DOR AMR page — https://tax.colorado.gov/average-market-rate). Retail stores, end 2025: 687 (MED report via secondary — Verify vs PDF). Licensed businesses, end 2025: 2,106 (MED report via secondary — Verify vs PDF; "modelled" label deleted). Medical registry fee $52 non-refundable; waiver ≤185% FPL (secondary, most recent — Verify vs CDPHE; fee adopted 15 May 2024, effective 15 July 2024 [CORRECTED date]). Retail purchase limit 1 oz flower equivalent / transaction (Rule 6-110). Adult possession limit 2 oz (HB 21-1090).

PART 1 — LAWS

1.1 Legal status. Both medical and retail (adult-use) marijuana are legal under Colorado state law, for different populations, under different licences. Federal law is different and still governs on federal land in Colorado. Medical: legal since Amendment 20 (2000), Colo. Const. Art. XVIII, §14 — for Colorado residents with a debilitating/disabling condition, a provider recommendation, and a CDPHE registry card (§1.4). Retail: legal since Amendment 64 (6 Nov 2012), Colo. Const. Art. XVIII, §16, first licensed retail sales 1 Jan 2014 — for persons 21+ only, with government-issued ID. What is legal for an adult 21+ (retail): possessing, using, displaying, purchasing or transporting 1 oz or less (constitutional protection); possessing/growing/processing/transporting no more than 6 plants (3 or fewer mature/flowering) and possessing what those plants produce on the premises where grown, in an enclosed, locked space, not openly/publicly, not for sale; transferring 1 oz or less without remuneration to another person 21+; consuming except openly/publicly or in a manner that endangers others; assisting another 21+ person in any of those acts. The statute then raises the possession ceiling to 2 oz (HB 21-1090) — the constitution's 1 oz is the floor of protection, not the current criminal threshold. What remains illegal: sale/transfer to anyone under 21; open/public consumption (except at a licensed hospitality business); driving under the influence / while ability impaired; an open container in the passenger area of a vehicle; taking marijuana across a state line; unlicensed sale; growing more than the limits; any use on federal land. Employers, landlords, hotels and schools may still prohibit use on their property / in the workplace. Visitors: an adult visitor 21+ with valid government ID may buy retail on the same terms as a resident since HB 16-1261 (2016) repealed the former quarter-ounce visitor limit (enrolled text Verify). Visitors may not buy medical — Colorado has no reciprocity (§1.4). Hemp vs marijuana line: "marijuana" in Colorado law does not include industrial hemp — cannabis with no more than 0.3% delta-9 THC on a dry-weight basis (§1.5). Anything above that is marijuana and may only be sold through the MED-licensed system, or, for low-dose hemp products, under the SB 23-271 regime. 1.2 Constitutional provisions, statutes and regulations. Note on "last-amended" dates: a single consolidated last-amended date for each section was not verified section-by-section. Where a date is known from an enacted bill it is given; otherwise the entry says Verify rather than inventing one. Verbatim quotes below were taken from Cornell / Justia / FindLaw / vLex reproductions where the official leg.colorado.gov / Secretary of State text was not opened in full — re-check every verbatim quote against the official text before court or filing use. A. Constitution. A1. Colo. Const. Art. XVIII, §14 — Medical use (Amendment 20, adopted 7 Nov 2000). Creates an affirmative defence and, for registry-card holders, an exception from state criminal law for medical use; defines "debilitating medical condition"; requires CDPHE to keep a confidential registry; caps ordinary medical possession at 2 oz usable marijuana and 6 plants (3 mature); defines primary caregiver; allows the state health agency to approve additional conditions by petition/rulemaking. Quoted in the original (§14(1)(a) condition list; §14(4)(a) 2 oz / 6-plant limits) — secondary quotation, Verify against official text. Statutory expansion — "disabling medical condition", CRS §25-1.5-106(2)(a.7), adds PTSD, an autism spectrum disorder, and any condition for which a physician could prescribe an opioid. Exact session-law citations Verify (PTSD added by HB 17-1367; autism and opioid-condition by later bills — Verify). A2. Colo. Const. Art. XVIII, §16 — Personal use and regulation (Amendment 64, adopted 6 Nov 2012; retail sales 1 Jan 2014). Legalises personal use for 21+; requires DOR to adopt regulations by 1 July 2013 and license cultivation, manufacturing, testing and retail stores; requires the General Assembly to enact a wholesale excise tax with the first $40 million annually to the Public School Capital Construction Assistance Fund (BEST — see Part 2); permits local governments to regulate or prohibit facilities; requires industrial-hemp legislation; preserves medical rights under §14; preserves employer rights (§1.8). §16(3)(a)–(e) quoted in the original (1 oz; 6 plants/3 mature; 1 oz transfer without remuneration; consumption not openly/publicly or endangering others; assisting) and §16(1)(a) (in part) — secondary quotation, Verify against official text. Local control, §16(5)(f) (paraphrase verified, exact wording Verify): a locality may, by ordinance or by vote of its electors, prohibit marijuana cultivation, manufacturing, testing or retail facilities within its jurisdiction. Medical provisions unaffected, §16(7)(a) (in part, Verify exact wording). There is no constitutional potency cap, no constitutional retail purchase limit beyond the 1 oz personal-use protection, and no constitutional delivery/hospitality right — those are statutory/regulatory. B. Statutes. B1. Title 44, Article 10 — Colorado Marijuana Code (CRS §§44-10-101 et seq.). Former separate Medical Code (Title 12, Art. 43.3) and Retail Code (Title 12, Art. 43.4) consolidated into a single Article 10 by SB 19-224 (Sunset Regulated Marijuana, signed 29 May 2019, effective 1 Jan 2020), then repeatedly amended, most recently in this run's scope by HB 25-1209 (effective 5 Jan 2026). Licence classes: CRS §44-10-401. Last-amended date section-by-section: Verify. §44-10-103 Definitions — "regulated marijuana", "regulated marijuana product", medical vs retail, industrial hemp exclusion (exact definitions Verify vs current CRS). §44-10-104 Local jurisdiction authority — county / city-and-county / municipality may license, regulate or prohibit cultivation or sale (verbatim in part via FindLaw — Verify full text). §§44-10-202/203 State Licensing Authority (Executive Director of DOR, acting through MED) and rulemaking power — licensing, security, labelling, advertising, testing, tracking, health and safety; must prohibit health/physical-benefit claims in advertising, merchandising and packaging (current text Verify). §44-10-307 Who may not hold a licence — under 21; criminal history showing lack of good moral character (CRS §24-5-101(2) factors); felony conviction in preceding 3 years or currently under sentence (except: for a social equity applicant, a marijuana conviction alone is not the sole basis for denial); failure to file/pay marijuana taxes; licensed physician making patient recommendations (medical bar); revoked primary-caregiver authority (FindLaw — Verify). §44-10-311 Location / buffer — no licence within 1,000 feet of a school, alcohol/drug treatment facility, principal campus of a college/university/seminary, or residential childcare facility, except renewals of pre-existing licences; local jurisdictions may alter distance minimums (exact text and measurement method Verify before siting advice). §44-10-401 Classes of licences — medical and retail store, cultivation, manufacturer, testing, transporter, R&D, hospitality, hospitality-and-sales, plus occupational licences for owners, managers, operators, employees and support staff (verbatim in part, as in original; full detail in Part 4). §§44-10-501 et seq.; 601 et seq.; 701; 801; 803 Medical and retail operating requirements; testing, tracking and related duties; advertising / false-statement prohibitions; Marijuana Cash Fund; fees (retail application fee capped at $5,000 initially, half to the local jurisdiction, subject to inflation adjustment by Denver-Aurora-Lakewood CPI — FindLaw §44-10-803, Verify; do not use as a current fee schedule). §44-10-1001 Inspection and records — licensee must keep a complete set of records, open during business hours, and retain books/records for the current tax year and the three immediately prior tax years. §44-10-1001(4) added by HB 25-1209, ch. 398, p. 2256, §17, effective 5 Jan 2026 (Verify vs enrolled text — the only section-level amendment date stated in the original). B2. Criminal / controlled substances — Title 18, Article 18, §18-18-406. Criminal backstop to §§14/16: possession over 2 oz, unlawful cultivation, sale/transfer to a minor, open/public use. §18-18-406(3) quoted: "Regardless of whether the plants are for medical or recreational use, it is unlawful for a person to knowingly cultivate, grow, or produce more than twelve marijuana plants on or in a residential property; or to knowingly allow more than twelve marijuana plants to be cultivated, grown, or produced on or in a residential property." Possession tiers (summary, Verify exact ranges before criminal advice): 2 oz or less (adult) — no penalty except open/public use; more than 2 oz to 6 oz — level 2 drug misdemeanour; more than 6 oz — level 1 drug misdemeanour, with higher tiers for larger amounts and sale to minors. Open/public use of 2 oz or less: drug petty offence, fine up to $100 and up to 24 hours' community service (secondary — Verify). §18-18-406.3 — medical-specific unlawful acts (detail Verify). B3. Medical registry statute — Title 25, §25-1.5-106. Implements §14: CDPHE confidential registry; application contents (physician documentation, proof of Colorado residency, fee); two-physician recommendations for patients under 21; ordinary possession/cultivation limits and extended-plant-count process; primary caregivers (transporting/cultivating caregivers register with DOR/MED); CDPHE rulemaking (5 CCR 1006-2 — current version Verify). Amended by HB 21-1317, SB 23-081 and later bills; no single last-amended date stated here. B4. Driving — Title 42, §42-4-1301 (DUI / DWAI). Driving under the influence of alcohol, drugs, or both is prohibited. There is no THC per se DUI offence (unlike alcohol at 0.08) — only a permissible inference: "if the driver's blood contained five nanograms or more of delta 9-tetrahydrocannabinol per milliliter in whole blood, as shown by analysis of defendant's blood, such fact gives rise to a permissible inference that the defendant was under the influence of one or more drugs" — §42-4-1301(6)(a)(IV), as quoted in CDOT FAQs and People v. Turner, 23CA0340. Drivers can still be arrested on observed impairment below 5 ng. §§42-4-1305 / 1305.5 — open container / consumption in a vehicle: class A traffic infraction to consume marijuana or possess an open container in the passenger area on a public road, driver and passengers alike; "open container" includes a package with a broken seal or evidence of consumption (current text Verify). B5. Hemp statutes — Title 35, Article 61; Title 25, Article 5, Part 4. §§35-61-101 et seq. — Industrial Hemp Regulatory Program Act (CDA regulates cultivation). §§25-5-426 / 427 — wholesale food manufacturing; classes of hemp-derived compounds and cannabinoids (SB 23-271) — CDPHE regulates hemp products, MED regulates intoxicating/potentially intoxicating cannabinoids as marijuana products. SB 19-220 (alignment with 2018 Farm Bill) and SB 19-240 (industrial hemp products regulation) created the CDPHE hemp-product registration system; enrolled-text detail Verify. B6. Other major bills that are current law: HB 13-1317 / 1318 (2013, first retail framework and Proposition AA taxes — HB 13-1318 detail Verify); HB 14-1361 (2014, equivalencies — basis for 1 oz = 8 g = 800 mg, corroborated by Rule 6-110's basis-and-purpose); HB 16-1261 (2016, visitor limit repeal — enrolled text Verify); HB 19-1090 (2019, publicly traded / outside-investor ownership); HB 19-1230 (2019, hospitality); HB 19-1234 (2019, delivery); SB 19-224 (2019, sunset/consolidation); HB 20-1080 (2020, employee residency — detail Verify); HB 20-1424 (2020, social equity); HB 21-1090 (2021, possession 1 oz → 2 oz); HB 21-1317 (2021, concentrates); SB 22-205 (2022, CDPHE power over converted THC isomers — predecessor to SB 23-271, detail Verify); SB 23-081 (2023, medical access); SB 23-271 (2023, intoxicating hemp); SB 25-268 and HB 25-1209 (2025); HB 26-1077, HB 26-1409, SB 26-007, SB 26-031 (2026 — see §1.9). C. Regulations. 1 CCR 212-3 — Colorado Marijuana Rules (MED). Part 1 general/definitions; Part 2 applications, licences, fees (Rule 2-205); Part 3 premises, packaging/labelling/advertising, operating requirements; Part 4 testing (Rule 4-115); Part 5 medical store rules (5-115, 5-125); Part 6 retail store rules (6-110, 6-900 hospitality, delivery); Part 8 discipline. Former 212-1 (medical) and 212-2 (retail) consolidated into 212-3 eff. 1 Jan 2020. Rules implementing HB 25-1209 took effect 5 Jan 2026. Current consolidated adoption date rule-by-rule: Verify vs Colorado Register. MED rules page via sbg.colorado.gov/med/rules — page itself not opened (Verify live URL; DOR pages have moved to tax.colorado.gov / cdor.colorado.gov). Rule text reproductions via Cornell/Justia — Verify vs official text. 5 CCR 1006-2 — CDPHE medical registry rules (current text and last-amended date Verify — not opened). 6 CCR 1010-24 — CDPHE hemp product / safe-harbor rules (implements SB 23-271 / §25-5-427: registration, per-serving/package caps, ratio, labelling, testing, converted-cannabinoid prohibition; current text, last-amended date, and exact per-package caps Verify — not opened; see §1.5). 8 CCR 1203-23 — CDA hemp rules (administration/enforcement of Title 35, Article 61). Title 27, Article 80; §27-80-203 defines "tetrahydrocannabinols" and, by cross-reference in §35-61-101, delta-9 THC for hemp purposes. Whether Colorado has adopted any state scheduling rule conforming to the federal 28 Apr 2026 Schedule III move: no such rule located — none asserted here; Verify. 1.3 Possession, home grow, public consumption, vehicles, gifting, product types and potency/purchase limits. Possession — adults 21+ (retail): constitutional protection 1 oz or less (§16(3)(a)); current criminal threshold 2 oz (HB 21-1090). CDOT confirms: "Adults 21 and older can have up to 2 ounces of cannabis." Practical distinction: you may possess 2 oz, but a retail store may sell you only 1 oz (or its equivalent) in a single transaction. Possession ≠ purchase allowance. Purchase limits — retail (Rule 6-110, via Justia, current through Register Vol. 48, No. 11, 10 June 2025 — https://regulations.justia.com/states/colorado/200/212/rule-1-ccr-212-3/part-6/section-1-ccr-212-3-6-110/): "A Retail Marijuana Store and its employees are prohibited from Transferring more than one ounce of Retail Marijuana flower or its equivalent in Retail Marijuana Concentrate or Retail Marijuana Product to a consumer in a single transaction. A Retail Marijuana Store may also Transfer up to six (6) seeds in addition to the one ounce … A single transaction includes multiple Transfers to the same consumer during the same business day where the Retail Marijuana Store employee knows or reasonably should know that such Transfer would result in that consumer possessing more than one ounce of marijuana." Equivalencies (1 oz flower =): 8 grams of concentrate and 800 mg THC in edibles / infused products, in any combination. Non-edible, non-psychoactive products (ointments, lotions, balms, other non-transdermal topicals) are exempt from the 1 oz transfer limit. A 2025 legislative effort to raise the retail sales limit to match the 2 oz possession limit failed (bill number Verify); the 1 oz sale limit remains current. Concentrate daily cap (retail and medical, 21+): 8 grams per person per day (HB 21-1317; see §1.4 for the SB 23-081 medical 40 g single-day mechanism). Home grow — adults 21+ (retail) and patients (medical, same numbers): per adult 6 plants, no more than 3 mature/flowering at one time (§16(3)(b); §14(4)(a) for patients). Per residence 12 plants maximum, regardless of how many adults live there, for medical or retail alike (§18-18-406(3)). Conditions (retail): enclosed, locked space, not openly/publicly, not for sale, produce possessed on the premises where grown. Local limits: local jurisdictions may impose additional restrictions; a secondary summary states the 12-plant cap applies "unless a local jurisdiction permits more" — statutory basis Verify and check the specific city/county ordinance (Part 3). No locality-specific home-grow limit is stated as settled in Part 1. Public consumption: illegal — consumption conducted openly and publicly is expressly not permitted by §16(3)(d). That includes streets, parks, sidewalks, restaurants, bars, concert venues, public transport, ski resorts, and common areas of apartment/condominium buildings (secondary summary of Legislative Council 2024 handbook — Verify handbook text). Penalty: drug petty offence, up to $100 fine + up to 24 hours' community service (secondary — Verify). Exceptions: (1) private property with the owner's permission; (2) a licensed marijuana hospitality business where the locality has opted in. Unless holding a hospitality licence, a licensee shall not permit consumption on its premises (MED reminder sheet, 11 Apr 2023). Vehicles: no consumption in a vehicle, driver or passenger; no open container in the passenger area (broken seal or evidence of consumption makes a package an "open container" — CDOT FAQs). Sealed product within the possession limit may be transported; it must not be taken across a state line (Part 10). Driving impaired: DUI/DWAI under §42-4-1301; 5 ng permissible inference — not a per se limit (below 5 ng, observed impairment can still support DUI/DWAI; above 5 ng, the jury may infer influence). Gifting: adults 21+ may transfer (gift) up to 1 oz without remuneration to another adult 21+ (§16(3)(c)). [AUDIT DECISION: secondary summaries stating 2 oz, tracking the current possession limit, are NOT adopted. The constitutional text says 1 oz; HB 21-1090 raised possession to 2 oz but the gifting subsection's amendment status was not verified from primary text — advise on the 1 oz constitutional figure and flag 2 oz as Verify.] Any transfer for remuneration without a licence is unlawful sale; any transfer to a minor is a felony-tier offence under §18-18-406. Allowed product types (retail and medical, through licensed stores): flower (including pre-rolls); concentrates (wax, shatter, live resin, oils, dabs, vape oils/cartridges); edibles (solid and liquid); beverages (marijuana-infused, sold only through licensed stores — distinct from hemp beverages in §1.5); tinctures; topicals (non-psychoactive topicals exempt from purchase limits); transdermal products; seeds (up to 6 in addition to the 1 oz equivalent, retail). No general potency cap in Colorado. There is no statutory or rule cap prohibiting flower above a THC percentage or concentrates above a THC percentage. Control is by purchase quantity (8 g concentrate/day), not potency percentage. Any claim of a 30% flower / 60% or 70% concentrate cap is not Colorado law. Edibles — retail: 10 mg active THC maximum per standardised serving; 100 mg maximum per package. Rule 4-115 potency-failure provisions: a single serving over 10 mg, or a package over 100 mg, fails potency testing (Cornell — Rule 4-115, Verify vs current rule text). Edibles — medical: manufacturer sets the standard portion; no 10 mg per-serving cap. Medical daily purchase limit is by total THC (20,000 mg, §1.4), not per-serving cap (Verify vs Rule 3-1015 / 5-125). Beverages — marijuana: regulated as marijuana products (same equivalency/labelling as other edibles; measuring-device rules for multi-serving liquids). Hospitality-and-sales: no more than 100 mg active THC in a day to one customer, in servings ≤10 mg each, with a measuring device for multi-serving liquids (Rule 6-925, Cornell — Verify vs current rule text). Vapes: concentrates for purchase-limit purposes (count toward 8 g cap and 1 oz equivalent). No separate vape potency cap located — Verify vs Rule 3-335 if needed. Concentrates — summary: retail 21+: 8 g/day. Medical 21+: 8 g/day ordinary, with SB 23-081 40 g single-day / 30-day-equivalent mechanism (§1.4). Medical 18–20: 2 g/day ordinary, with pre-18-card exception to 8 g/day (§1.4). 1.4 Medical programme. Qualifying conditions. Constitutional ("debilitating") list (§14(1)(a)): cancer; glaucoma; positive HIV status or AIDS, or treatment for such conditions; and a chronic/debilitating disease or condition (or its treatment) producing cachexia, severe pain, severe nausea, seizures (including epilepsy), or persistent muscle spasms (including multiple sclerosis), where the physician's opinion is that it reasonably may be alleviated by medical marijuana; plus any other condition approved by the state health agency by rulemaking or petition. Statutory ("disabling") additions (§25-1.5-106): PTSD; an autism spectrum disorder; any condition for which a physician could prescribe an opioid. Secondary lists adding anxiety, insomnia, fibromyalgia, migraines, arthritis, Crohn's, lupus, etc. as "commonly approved" are not the statutory list — they reflect physician practice under the opioid-condition / agency-approval routes; the exact CDPHE-approved-condition list is Verify against CDPHE. Physician certification. Bona fide physician-patient relationship, diagnosis of a debilitating/disabling condition, conclusion the patient might benefit. Since SB 23-081, the physician is not required to state maximum THC potency, specific product, daily authorised quantity, or directions for use, and is not required to provide a DEA number on the recommendation; those items are optional unless the patient seeks to purchase above the statutory limit, in which case a Uniform Certification Form is required (SB 23-081 fiscal note, leg.colorado.gov). Under 21: two-physician recommendations required. Minors (under 18): two provider certifications and a parent/legal guardian as primary caregiver. Current provider types (MD/DO/APRN/PA scope) — Verify against CDPHE's current provider page; do not assume the 2000 "MD only" text is still operative. HB 21-1317 added, for 18–20 patients, two-physician diagnosis and follow-up appointments every three months — whether the 3-month rule survives SB 23-081 is Verify vs current §25-1.5-106. CDPHE registry and fees. Agency: CDPHE Medical Marijuana Registry — confidential registry. Patient must reside in Colorado and submit proof of residency and identity. Fee: $52 non-refundable, for application and renewal; fee waiver if household income ≤185% of the Federal Poverty Level (certified Colorado tax return or IRS transcript). [CORRECTED: Board of Health adopted the fee 15 May 2024, effective 15 July 2024 — not "15 Oct 2024".] Older figures ($25, $29.50, $35, $90) are outdated — do not use them. $52 is the most recent secondary figure (Sept 2026) — Verify against the live CDPHE application page. Renewal annual; online renewal within 30 days before expiration; new provider certification required on renewal (Verify vs CDPHE). The historical 35-day paper rule is largely superseded by the online system — Verify before advising on it. Caregivers. Constitutional definition (§14(1)(f)): a person, other than the patient and physician, 18+, with significant responsibility for managing the well-being of a patient — merely supplying marijuana is not, by itself, "significant responsibility" (People v. Clendenin — Verify vs opinion). Four types in current practice: (1) parents of minor patients; (2) advising caregivers (advice only); (3) transporting caregivers (transport for homebound patients); (4) cultivating caregivers (grow on behalf of the patient). Only transporting and cultivating caregivers must register with DOR/MED; advising caregivers and parents register through CDPHE. Transporting/cultivating caregivers: maximum 5 patients (secondary — Verify vs §25-1.5-106 / MED rules). Only homebound and minor patients may have a transporting caregiver. A patient cannot have both a designated caregiver and a medical centre cultivating for them at the same time, except parents of minor patients (Verify). CDPHE does not charge caregivers a fee for a caregiver identification card. Caregiver plant ceiling: cultivating caregiver no more than 36 plants ordinarily, 99 plants absolute maximum unless patients have extended counts; only a licensed medical business may grow more than 99 (Verify). Purchase limits — medical (per business day, per patient). Rule 5-125, verbatim in part (via Cornell — reproduction may predate SB 23-081 implementation, Verify vs current rule text): "A Medical Marijuana Store and its employees shall not sell to a patient in a single business day, individually or in any combination, more than: a. Two ounces of medical marijuana flower; or b. Eight grams of Medical Marijuana Concentrate for a patient 21 years old of age or older, or two grams of Medical Marijuana Concentrate for a patient between 18 and 20 years old; or c. Medical Marijuana Products containing a combined total of 20,000 mg." — 1 CCR 212-3-5-125. Possession (medical): 2 oz usable; 6 plants (3 mature) — §14(4)(a). Greater amounts require a physician's extended-quantity recommendation and, for cultivation, registration of the grow. Non-psychoactive topicals exempt from the daily 20,000 mg limit since SB 23-081. A store may sell above the limit only if the patient has a physician recommendation for more, has designated that store as primary store (where required), and the store holds the required documentation; the store must check Metrc for daily authorised quantity and THC potency authorisations before sale. Concentrate limits and young-adult rules — HB 21-1317 / SB 23-081 sequence (do not conflate). HB 21-1317 (2021) — (1) Colorado School of Public Health systematic review of high-potency THC / concentrate health effects + Scientific Review Council; (2) medical concentrate advertising warning on overconsumption risks and prohibition of medical advertising specifically directed at 18–20; (3) dispensary pamphlet on diversion penalties and overconsumption; (4) medical concentrate purchases limited to 8 g/day (21+) and 2 g/day (18–20), with exceptions for homebound patients, physician-certified greater need, significant physical/geographic hardship, and patients who held a card before 18 (as later clarified); (5) retail concentrate purchases limited to 8 g/day; (6) Metrc check before sale; (7) two-physician / follow-up requirements for 18–20. Limits took effect 1 Jan 2022. SB 23-081 (2023) — CONFIRMED by introduced text and fiscal note (https://leg.colorado.gov/bill_files/91274/download): raised the single-day medical concentrate limit from 8 g to 40 g, but capped total concentrate purchases in any 30-day period at the equivalent of 8 g per day (240 g / 30 days); raised the 18–20 limit from 2 g to 8 g per day for patients who held a registry card before turning 18 (other 18–20 patients remain at 2 g/day, subject to physician-certified exceptions); made physician potency/product/quantity/directions optional; allowed a retail store to sell to a patient/caregiver at the medical limit on presentation of a registry card. Warning: secondary pages stating flatly "medical patients can buy 40 g a day" without the 30-day cap are incomplete and misleading; pages stating the ordinary limit is still 8 g/day without the 40 g single-day mechanism are also incomplete. [CORRECTED emphasis: the statute controls over the Cornell Rule 5-125 reproduction, which still shows 8 g / 2 g.] Whether SB 23-081's 40 g mechanism is fully reflected in the current Rule 5-125 text is Verify — the Cornell version may predate SB 23-081 rule implementation. Extended plant counts. A patient who grows more than 6 plants is encouraged to register the grow with MED. A physician recommendation for an extended count based on medical necessity is the basis. Ceilings: patient — no explicit statutory ceiling in the summary beyond medical necessity + registration, but 99 plants is the practical ceiling for non-licensees; caregiver — 36 ordinarily, 99 absolute maximum. Exact extended-count registration rule (MED Rule 2-series / §25-1.5-106) Verify before advising a patient to grow above 6. Medical-necessity defence: §14 affirmative defence (see §1.2). Out-of-state patients — no reciprocity. Colorado does not recognise medical cards or registry status from other states. An out-of-state patient may not purchase from a medical store, but may purchase retail if 21+ with valid ID. Historical reciprocity discussions with Montana/Rhode Island in archived CDPHE FAQs do not create current reciprocity. Schedule III era: Schedule III does not change any Colorado purchase limit, qualifying condition or registry rule; does not make medical marijuana "prescribed" under federal law; does not create reciprocity; does not authorise interstate shipment. 1.5 Hemp and intoxicating hemp. Hemp definition and THC measurement (Colorado, current state law). CRS §35-61-101(7), verbatim: "'Industrial hemp' or 'hemp' means the plant Cannabis sativa L. and any part of the plant, including the seeds of the plant and all derivatives, extracts, cannabinoids, isomers, acids, salts, and salts of isomers, whether growing or not, with a delta-9 tetrahydrocannabinol concentration of no more than three-tenths of one percent on a dry-weight basis." CDA rule definition, 8 CCR 1203-23 Part 1 §1.11, is substantively identical with "total delta-9" wording. CDA pre-harvest testing: laboratory testing on pre-harvest samples to determine total Δ9-THC, which includes Δ9-THCA (THCA decarboxylates to THC on drying/heating). The "acceptable hemp THC level" is when applying measurement of uncertainty to the reported delta-9 THC concentration on a dry-weight basis produces a range that includes 0.3% or less (§35-61-101(1)). Consequence for THCA flower: because Colorado applies a total-THC test to finished hemp products, high-THCA flower low in delta-9 alone but high in total THC is not a legal hemp product at retail in Colorado on secondary analysis (updated 26 Sept 2026) — statute/rule basis (total-THC finished-product test) Verify against §25-5-427 / 6 CCR 1010-24 before advising a retailer. Federal vs state divergence: Colorado's current 0.3% delta-9 (with total-THC applied in testing) is not the same as the post-11 Dec 2026 federal total-THC + 0.4 mg per-container definition. No Colorado conforming amendment to §35-61-101 was located in this run — Verify whether a 2026/2027 bill or rule does so. The intoxicating hemp law — SB 23-271 (2023) and later changes. Citation: Senate Bill 23-271, Concerning the regulation of compounds that are related to cannabinoids, 2023 Regular Session (https://leg.colorado.gov/bills/sb23-271). What it did (official bill summary, in substance): created a framework for (a) CDPHE to regulate and register hemp products and certain intoxicating hemp products, and (b) MED to regulate intoxicating products or potentially intoxicating compounds that are or may be cannabinoids, including power to authorise/prohibit chemical modification/conversion/synthetic derivation; labelling and advertising; production and testing; inspection, recordkeeping and tracking; and classifying/reclassifying cannabinoids as intoxicating, potentially intoxicating, or non-intoxicating. New statute: CRS §25-5-427 — Classes of hemp-derived compounds and cannabinoids — definitions — registration required — prohibitions — safe harbor — rules — repeal. It also amended §25-5-426 (wholesale food manufacturing). Predecessor: SB 22-205 (2022) authorised CDPHE to prohibit by rule chemical modification/conversion/synthetic derivation of intoxicating THC isomers from hemp (detail Verify); joint MED/CDPHE guidance May 2021 had already stated chemically altering/converting naturally occurring cannabinoids in hemp is not compliant with the hemp-product definition (Verify guidance document itself). Later changes: no later statute amending §25-5-427's core 1.75 mg / 15:1 framework was located other than the failed SB 26-164 (none-located claim, Verify by session-law search). CDPHE rulemaking under §25-5-427 (6 CCR 1010-24) is the "later change" mechanism — current version Verify. Any claim Colorado raised the hemp limit to 5 mg or 10 mg in 2024–2025 is wrong — those figures are either the failed SB 26-164 proposal or secondary summaries of safe-harbor package caps, not enacted law. Three classifications (SB 23-271): (1) Non-intoxicating cannabinoids — e.g. CBD, THCV, CBC, cannabicitran, cannabicyclol, cannabielsoin, CBG, CBDV, CBN (examples Verify vs enrolled text) — derived from hemp may be produced, distributed or sold as a hemp product. (2) Potentially intoxicating cannabinoids / compounds — including novel cannabinoids not yet assessed for safety: a person shall not manufacture, produce or distribute a potentially intoxicating cannabinoid within Colorado as an ingredient in a hemp product or as a finished hemp product, unless it is a safe-harbor hemp product exported from Colorado; and shall not market/promote a hemp product as containing THC or any other potentially intoxicating cannabinoid. (3) Intoxicating cannabinoids — including delta-8, delta-9, delta-10 and other THC isomers (THC definition expressly includes isomers, derivatives, salts and acids): products containing potentially intoxicating compounds and intoxicating cannabinoids must only be produced, distributed or sold by a person licensed by MED to do so — i.e. through the marijuana system — except for the low-dose hemp-product exception below and safe-harbor exports. Which products are allowed, per-serving limits, minimum age, sales channels. Allowed outside a dispensary (hemp channel): a finished hemp product that is a cosmetic, dietary supplement [CORRECTED: added], food, food additive or herb, for human use/consumption, containing hemp-plant parts including naturally occurring cannabinoids, with no more than 1.75 mg THC per serving and a CBD:THC ratio of at least 15:1, manufactured by a CDPHE-registered manufacturer, labelled and tested under CDPHE rules. Per-serving vs per-package (Verify): firmly sourced figure is 1.75 mg per serving. A secondary summary of 6 CCR 1010-24 adds ≤5 mg THC per package (non-safe-harbor) and ≤2.5 mg per serving / ≤10 mg per package (safe-harbor full-spectrum). Those package caps are not stated as settled law here until 6 CCR 1010-24 is opened. Minimum age: no general 21+ floor for all hemp products. Age rule is ratio- and dose-dependent: a hemp product with a CBD:THC ratio less than 20:1 and more than 1.25 mg THC cannot be sold to a person under 21 [CORRECTED conjunction — see §0.6; enrolled-text exact "and/or" wording Verify]. In plain terms: a low-dose, high-ratio product (≤1.25 mg and ≥20:1) may be sold to an adult 18+; anything stronger or lower-ratio is 21+ (subject to the Verify above). Sales channels (hemp channel): liquor stores, grocery stores, gas stations, bars/restaurants (for beverages meeting 1.75 mg / 15:1), and online sale/shipping to states where allowed. No Colorado hemp-store licence is required for retail sale in this channel; the burden falls on the manufacturer (CDPHE registration) and compliance with per-serving/ratio/labelling rules. Full registration types are Part 7. Not allowed outside dispensaries: (a) any product with more than 1.75 mg THC per serving or a ratio below 15:1 — that is a marijuana product, MED licensee only; (b) delta-8, delta-10, HHC, THCO, THCP and other chemically converted/synthetically derived intoxicating cannabinoids — "strictly prohibited" outside the marijuana system; (c) THCA flower as a retail hemp product (secondary, Verify); (d) any hemp product marketed as containing THC or a potentially intoxicating cannabinoid; (e) any product that is not a cosmetic, dietary supplement, food, food additive or herb (e.g. smokable hemp — smokable-hemp rule in §25-5-427 / 6 CCR 1010-24 Verify; do not assume smokable hemp is freely saleable). Safe harbor (export only): a hemp product manufactured/produced for export from Colorado, registered with CDPHE, that would otherwise contain a potentially intoxicating cannabinoid. It may not be sold in Colorado as a hemp product; it must be exported, and export to a state where it is illegal is prohibited. Do not confuse "safe harbor" (export) with "safe harbor full-spectrum" package-cap language in secondary summaries. Registration with CDPHE; licence through MED (if any). CDPHE registration is required for manufacturers of hemp products (including safe-harbor products) under §25-5-426 / §25-5-427; manufacturing/producing/selling/distributing/holding for sale a safe-harbor product without registering is prohibited. MED licence is required for intoxicating products: a person must be licensed by MED to manufacture, produce, distribute or sell products containing potentially intoxicating compounds or intoxicating cannabinoids as marijuana products (ordinary MED licence types in §44-10-401). There is no separate "intoxicating hemp licence" created by SB 23-271 outside the MED system — the MED licence is the marijuana licence. Penalties (secondary): civil penalties up to $10,000 per day, per product, per violation — Verify against §25-5-427 penalty provisions. CBD and hemp beverages. CBD (non-intoxicating) beverages/products: allowed as hemp products if they meet the hemp definition, are manufactured by a CDPHE-registered manufacturer, and comply with food/cosmetic rules. CBD alone does not cause a high, but a product marketed as "CBD" may still contain THC — check the label. Hemp THC beverages (outside dispensaries): must meet 1.75 mg per serving / 15:1; a can is treated as a serving in CDOT's summary. Marijuana THC beverages (in dispensaries): regulated as marijuana products (10 mg per serving / 100 mg per package retail, measuring-device rules). Failed liberalisation: SB 26-164 would have allowed 10 mg per 12-oz serving in bars/liquor stores and 3 mg in grocery/convenience stores — it failed (§1.9); current law remains 1.75 mg. Colorado's response to the new federal hemp definition and the 12 Nov / 11 Dec 2026 dates — analysis, not a Colorado statute. (1) Colorado's 1.75 mg per-serving rule is already stricter than the old federal 0.3% test in dose terms, but looser than the new federal 0.4 mg per-container cap — a typical 1.75 mg can exceeds 0.4 mg/container by more than 4×, so after 11 Dec 2026 it would be federally non-hemp even if Colorado-compliant, unless Congress acts again or the product moves into the MED marijuana system. Between 12 Nov and 11 Dec 2026 the federal law is limited (PL 119-103 §2019) to excluding non-naturally-produced/synthesised cannabinoids — the full cap does not yet apply in that window. (2) Colorado's total-THC testing already points in the same direction as the federal total-THC definition, so producers are less exposed to a measurement-method surprise than delta-9-only states — but fully exposed to the per-container cap surprise. (3) Chemically converted cannabinoids: Colorado already prohibits delta-8 and similar converted cannabinoids outside the marijuana system, so the federal exclusion reinforces the existing prohibition and removes any federal-hemp defence for delta-8 in Colorado. (4) Non-intoxicating hemp (fibre, grain, THC-free CBD, etc.): a truly THC-free product is unaffected in principle, but any product with trace THC above 0.4 mg per container would fail — how "container" is interpreted for bulk vs retail products after December is Verify. Colorado state response: Unavailable in this run — no statute, executive order, CDPHE, CDA or MED guidance responding specifically to PL 119-37 §781 / PL 119-103 §2019 was located. CDOT's page is the closest official statement and uses pre-delay "November 2026" framing. Whether the Governor, CDPHE, CDA or MED has issued a post-September 2026 response is the single most important follow-up for §1.5 and Part 7, to be checked after 11 Dec 2026. As of 1 Nov 2026, a hemp-beverage business selling 1.75 mg cans outside dispensaries is Colorado-compliant but federally time-limited — Colorado law alone should not be advised as protecting it after that date. 1.6 Packaging, labelling, advertising, delivery, hospitality, zoning and buffers. Packaging and labelling — MED rules (1 CCR 212-3, Part 3, Rules 3-1000 series; current text Verify). Every regulated marijuana product must be child-resistant at the moment it is handed to the customer, certified to the federal CPSA/ASTM standard; flower/trim/seeds in a non-child-resistant container must be placed in a child-resistant, opaque exit package at transfer; multi-serving edibles require resealable closures (Rule 3-1010(B)(11) — summarised, Verify vs Rule 3-1010 itself). Universal Symbol: Colorado Universal THC Symbol — red diamond, exclamation point, letters "THC" — on the front of the container and any marketing layer, minimum ½″ × ½″, with "Contains Marijuana, keep away from children" (exact warning wording Verify) directly beneath; for retail edibles that can practicably be stamped, the symbol on each standardised serving, minimum ¼″ × ¼″. No pre-approval of artwork required; official artwork free from MED's Compliance Tools page. Required label fields (container + marketing layer): product identity; net weight/contents; Statement of Intended Use (closed list); both government warnings; Universal Symbol; licence numbers of cultivation and manufacturing facilities; production batch number; potency test results (prior to transfer to a business other than a store); ingredient list and expiration date (edibles); any other required information/warnings. Required text no smaller than 1/16″. Prohibited label content (Rule 3-1010(B)(2)–(5), via vLex reproduction, current through Register Vol. 46, No. 3, 10 Feb 2023 — Verify vs current Rule 3-1010): "Labels Shall Not Be Designed to Appeal to Children… including but not limited to, cartoon characters or similar images." / "False or Misleading Statements…" / "Health and Benefit Claims…" — vLex, Verify. Edible serving marking: §1.3 (10 mg / 100 mg retail; stamped symbol per serving where practicable). Hospitality packaging exception: a Retail Marijuana Hospitality and Sales Business transferring marijuana in compliance with Rule 3-1020 is exempt from Rule 3-1010's general requirements at transfer, but must package/label any unconsumed marijuana before the consumer leaves the premises (Rules 3-1010(A), 6-925(I) — Verify). Hemp labelling is governed by CDPHE rules under §25-5-427 / 6 CCR 1010-24, not MED Rule 3-1010 — Verify CDPHE fields. Advertising — Rules 3-700 series; §§44-10-701 / 44-10-203 (Verify current text). Audience rule: advertising on TV, radio, print or online only where at least 71.6% of the audience is reasonably expected to be 21+ (no more than 28.4% underage) — Rule 3-720 (Verify). Content prohibitions: no misleading/deceptive/false advertising; no advertising designed to appeal to minors (including cartoon imagery); no health/physical-benefit claims (State Licensing Authority specifically directed to prohibit such claims). No unsolicited online advertising (e.g. pop-ups) under Rule 3-750; no advertising toward location-based devices unless via a mobile app installed by a 21+ device owner with an easy, permanent opt-out (rule numbers Verify). Medical concentrate advertising: HB 21-1317 prohibits medical advertising specifically directed at 18–20 and requires medical and retail concentrate advertising to include a warning on overconsumption risks. Penalties (secondary): advertising violations classified Level I, fines up to $100,000 per individual violation and potential suspension/revocation — Verify vs Rule 8-series discipline rules. Hemp advertising: SB 23-271 prohibits marketing/promoting a hemp product as containing THC or any other potentially intoxicating cannabinoid; otherwise general consumer-protection law, not MED rules — Verify CDPHE hemp advertising rules. Delivery — HB 19-1234. Delivery is a permit held by a licensed medical or retail store (and, for transport, by a licensed transporter with a delivery permit), not an independent deliverer licence — the independent-delivery licences in failed HB 24-1061 were not enacted. Where: to a private residence only (not a public place, hotel room as a general rule, or workplace — hotel-delivery bill failed). Locality must have opted in to delivery. Who / how much: no retail delivery under 21; per business day no more than 1 oz retail or 2 oz medical (in combination) to one consumer/patient; concentrate limits apply (MED reminder sheet, 11 Apr 2023). Hours: no sales before 8:00 a.m. or after 12:00 a.m. (midnight), subject to stricter local hours. Vehicle/inventory tracked in Metrc (§1.7). Surcharge: a $1 delivery surcharge is referenced in HB 24-1061 summaries as a surcharge that failed bill would have eliminated — whether a $1 surcharge is currently collected, and by whom, was not verified — Verify before advising on delivery pricing; do not state a $1 surcharge as current law without that check. Hospitality (consumption) — Rules 6-900 series; HB 19-1230. (1) Marijuana Hospitality Business (Rule 6-915 series): consumption on the licensed premises; may be mobile (e.g. tour bus); may not sell marijuana; may not be located on a premises that serves/sells alcohol, including a liquor-licensed retail food establishment (a non-liquor retail food establishment may co-locate, subject to Rule 6-915). (2) Retail Marijuana Hospitality and Sales Business (Rule 6-925): sale and consumption on the premises; cannot be mobile; may only transfer retail marijuana obtained from another retail business; daily sales limits per customer per day: 1 oz flower, 8 g concentrate, 100 mg active THC in oral-consumption products (servings ≤10 mg), with measuring devices for multi-serving liquids; non-edible, non-psychoactive products exempt. Mobile hospitality specifics: consumption area must exclude the driver's and front-seat passenger's seating area (Rule 6-940(B)); ventilation so smoke/vape air is not circulated into the driver's area (Rule 6-940(E)) — all Verify vs current rules. Local opt-in required — a locality that has not authorised hospitality may not have a hospitality business even with a state licence. No consumption on other licensees' premises (§1.3). Zoning and buffer distances. State buffer — §44-10-311: 1,000 feet from a school, alcohol/drug treatment facility, principal campus of a college/university/seminary, or residential childcare facility, except renewals of pre-existing licences are not affected, and local jurisdictions may alter distance minimums (increase or decrease by local ordinance). Exact text and measurement method Verify before siting advice. Beyond the state buffer, each locality sets its own zoning districts, caps, hours and additional buffers (Part 3). A state licence does not override local zoning — applicant must show compliance with local zoning and proof of possession of the premises. Whether hospitality businesses are subject to the same 1,000′ buffer, a different buffer, or a local variant was raised in Denver stakeholder sessions but not resolved in sources opened here — Verify vs Rules 6-915/6-925 and the specific locality's ordinance. 1.7 Seed-to-sale tracking — Metrc. Metrc — Marijuana Enforcement Tracking Reporting Compliance — the state-mandated, cloud-based seed-to-sale inventory tracking system. Colorado was Metrc's first state (adopted 2011; in use for the regulated market from 2014). Mandatory, no alternative: all licensed medical and retail marijuana businesses must use Metrc; Colorado does not allow an alternative tracking system. MED oversees Metrc compliance. What is tracked: every plant and every package/product, from planting through harvest, processing, testing, packaging, transfer and retail sale, using RFID tags (plant tags and package tags) with a unique identifier per plant/package, plus barcode data. Plant tags are single-use; recreational plant tags are blue, medical yellow (secondary detail — Verify current tag colours/pricing). Tag prices in secondary sources: $0.45 per plant tag, $0.25 per package tag (Verify current Metrc price list). Separate accounts: medical and retail operations maintain separate Metrc accounts — a direct operational expression of the medical/retail split. Training: Metrc requires users to complete mandatory training before gaining full account access; tags are ordered directly through Metrc once the account is active. Sale-time checks: medical — store must check Metrc before sale to verify the patient has not exceeded daily authorised quantity limits or THC potency authorisations (HB 21-1317, Rule 5-125). Retail — store must not transfer more than the 1 oz equivalent in a single transaction, including multiple transfers in the same business day where the employee knows or reasonably should know the customer would exceed 1 oz (Rule 6-110). Reporting / reconciliation: licensees must record every inventory action (cultivation, transfer, sale, disposal/waste) and reconcile physical inventory against Metrc; discrepancies must be addressed immediately. A secondary guide states monthly reports are due by the 15th of the month — Verify current deadline vs MED Rule 3-series / Metrc administrator guidance. Hemp tracking: Metrc is a marijuana tracking system. Hemp cultivation is tracked through CDA registration and pre-harvest testing, not Metrc, except where a hemp-derived product enters the MED marijuana system as an intoxicating product — in which case Metrc applies from that point (Verify exact handover point in MED/CDPHE guidance; Part 7 follow-up). Official MED Metrc page cited in secondary sources as sbg.colorado.gov/med/metrc — page itself not opened in this run (Verify live URL). 1.8 Employment and drug testing protections. Constitutional preservation of employer rights. Amendment 64, §16(6) (paraphrase verified, exact subsection Verify): nothing in §16 shall be construed to require an employer to permit or accommodate use, consumption, possession, transfer, display, transportation, sale or growing of marijuana in the workplace, or to affect an employer's ability to have policies restricting marijuana use by employees. Parallel provision: §44-10-104(5)(a) (in part, FindLaw, text truncated in search result — Verify full subsection). Medical programme, same principle: §14(5)/(8) preserves employer and other private rights (detail Verify). A medical card does not, by itself, require an employer to accommodate use. No general private-employer drug-testing statute. Colorado has no statute restricting or regulating how private employers conduct drug testing — no state law dictating when a company may test, what kind of test it must use, or what notice it must provide. Pre-employment, random, reasonable-suspicion and post-accident testing are all permissible as a matter of state law, subject to other generally applicable law (e.g. disability, federal safety rules). This is a negative claim based on secondary sources — any new 2025–2026 testing statute would overturn it (none located in this run; Verify vs current CRS). City of Boulder exception (secondary — Verify vs Boulder municipal code; do not advise a Boulder employer on this summary alone). Practical consequence: an employer may terminate or rescind an offer for a positive THC result alone, even if the worker was sober on every shift, because THC metabolites linger for days/weeks after impairment ends. Coats v. Dish Network, LLC, 2015 CO 44 — the controlling case. Citation: 2015 CO 44 (Colo. 15 June 2015) [Verify "unanimous (one justice not participating)" vs opinion — holding confirmed, composition flag retained]. Facts: Brandon Coats, a quadriplegic telephone customer-service representative employed by Dish Network 2007–2010, held a Colorado medical marijuana licence for painful muscle spasms, used medical marijuana off-duty in accordance with state law, never used at work, and was terminated after a random drug test in May 2010 returned positive for a marijuana component. He informed Dish he was a registered patient and would continue use; Dish terminated him under its drug policy. Statute at issue: CRS §24-34-402.5 — Lawful off-duty activities statute — generally makes it a discriminatory employment practice to terminate an employee for engaging in any lawful activity off the employer's premises during nonworking hours, unless the restriction relates to a bona fide occupational requirement or a conflict of interest. Holding (verbatim substance): for an activity to be "lawful" under §24-34-402.5, it must be lawful under both state and federal law. Because marijuana was a Schedule I controlled substance under the federal Controlled Substances Act, its use — even off-duty, at home, with a medical card — was not "lawful activity" protected by the statute. The Court rejected arguments based on (a) DOJ non-prosecution policy for state-compliant patients and (b) the December 2014 federal appropriations rider barring DOJ from spending funds to prevent states from implementing medical marijuana laws. Result: Coats' wrongful-termination claim was dismissed; Dish's termination was lawful under Colorado law as it stood in 2015. Later law — and the open Schedule III question (most important Verify in this section). No later Colorado statute overturning Coats was located in this run. No Colorado employment-protection statute for marijuana users (medical or retail) was found in sources opened here — Verify by searching CRS Title 24, Article 34 and 2024–2026 session laws before advising an employee they are protected. Does Schedule III change Coats for medical users? — UNRESOLVED, marked Verify, reasoning stated carefully: Argument Coats' logic now fails for state-licensed medical use: after 28 Apr 2026, state-licensed medical marijuana is no longer Schedule I federally; it is Schedule III. The Coats premise — "marijuana is unlawful under federal law, therefore not 'lawful' under §24-34-402.5" — no longer holds in the same form for medical use that is both state-licensed and federally Schedule III. A court could therefore hold off-duty, state-licensed medical use is now "lawful" for §24-34-402.5 purposes. Counter-arguments Coats may survive even for medical use: (1) Schedule III drugs still require a federal prescription / FDA approval framework that state medical marijuana does not satisfy — state "recommendations" are not federal prescriptions, and only FDA-approved marijuana drug products are federally lawful as medicines in the ordinary sense; (2) the CSA still prohibits manufacture/distribution/possession except as authorised, and state-licensed medical marijuana may still be federally unlawful in that technical sense even if scheduled differently; (3) the appropriations-rider argument already failed in Coats, showing the Court's narrow reading of "lawful"; (4) §16(6) / §44-10-104(5) employer-preservation language is independent of Coats and may still protect employer policies even if §24-34-402.5 were read differently. For retail users: no argument arises — retail remains Schedule I, so Coats' original reasoning applies unchanged. Bottom line: no Colorado court decision applying Coats after 28 Apr 2026 was located. Whether Coats still bars a §24-34-402.5 claim for state-licensed medical use after rescheduling is Verify and must not be stated as decided in either direction. Related case noted, not relied on: Beinor v. Industrial Claim Appeals Office, No. 10CA1685 (Colo. App. 18 Aug 2011) — pre-Coats, employer-friendly decision on medical marijuana and unemployment/workers' compensation context (Verify current precedential value after Coats). Safety-sensitive / federal-contractor roles: federal drug-testing requirements (e.g. DOT, federal contractors) are independent of Colorado law and unaffected by Coats or Schedule III for retail purposes — Verify the specific federal programme before advising. 1.9 Pending legislation — confirmed status on leg.colorado.gov. Method: status confirmed on leg.colorado.gov where the bill page was opened (SB 26-161, SB 25-268, HB 25-1209, HB 26-1077, HB 26-1409, SB 26-007, SB 26-031, HB 24-1061, HB 25-1331, SB 26-164 committee report). For other bills, status is taken from leg.colorado.gov summaries reproduced in secondary trackers and is marked accordingly. No bill listed as "pending" below is current law, and no bill listed as "dead" may be cited as law. The 2026 Regular Session has adjourned (sine die May 2026 in secondary reports); any bill not signed by the Governor by the end of the session is dead for that session unless carried to a special session — Verify session status for any bill you intend to rely on. HB 25-1209 Marijuana Regulation Streamline — ENACTED, signed 3 June 2025. Most provisions eff. 5 Jan 2026. Digital occupational licences; fingerprint checks limited to initial owner licensing, name-based checks for employees thereafter; R&D sampling relaxed; repeal of outdated prohibitions; $300,000 general-fund transfers to Marijuana Entrepreneur Fund on 1 July 2025 and 1 July 2026 (Verify vs enrolled text); MED rule changes eff. 5 Jan 2026 (https://leg.colorado.gov/bills/hb25-1209). SB 25-268 Changes to Money in the Marijuana Tax Cash Fund — ENACTED, signed 3 June 2025. Local share 10% → 3.5% from 1 July 2025; JBC review between 1 Nov 2027 and 1 Apr 2028 (https://leg.colorado.gov/bills/sb25-268). SB 25-246 Gray and Black Market Marijuana Enforcement Grant Program repeal — ENACTED (per secondary summary), programme repealed 30 June 2026 — Verify on leg.colorado.gov (not opened). HB 26-1077 Average Market Rate of Unprocessed Retail Marijuana — ENACTED, signed 3 June 2026. Eff. 1 July 2026. The 2026 Regular Session's marijuana bills that mattered were either enacted or postponed indefinitely above. Any bill introduced in a special session after the regular session, or pre-filed for the 2027 session, would not appear in sources opened here — Verify by a fresh leg.colorado.gov search for "Marijuana" / "Cannabis" / "Hemp" / "Intoxicating" before advising that "nothing is pending". In particular, a Colorado legislative response to the federal hemp dates (PL 119-37 / PL 119-103) for the 2027 session is plausible but not located — it must be checked in the 2027 pre-file list, not assumed.
