PART 2 — TAXES

2.1 The state tax stack at a glance — current law, with the 2017 change most secondary summaries get wrong. Retail (adult-use) — current: 15% state retail marijuana sales tax on the final consumer purchase price of retail marijuana and retail marijuana-infused products; 15% state retail marijuana excise tax on the first transfer/sale from a retail cultivation facility, calculated on the AMR or contract price (§2.3); exempt from the 2.9% general state sales tax since 1 July 2017. Other tangible items sold by a store (apparel, glassware, rolling papers, etc.) are subject to 2.9%. Local general sales taxes and local special marijuana sales/excise taxes may still apply (Part 3); whether a particular local general sales tax applies to retail depends on that jurisdiction — DOR directs readers to DR 1002, Colorado Sales/Use Tax Rates. Medical — current: 2.9% state sales tax on medical marijuana and medical marijuana-infused products, plus applicable local sales taxes; exempt from the 15% retail sales tax and the 15% retail excise tax. Sources: Legislative Council Staff, "Marijuana Taxes" (https://content.leg.colorado.gov/agencies/legislative-council-staff/marijuana-taxes%C2%A0) — "Medical marijuana is subject to the 2.9 percent state sales tax… while retail marijuana is exempt. Retail marijuana is subject to a 15 percent sales tax, levied on retail sales, and a 15 percent excise tax, levied on the first transfer of marijuana from a wholesaler to a processor or retailer." SB 17-267 history via HB17B-1001 summary: SB 17-267 exempted retail sales from 2.9% and, as previously authorised by voter approval, increased the state retail sales tax from 10% to 15%, effective 1 July 2017. Proposition AA (2013) authority: voters approved 5 Nov 2013 up to 15% excise on unprocessed retail marijuana and up to 15% retail sales tax (initially levied at 10% sales); the 15% rates are voter-approved revenue and exempt from TABOR spending limits; the 2.9% tax is subject to TABOR limits. Pre-1 July 2017 position — historical only: from January 2014 retail paid both 2.9% and a 10% special retail sales tax. Older DOR-derived pages describing a consumer paying "2.9% plus an additional 15%" are outdated on that point. Worked illustration — state taxes only, retail: on a $100 retail purchase price, state retail sales tax is $15.00. The 15% excise is not shown at the register; it is charged upstream on the cultivator transfer (AMR or contract price) and built into the shelf price. Verify any register total against DR 1002 and the local jurisdiction, because local taxes are additional. 2.2 Statutory home. Retail marijuana taxes: Title 39, Article 28.8, C.R.S. — Part 2 (retail sales tax) and Part 3 (retail excise tax), including §39-28.8-101 (definitions, §39-28.8-101(1.5) on AMR), §39-28.8-302 (excise levied at first transfer), §39-28.8-305 (excise distribution — §2.5), §39-28.8-501 (Marijuana Tax Cash Fund). Local retail marijuana taxes: DOR cites §39-28.8-203(1)(a)(VI) for the rule that a local retail sales tax is not collected or administered by DOR, even if DOR collects other local general sales taxes for that jurisdiction (https://tax.colorado.gov/marijuana-tax-information-for-local-governments). General state sales tax: 2.9% on tangible personal property, retail marijuana/products expressly exempted. Marijuana Code licensing: Title 44, Article 10 (Part 4). AMR rules: 1 CCR 201-18 and 1 CCR 212-3 (definitions), cited on the DOR AMR page (https://tax.colorado.gov/average-market-rate). Last-amended dates for §§39-28.8-101, -302, -305, -501 and for 1 CCR 201-18 / 212-3: Verify — current official text was not opened line-by-line in this run. Do not cite a last-amended date for these provisions from secondary summaries. 2.3 The 15% excise tax and the Average Market Rate — how it is set, current rate, history. Who pays, when, on what: excise remitted by the retail cultivation facility on the first sale or transfer of unprocessed retail marijuana to a retail store or retail products manufacturer (MIP). Rate 15%. Base: unaffiliated transfer — 15% of the contract (sale) price; affiliated transfer (common ownership) — 15% of the AMR (DOR AMR page, https://tax.colorado.gov/average-market-rate). How the AMR is calculated (DOR): AMRs are median market prices per pound or count for each category of unprocessed retail marijuana sold/transferred from retail cultivators to retail stores or MIPs (median = middle value when ordered least to greatest). DOR calculates AMRs quarterly, as required by §39-28.8-101(1.5). Calculation uses Metrc data. AMRs are calculated the month before they are in effect, using data from the prior three months (e.g. Q1 AMRs calculated in December using September–November data). Dataset includes only transfers that: (1) originated at a retail cultivator; (2) went to a retail store or retail MIP; (3) were of unprocessed marijuana; (4) were between unaffiliated businesses; and (5) had a receiver price greater than one cent. Price per pound (bud, trim, bud allocated for extraction, trim allocated for extraction, wet whole plant) or price each (immature plants, seeds) is calculated from Metrc price and weight/count data. Category — Q4 2026 (1 Oct – 31 Dec 2026) AMR (DOR AMR page, https://tax.colorado.gov/average-market-rate) and implied 15% excise (arithmetic, not printed on DOR page): Retail Bud $601 per pound / $90.15 per pound; Retail Trim $204 / $30.60; Bud Allocated for Extraction $425 / $63.75; Trim Allocated for Extraction $100 / $15.00; Wet Whole Plant $100 / $15.00. Immature-plant and seed AMRs (per-count) were not shown in the portion of the Q4 2026 page retrieved — Verify on DOR's "Current & Prior Rates" table. AMR history — gap: Q4 2026 bud ($601/lb) is far below older secondary examples (e.g. $1,876/lb flower, $296/lb trim in an old NORML reproduction — not current, must not be used as current rates). Sequence now established: Q1 2021 bud AMR $1,721/lb; Q1 2026 $648/lb; Q2 2026 $607/lb (secondary-reported); Q3 2026 $574/lb; Q4 2026 $601/lb. A year-by-year AMR table was not retrieved — DOR "Current & Prior Rates" link was not opened in full (Verify for Part 6 / future update). HB 26-1077 — fresh-frozen AMRs (enacted 2026, rulemaking pending). DOR must adopt rules to calculate separate AMRs for fresh-frozen marijuana cultivated indoors and fresh-frozen outdoors; rules by 1 July 2027 (amendment text, leg.colorado.gov); bill took effect 1 July 2026. The Q4 2026 AMR page does not list separate fresh-frozen indoor/outdoor categories — Verify whether DOR has published interim fresh-frozen rates elsewhere or publication awaits the 1 July 2027 deadline. Do not assume fresh-frozen product is currently taxed on a separate AMR. 2.4 The 2.9% state sales tax and medical treatment — detail. Rate 2.9%, charged on the final consumer purchase price for tangible personal property generally. Applies to: medical marijuana and medical products; non-marijuana tangible items sold by any marijuana store. Does not apply to: retail marijuana and retail products (exempt since 1 July 2017, SB 17-267). DOR Marijuana Tax Reports page describes tax revenue as coming from "the state sales tax (2.9%) on marijuana sold in stores, the state retail marijuana sales tax (15%) on retail marijuana sold in stores, and the state retail marijuana excise tax (15%) on wholesale sales/transfers" — in context the 2.9% component is the medical (and non-marijuana-item) component; it is not an additional 2.9% on retail. That shorthand must not be read as re-imposing 2.9% on retail. Local general sales tax on medical vs retail: DOR notes retail is exempt from the state 2.9% "and some local taxes" and directs readers to DR 1002 for the complete list of local governments that allow the exemption — local general-sales-tax treatment of retail is jurisdiction-specific and cannot be stated as a single statewide rule (Verify each jurisdiction in DR 1002, updated 1 January and 1 July each year). Special districts: RTD (1.0%) and SCFD (0.1%) are frequently included in Denver totals (Part 3, Denver). SB 17-267's exemption initially raised a question about whether district sales taxes still applied to retail; HB17B-1001 (2017 first extraordinary session) clarified that affected entities that levy sales tax shall tax retail marijuana sales (bill summary — Verify current district treatment in DR 1002 for the specific address, as district boundaries vary). 2.5 Revenue distribution — the three eras (where older sources conflict). Era 1 — Before 1 July 2025: local share 10%. Of the gross 15% retail sales tax: 10% to local governments, 90% retained by the state. The state's 90% was then allocated (Legislative Council Staff handbook page, now outdated on the local share): 71.85% to the Marijuana Tax Cash Fund, 15.56% to the General Fund, 12.59% to the State Public School Fund. Local apportionment: each city/town's share apportioned according to the percentage of retail sales tax revenues collected by DOR within that city/town's boundaries. Counties received nothing unless there was a retail store in an unincorporated area (DOR, https://tax.colorado.gov/marijuana-tax-information-for-local-governments). Era 2 — 1 July 2025 to 30 June 2026: local share cut to 3.5% (SB 25-268). SB 25-268, "Changes to Money in the Marijuana Tax Cash Fund", became law (Chapter 374, effective 3 June 2025 — chapter/effective detail Verify vs signed act). Enacted summary (https://leg.colorado.gov/bills/sb25-268): "beginning July 1, 2025, the act changes the apportionment… so that local governments receive 3.5% rather than 10% of the tax revenue and the state retains 96.5% rather than 90%… The 6.5% increase… is apportioned to the [Marijuana Tax Cash] fund." SB 25-268 also repealed the requirement for an annual $3 million appropriation from the Marijuana Tax Cash Fund to the University of Colorado Board of Regents for the medication-assisted treatment expansion pilot program (while allowing a discretionary appropriation), and provided for Joint Budget Committee review of the local percentage between 1 November 2027 and 1 April 2028. DOR confirms: "For retail sales from 7/1/25 through 6/30/26 local governments received 3.5% of the 15% retail marijuana state sales tax… Prior to 7/1/25 the local share was established at 10%." Era 3 — From 1 July 2026: local share eliminated (HB 26-1409). HB 26-1409, "Marijuana Tax Cash Fund Distributions", 2026 Regular Session, became law; signed act dated 4 June 2026 (https://leg.colorado.gov/bills/hb26-1409). Enacted summary: "Current law requires 3.5% of the gross retail marijuana sales tax revenue to be distributed to local governments. The act eliminates the distribution to local governments and allocates the gross retail marijuana sales tax revenue as follows, on and after July 1, 2026: 73.17% to the Marijuana Tax Cash Fund; 11.33% to the State Public School Fund; 1.5% to the Marijuana Cash Fund; 14% to the General Fund." DOR confirms in identical terms: "As of July 1st, 2026 – in accordance with HB26-1409 – the state's imposed 15% retail marijuana sales tax is fully retained by the state and appropriated as follows: 73.17% / 11.33% / 1.5% / 14%." HB 26-1409 also directs the State Treasurer to transfer from the Marijuana Tax Cash Fund to the State Public School Fund on 30 June 2027 and each 30 June thereafter an amount equal to the difference between the fund balance and (15% of the amount the General Assembly appropriated from the fund in that fiscal year + any amount designated as emergency reserve for that fiscal year) [CORRECTED: formula now stated from the enacted summary; "truncated — Verify" flag removed]. Practical consequence: from 1 July 2026 a city or county no longer receives a share of the state 15% retail sales tax merely because retail sales occurred within its boundaries. Its marijuana revenue is only what it levies itself (own general sales tax, if applicable, plus own special marijuana taxes — Part 3), plus other state distributions (e.g. BEST grants, competitive, not a sales share). Longmont's 2026 budget discussion explicitly treats the end of the shareback as a revenue loss to be replaced by annexation — corroborating a live local-budget effect, not a paper change (secondary — Verify vs Longmont budget). Warning on conflicting secondary figures: a Q3 2026 secondary market report and a news analysis give FY 2024-25 shares of total marijuana revenue (e.g. Marijuana Tax Cash Fund 54.4%, K-12 funds 26.7%, General Fund 11%, local governments 7.8%) that do not match the statutory 73.17/11.33/1.5/14 split, because they are shares of all marijuana tax-and-fee revenue in a fiscal year, not the statutory split of the 15% sales tax alone. Do not mix the two bases. Excise-tax distribution — BEST / public school construction. DOR current statement (https://tax.colorado.gov/marijuana-tax-information-for-local-governments): "The 15% retail marijuana excise tax goes to Colorado public school construction… The first $40 million in retail marijuana excise tax revenue collected annually goes to public school construction. Any revenue above that is transferred to the Public School Fund." Constitutional origin: Amendment 64 required the General Assembly to enact an excise tax with the first $40 million per year dedicated to public school construction. Statutory route: §39-28.8-305 (excise distribution) and the public school capital construction assistance fund under the Building Excellent Schools Today (BEST) Act, §22-43.7-104. BEST grants are competitive, prioritised on asbestos removal, building-code violations, overcrowding and poor indoor air quality. [CORRECTED: DOR's "first $40m / remainder" formulation is the constitutional floor, NOT the complete current statutory rule. HB 18-1070 (2018) enacted, from 1 July 2018, crediting to the assistance fund the greater of the first $40 million or 90% of excise revenue (§§22-43.7-104(2)(d), 39-28.8-305); a later amendment recital indicates all excise revenue credited to the assistance fund for fiscal years from 1 July 2019 onward except FY 2020-21 (lesser of $40m or all). Do NOT quote DOR's simplified formulation as the complete current rule. Exact current §22-43.7-104 formula remains Verify.] Legislative Council Staff also notes a general constitutional routing point easily misread as marijuana-specific: under Colo. Const. Art. XXIV, §2, 85% of excise-tax revenue (excluding transportation-related excise taxes) is constitutionally required to be credited to the Old Age Pension Fund, with the excess over pension needs allocated to the General Fund. That is the general excise-tax accounting route; the marijuana-specific BEST/Public School Fund allocation in §39-28.8-305 is the operative distribution for marijuana excise revenue — Verify how the two provisions interact in current state accounting presentation before summarising them together. Marijuana Tax Cash Fund — what it funds. Per §39-28.8-501: revenue in the Marijuana Tax Cash Fund is required to be used for health care, health education, substance abuse prevention and treatment programs, and law enforcement. Secondary reporting of FY 2025-26 states about $124.7 million from the Marijuana Tax Cash Fund was distributed across 15 state agencies in FY 2025-26 — secondary, fiscal-year, appropriations-based, not a DOR tax-collection figure; Verify against Joint Budget Committee / Long Bill appropriations for FY 2025-26 before reuse. Note the distinct Marijuana Cash Fund (1.5% from 1 July 2026, HB 26-1409) vs the Marijuana Tax Cash Fund (73.17%). They are different funds; do not conflate them. The Marijuana Cash Fund is the MED operating fund (licence-fee funded historically); the 1.5% allocation is new in HB 26-1409 — Verify the Marijuana Cash Fund's statutory purpose in current §39-28.8-501 / Title 44. 2.6 Local sales and special marijuana taxes — general rules (detail by jurisdiction in Part 3, §3.4). Local jurisdictions may impose and collect their own sales and/or excise tax on retail marijuana. It is the local jurisdiction's responsibility to collect, administer and enforce that local tax. A local retail marijuana sales tax will not be collected or administered by DOR, even if DOR collects other local general sales taxes for that jurisdiction. §39-28.8-203(1)(a)(VI) (DOR, https://tax.colorado.gov/marijuana-tax-information-for-local-governments). Consequence: there is no single DOR table of local special marijuana tax rates. Authoritative compilations are (a) each jurisdiction's own code/ordinance and tax page, (b) DOR DR 1002 for state-collected general sales taxes, and (c) the Colorado Municipal League (CML) municipal retail marijuana status table (November 2024-dated snapshot of special taxes — see §3.3). Local taxes are in addition to the state 15% sales tax and embedded 15% excise tax. A consumer's total at the register is therefore: shelf price (already embeds excise) + 15% state retail sales tax + local general sales tax (if applicable to retail at that address) + local special marijuana sales tax (if any) + applicable special-district sales taxes (RTD, SCFD, etc., where applicable). Medical purchases substitute 2.9% state sales tax for 15% state retail sales tax and pay no state excise tax, but still pay applicable local general sales taxes. No local tax rate in Part 3 should be added to state rates to produce a "total tax" for a jurisdiction unless every layer for that exact address has been verified in DR 1002 and the local code. District taxes vary by address even within a city. 2.7 Hemp product tax — no special hemp excise found; intoxicating-hemp tax treatment is Verify. No Colorado special excise tax on hemp or hemp products was found in an official source in this run. Hemp products sold at retail are, in principle, tangible personal property subject to the 2.9% state sales tax plus applicable local sales taxes, but the only source retrieved for that proposition is a secondary state-by-state hemp-tax table stating "Colorado — State Sales & Use Tax — 2.9%" — Verify against DOR guidance and DR 1002; do not present the 2.9%-on-hemp point as DOR-confirmed. Intoxicating hemp — SB 23-271: enacted bill summary states: "Nonintoxicating cannabinoids, potentially intoxicating compounds, and intoxicating cannabinoids are marijuana or marijuana products for the purposes of the retail marijuana sales tax." That suggests intoxicating/potentially intoxicating cannabinoid products brought inside the MED-licensed system are treated as marijuana for retail-sales-tax purposes. Verify current DOR application — in particular, whether a CDPHE-registered nonintoxicating hemp product is taxed only at 2.9% (if at all) while a MED-licensed intoxicating product is taxed at the 15% retail rate, and how the distinction is administered at the register. Federal hemp dates — Colorado response: Unavailable as of 1 Nov 2026 in this run. No DOR, MED, CDPHE or CDA response to the federal hemp dates was retrieved. A secondary 2026 state brief notes Colorado was "weighing loosening hemp beverage limits ahead of the federal hemp ban" and that SB 26-164 and SB 26-161 stalled — secondary, Verify against leg.colorado.gov before any statement about pending Colorado hemp legislation (both bills' deaths are now confirmed above). Do not predict a Colorado tax change from the federal dates. Hemp cultivation/processing registrations (CDA) and hemp product registrations (CDPHE) are Part 7 territory; their fees are not taxes and are not counted here. 2.8 IRS §280E and Colorado decoupling — state tax treatment. Federal position (fixed baseline, applied to Colorado). Before Schedule III: both medical and retail businesses were subject to IRC §280E — ordinary and necessary business expenses disallowed federally, deduction limited essentially to cost of goods sold. From 28 April 2026: medical activity that is state-licensed (and FDA-approved products) is Schedule III, so §280E is generally lifted for that medical activity. Retail activity remains Schedule I and fully subject to §280E federally. For a business holding both medical and retail licences, the federal change applies to the medical activity only. How expenses, inventory and income must be split between the medical and retail sides for federal purposes, and whether DOR or the IRS has issued Colorado-specific allocation guidance, was not retrieved — Verify. Do not assume a pro-rata or premises-based split is prescribed. Colorado decoupling — already in place for both tracks, before Schedule III. [CORRECTED attribution:] HB 13-1042 (session law, https://leg.colorado.gov/sites/default/files/images/olls/2013a_sl_327.pdf) enacted, for income tax years commencing on or after 1 January 2014, a state subtraction for taxpayers licensed under the Colorado Medical Marijuana Code, at §39-22-104(4)(r) (individual) and §39-22-304(3)(m) (corporate), equal to any expenditure eligible as a federal deduction but disallowed by §280E. The extension to retail businesses is attributed secondarily to SB 13-283 — Verify vs its session law; current subsection letters likewise Verify (letters may have shifted with later amendments including natural medicine). "Colorado was the first state to decouple" remains secondary — Verify before repeating as fact. Official corroboration that the deduction still operates: DOR Form DR 0112 (2025), Colorado C Corporation Income Tax Return, Line 11, "Colorado Marijuana and Natural Medicine Business Deduction": "For Colorado-licensed marijuana or natural medicine businesses, enter any expenditure that is eligible to be claimed as a federal income tax deduction but is disallowed by section 280E… To calculate this deduction, you must create pro forma federal schedule(s)… as if the federal government would have allowed the expenditures… You must submit the pro forma schedule(s), the actual federal schedule(s), and your license number from the [MED] or Natural Medicine Division (NMD) with your Colorado return." Consequence: at the state level, a Colorado retail business already deducts ordinary expenses that are federally disallowed, and a medical business did so before Schedule III as well. Schedule III therefore changes the federal return for medical activity; it does not create Colorado's state deduction, which predates it. Whether DOR will revise DR 0112 instructions for tax year 2026 to reflect that medical expenses are now federally deductible (and therefore no longer need a state "add-back" via the pro forma method) was not retrieved — Verify with DOR Taxation guidance for TY 2026. Do not advise that medical businesses should or should not still claim the state deduction for 2026 without that guidance. Colorado individual and corporate income tax rates themselves are out of scope for Part 2 except as they interact with the deduction above. 2.9 Revenue figures — official DOR data (calendar-year basis). Source for all figures in this section: DOR, "Marijuana Tax Reports" and DOR, "Marijuana Sales Reports" (https://cdor.colorado.gov/data-and-reports/marijuana-data/marijuana-sales-reports). Both pages state a two-month publication lag from June 2025 data onward (published monthly on the third Thursday); the tax page therefore shows through August 2026 and the sales page through July 2026 at the time of access. State marijuana tax-and-fee revenue includes 2.9% sales tax, 15% retail sales tax, 15% excise tax, plus licence/application fees. Monthly 2026 context (DOR press releases, via search 1 Nov 2026): August 2026 tax-and-fee revenue $19,322,443 (released 15 Oct 2026, with July 2026 sales); July 2026 $18,980,768; June 2026 $18,946,733; May 2026 $18,526,192; March 2026 $18,058,713; February 2026 $18,856,954. These are secondary reporting of DOR releases — the DOR monthly report files themselves (linked from the tax reports page) are the primary source for any monthly table; no direct monthly-file URL was confirmed in this audit. Fiscal-year figures — different basis, do not mix with calendar-year figures above: Legislative Council Staff / Joint Budget Committee basis (via secondary reporting): marijuana tax revenue peaked at $424.4 million in FY 2020-21 and fell to $231.1 million in FY 2024-25, a 45.5% decline. A separate secondary analysis cites FY 2021-22 $369.8 million as the JBC working baseline. These fiscal-year totals are close to but not identical to calendar-year DOR totals (calendar 2021: $423,486,053) because the fiscal year runs 1 July – 30 June and the LCS/JBC measure may differ in fee inclusion. Always label the basis (calendar vs fiscal) when quoting a "peak" or "decline". Excise-tax-only figure: HB 26-1077 fiscal note states FY 2024-25 excise-tax collections of $40.1 million — consistent with the BEST $40-million threshold being approximately met in that year, but a fiscal-note figure, not the DOR monthly excise breakdown (Verify vs DOR Marijuana Tax Revenue Report excise column). It does not show local special marijuana taxes (which locals collect themselves). 3.1 Dual licensing — how Colorado actually works

Every commercial marijuana business needs: (1) a state licence from MED, Colorado Department of Revenue, under Title 44, Article 10; and (2) a local licence from the Local Licensing Authority — city council / board of county commissioners (or its designee) — for the city or, if in unincorporated territory, the county where the premises sit. Operating with only a state licence, or only a local licence, is not lawful operation. The statute states the rule by licence class: a medical marijuana business "may not operate until it has been licensed by the local licensing authority and the state licensing authority" and a retail marijuana business "may not operate until it is licensed by the state licensing authority pursuant to this article 10 and approved by the local jurisdiction" (CRS §44-10-313(2) — https://colorado.public.law/statutes/crs_44-10-313). Denver states the rule in its own code terms (DRMC §6-205, as cited in the Denver FAQ — https://denvergov.org/Government/Agencies-Departments-Offices/Agencies-Departments-Offices-Directory/Business-Licensing/Business-licenses/Marijuana-licenses/FAQ), and MED states it as a state application rule (below). "You must confirm that the Local Authority where you plan to operate allows Medical and/or Retail Marijuana businesses to operate within their jurisdiction. The MED will not accept new marijuana business license applications for businesses located within a local authority's jurisdiction unless they have advised us that they are currently accepting new Medical and/or Retail Marijuana business license applications — local authorities that have advised the MED that they allow marijuana businesses to operate within their jurisdiction. Be aware that before your marijuana business may begin operation, you must also obtain a license from the Local Licensing Authority within whose jurisdiction you intend to operate." — MED, "Regulated Marijuana Business License Application" (opened 1 Nov 2026) — https://sbg.colorado.gov/med/new-regulated-marijuana-business-license-application. MED also requires local-jurisdiction fees to be included with the state application submission as a separate form of payment (check or money order only) — Step 4 on the same page (https://sbg.colorado.gov/med/new-regulated-marijuana-business-license-application). That is a procedural consequence of dual licensing, not a fee amount.

Opt-in vs opt-out — why both words appear, and which to use. Constitutional power: Amendment 64 (Art. XVIII, §16) authorises local governments to prohibit retail establishments (and to regulate them) within their jurisdiction; Amendment 20 / medical code similarly allows local prohibition of medical centres; CRS §44-10-313(1) authorises a county, municipality or city and county to prohibit a medical marijuana business and to enact more restrictive local regulations, and authorises local jurisdictions to adopt and enforce regulations for retail businesses at least as restrictive as Article 10 and its rules (https://colorado.public.law/statutes/crs_44-10-313). In that sense Colorado is often described as an "opt-out" state: retail is lawful statewide unless a locality prohibits it. MED practice: in practice, MED will not process a new application unless the locality has affirmatively advised MED that it allows businesses and is currently accepting applications for that type. An applicant must therefore treat the locality as an opt-in gate in the application sequence: confirm local allowance first, run the local process in parallel with the state process (MED expressly suggests beginning the local process at the same time), and obtain the local licence before beginning operation. This report uses both terms with that distinction stated, and never describes a locality as "opted in" merely because it has not passed a ban, unless MED/local sources confirm it is accepting applications.

What a locality may do, business type by business type. A city or county may, by ordinance/resolution and (where required) voter approval for a tax: prohibit any or all business types entirely (stores, cultivation, manufacturing/MIP, testing, transporter, delivery, hospitality/hospitality-and-sales); allow some types and prohibit others — e.g. Colorado Springs prohibits hospitality, hospitality-and-sales, transporter and delivery while allowing stores/cultivation/manufacturing/testing (https://coloradosprings.gov/marijuana); Pueblo County (unincorporated) prohibits personal delivery within its territory (Pueblo County Code Ch. 5.12 — https://county.pueblo.org/county-attorney-department/chapter-512-marijuana-licensing); cap the number of licences (by type, ward/district, or spacing that functions as a cap); zone where each type may sit, including district restrictions and buffer/setback distances from schools, childcare facilities, drug/alcohol treatment facilities, parks, places of worship, residential zones, and other marijuana businesses. On setbacks, note the corrected position on CRS §44-10-311: §44-10-311(1)(d)(I) is a MEDICAL-licence rule barring a new medical licence where the building is within 1,000 feet of a school, an alcohol or drug treatment facility, the principal campus of a college, university or seminary, or a residential child care facility, and it expressly allows the local authority, by rule, ordinance or resolution, to vary the distance or eliminate types of schools/campuses/facilities from the restriction (https://colorado.public.law/statutes/crs_44-10-311). It is not a general retail minimum setback. Localities routinely impose their own, larger buffers; 1,000 feet is the recurring local standard, and Colorado Springs' current retail rule is 1,000 feet (City Code §2.2.104(I), Ord. 25-08, eff. 10 Feb 2025 — https://codelibrary.amlegal.com/codes/coloradospringsco/latest/coloradosprings_co/0-0-0-1845), not the 1-mile figure from the September 2024 proposal discussed in secondary reporting. A locality may also impose local licence fees and local sales/excise taxes (subject to voter approval where TABOR / local charter requires it); impose operating conditions beyond state rules (hours, odor, security, neighbourhood meetings, etc. — e.g. Loveland 8 a.m.–10 p.m. hours and neighbourhood-meeting requirement — https://www.lovgov.org/city-government/city-clerk/marijuana); and distinguish incorporated vs unincorporated territory: a county's rules govern only unincorporated territory; an incorporated city/town inside that county has its own licensing authority. Example: Boulder County "does not issue licenses for the incorporated towns and cities (e.g., Boulder, Nederland) located in Boulder County" (Boulder County Marijuana Licensing — https://bouldercounty.gov/records/licenses/marijuana-licensing/). Always check the city if premises are inside city limits, the county only if outside.

Delivery and hospitality are separate local opt-ins. Delivery and hospitality are not automatically included in a locality that allows stores: a locality must separately allow delivery and/or hospitality, and an operator needs the corresponding state delivery permit / hospitality licence plus local authorisation. Denver issues medical and retail delivery permits and hospitality / hospitality-and-sales licences, but reserves store, transporter, cultivation, manufacturing and hospitality licences for social-equity applicants until 1 July 2027 (Denver FAQ and social-equity page — https://denvergov.org/Government/Agencies-Departments-Offices/Agencies-Departments-Offices-Directory/Business-Licensing/Business-licenses/Marijuana-licenses/FAQ). Verify nuance: Denver's social-equity page states only social-equity applicants may deliver, while the FAQ also lists retail/medical store licensees as delivery-permit applicants — Verify which line controls before stating delivery exclusivity unconditionally. Colorado Springs prohibits all three (hospitality, hospitality-and-sales, transporter, delivery) even though it now allows stores (https://coloradosprings.gov/marijuana). HB 26-1117 (2026), which would have created a temporary marijuana hospitality event permit, DIED — it was postponed indefinitely by the Senate Finance Committee on 7 May 2026, and its final fiscal note (8 June 2026) states its impacts do not take effect (https://leg.colorado.gov/bill_files/117143/download). It is not pending law and is not a basis for stating current law. That fiscal note states that as of February 2026 there were 10 hospitality licence holders statewide, located in Arvada, Aurora and Denver (https://leg.colorado.gov/bill_files/117143/download). That fiscal-note location count is a February 2026 snapshot, not a current licence count, and it lists Arvada as a hospitality location despite Arvada's store prohibition — hospitality is a distinct licence type and must not be conflated with store allowance (Verify current hospitality counts/locations in MED's licensed-facilities list, Part 5).

3.2 Constitutional and statutory local-control provisions (summary — full text is Part 1)

  • Colo. Const. Art. XVIII, §14 (Amendment 20, 2000) — medical; local governments may prohibit medical centres by vote/ordinance under the medical code framework.
  • Colo. Const. Art. XVIII, §16 (Amendment 64, 2012) — personal use and regulation; expressly preserves local government authority to prohibit retail establishments and to regulate them, including zoning and licensing, within their jurisdiction. Longmont Code Ch. 6.70's purpose clause cites §16(5)(f) for the local powers to prohibit, regulate time/place/manner, and limit the total number of establishments (https://longmont.primegov.com/api/compilemeetingattachmenthistory/historyattachment/?historyId=38997796-01cc-4443-8577-2f1aa6a66081).
  • Title 44, Article 10 (Colorado Marijuana Code) — state licensing; local licensing authority provisions, including the requirement for local approval/licence and local zoning compliance. CRS §44-10-313(2) (dual state/local licensing, quoted in §3.1) and §44-10-311(1)(d) (medical 1,000-foot rule, variable by locality) were checked in this audit (https://colorado.public.law/statutes/crs_44-10-313; https://colorado.public.law/statutes/crs_44-10-311).
  • Title 29 / Title 30 — general municipal/county powers (zoning, licensing, taxation) under which local marijuana ordinances are adopted. No Title 29/30 provision is quoted here as a marijuana-specific rule.

MED's business-licences hub links a page titled "Local Authorities Accepting Regulated Marijuana Business License Applications". Exact hub URL (as given in the original report; page not opened in full in this audit either): https://sbg.colorado.gov/med/marijuana-business-licenses — Verify. Therefore this report cannot reproduce the current MED list jurisdiction-by-jurisdiction from a directly opened MED table. Do not treat the CML table below as a substitute for the MED list. They measure different things: MED = "has told MED it is accepting applications"; CML = "municipal code/status as compiled by the Municipal League".

(b) Colorado Municipal League (CML) — Municipal Retail Marijuana Status table (November 2024). What it is: CML's compiled table of municipal (city/town) retail marijuana status, with columns for Sales, Cultivation, Manufacturing, Testing, Delivery, On-site Consumption, Tax Information, Notes, and Site/Code. Exact file URL: CML Municipal Retail Marijuana Status (Nov 2024, PDF) — https://www.cml.org/docs/default-source/marijuana-resources/marijuana-(2024).pdf?Status=Temp&sfvrsn=779b27f2_6. Resources-page URL (as given in the original report): https://www.cml.org/home/topics-key-issues/marijuana-resources-page — Verify; the original report described it as a 2021-dated code-link page linking municipal codes for Aspen, Boulder, Fort Collins, Glenwood Springs, Leadville, Pueblo, Trinidad, Wheat Ridge (retail) and Aspen, Boulder, Fort Collins, Glenwood Springs, Lafayette, Leadville, Pueblo, Trinidad, Wheat Ridge (medical), and that description was not re-verified in full in this audit. Limitations — critical: (1) Dated November 2024. It predates Colorado Springs retail sales beginning in 2025; Loveland's 2025 licensing ordinance and 2026 application opening; Pueblo City's September 2026 retail moratorium (secondary report, see below); Longmont's 2026 annexation proposal; and the 1 April 2025 Broomfield excise repeal date it itself notes. Any CML row must be checked against current local code before republication. (2) Municipal only. It does not cover unincorporated county territory except where a county is noted. (3) Search-snippet fragmentation: several CML rows below were retrieved as fragmented search snippets in which tax figure and municipality name are separated by intervening rows. Where attribution is ambiguous, it is flagged Verify rather than asserted. (4) CML is a municipal association, not a regulator. Its table is a secondary compilation, not an official MED or DOR list, even though it cites municipal codes.

(c) DOR county tax report — not a licence list. DOR's Marijuana Tax Revenue by County Report (linked from DOR Marijuana Tax Reports — https://cdor.colorado.gov/data-and-reports/marijuana-data/marijuana-tax-reports) shows state tax revenue by county, not licence counts or business-type allowance. It must not be cited as a list of jurisdictions "allowing" a business type — a county can show revenue only if sales occurred there, and a jurisdiction with no sales in a month may still allow businesses.

3.4 Local licence fees and special marijuana tax rates by jurisdiction — where officially reported

General rule on fees: no statewide local-fee schedule exists. Fees are set by each local licensing authority. MED's application requires local fees to be paid separately (check/money order only) — §3.1 (https://sbg.colorado.gov/med/new-regulated-marijuana-business-license-application). Only the fee figures below were retrieved with a source; all other jurisdictions' local fees are Unavailable in this run and must be taken from the local licensing authority's fee schedule, not estimated. Local special taxes — compiled table (CML November 2024, SECONDARY, unless a newer official source is cited). "Sales" = local special sales tax on retail sales (in addition to general sales tax and state taxes, unless stated otherwise). "Excise" = local excise tax, typically on the cultivator transfer or on retail sales as the ordinance defines it — CML does not always define the excise base; Verify the base in the local ordinance before calculating a total.

  • Denver (City and County of Denver, consolidated city-and-county): CML Nov 2024 (secondary): 5.5% special sales tax on retail, authorised up to 15% — Verify the "up to 15%" authority in DRMC; the 5.5% component is corroborated by Denver's official combined-rates sheet, which gives a Denver retail rate of 10.65% (5.15% general + 5.5% special) — https://denvergov.org/files/assets/public/v/1/finance/documents/treasury/tax-guides/tax-update-2025/tax-rates-effective-1-1-2025_1.pdf. See Denver row in §3.5 for the resolved general-rate figure.

  • Boulder (City of Boulder): CONFIRMED official: general sales tax 3.86% (city) — applies to both medical and recreational; additional 3.50% on recreational marijuana sales, "in addition to the City of Boulder sales tax rate of 3.86%. The tax applies to all sales of any items containing marijuana"; 5.0% Recreational Marijuana Excise tax "due when marijuana is transferred from a recreational marijuana cultivation facility to a [MIP], testing facility or recreational marijuana dispensary," calculated on weight/number × value set (AMR values) — City of Boulder, Tax Rates & Types (https://bouldercolorado.gov/tax-rates-types); December 2025 Revenue Report (https://bouldercolorado.gov/december-2025-revenue-report). City total on a recreational sale from city taxes alone: 3.86% + 3.50% = 7.36%, before state 15%, county and district taxes. The December 2025 Revenue Report confirms the same structure and notes the state shareback reduction from 10% to 3.5% effective 1 July 2025 reduced city revenue from that source (https://bouldercolorado.gov/december-2025-revenue-report); any extension to zero from 1 July 2026 under HB 26-1409 is this research's inference from §2.5, not a Boulder statement.
