3.5 Jurisdiction-by-jurisdiction — minimum checklist plus border towns

How to read each entry: "Allows" means the retrieved source confirms businesses of that type operate / are licensed there, subject to the source-quality notes in each entry. "Prohibits" means a code provision or voter measure prohibiting that type was retrieved. Where only a historic ban was retrieved and no current reversal was found, the entry says historic ban — current status Verify, rather than asserting a current ban. Where a jurisdiction changed status after the CML November 2024 snapshot, the newer source is given precedence and the CML row is noted as superseded. Directory/search listings alone are not licence proof and are labelled as such.

Denver — City and County of Denver (consolidated city-and-county; do not confuse with Denver County as a separate county, or with neighbouring Adams/Arapahoe/Jefferson counties). Status: allows medical and retail stores, cultivation, manufacturing, testing, delivery (permit) and hospitality / hospitality-and-sales — the most complete local programme in the state. Official source: City and County of Denver, "Frequently asked questions about marijuana licenses" — https://denvergov.org/Government/Agencies-Departments-Offices/Agencies-Departments-Offices-Directory/Business-Licensing/Business-licenses/Marijuana-licenses/FAQ — "Denver has a marijuana social equity program. It reserves store, transporter, cultivation, manufacturing, and hospitality licenses for social equity applicants until July 1, 2027. There is no cap on the number of licenses available to social equity applicants." "Under the program, only social equity applicants can deliver marijuana to consumers. They must hold a marijuana transporter license and delivery permit." City issues new: medical delivery permit, retail delivery permit, marijuana hospitality business licence (including mobile premise), retail marijuana hospitality-and-sales licence. City no longer issues new business licences for medical marijuana stores (and, per the FAQ excerpt, other legacy categories — full "no longer issues" list truncated in snippet, Verify complete list on FAQ page). Hospitality / hospitality-and-sales / mobile hospitality licences are reserved for social equity applicants until 1 July 2027. Denver Revised Municipal Code §6-205 (cited in FAQ): "It shall be unlawful for any person… to engage in any form of business or commerce involving marijuana within the city without a valid local license or permit… and a corresponding state license or permit…" — dual-licence rule in Denver code form (Verify exact DRMC text; the §3.1 reference to "§3.5" is corrected to §6-205 here). Denver provides a marijuana proximity check tool for stores, hospitality, hospitality-and-sales and cultivations. Delivery approved in Denver April 2021 (CML note, secondary). Tax: special marijuana sales tax 5.5% (CML Nov 2024, secondary; corroborated as the special component of Denver's official 10.65% retail rate — see below). General sales tax — RESOLVED: Denver's official Combined Rates sheet effective 1-1-2025 gives Denver general 5.15%, Denver retail marijuana rate 10.65% (5.15% + 5.5%), and a retail total of 26.75% (10.65% Denver + 15.00% state special + 1.00% RTD + 0.10% Cultural Facilities District), and a medical combined rate of 9.15% (5.15% Denver + 2.90% state + 1.00% RTD + 0.10% CFD) — https://denvergov.org/files/assets/public/v/1/finance/documents/treasury/tax-guides/tax-update-2025/tax-rates-effective-1-1-2025_1.pdf; Tax Guide Topic 70, rev. 01/2025, likewise states a 5.15% general sales tax and a 10.65% rate on recreational marijuana — https://denver.prelive.opencities.com/files/assets/public/v/1/finance/documents/treasury/tax-guides/tax-update-2025/taxguidetopic70_salestax.pdf. The older figures in the original report (general 4.81%, retail total 26.41%, medical total 8.81%, from a 2022 report) are SUPERSEDED and removed from the main text. Denver has no medical exemption from its general tax, unlike the state's retail exemption from the 2.9% state sales tax. Caps/zoning: no general cap stated for social-equity licences until 1 July 2027 (FAQ above). Proximity/buffer rules apply via the proximity check tool — specific distances not retrieved (Verify in DRMC Chapter 6, Article V). Concentration note (official, historic): Denver was the largest single recipient of the old local distribution (e.g. 33.34% of the local 10% distribution for October 2015 sales) — historic, secondary-reported, not a current licence count (see §3.6).

Colorado Springs — CORRECTION to the brief's premise ("no retail" is outdated). Historic position (until 2024): no retail stores. City Council voted 5–4 in 2013 to keep retail out; voters in 2022 rejected an initiated ordinance to allow retail sales (both secondary-reported; Verify in council/clerk records). 2024 reversal — election results (secondary reporting only; Verify against the official El Paso County canvass — no canvass was opened in this audit): Ballot Question 300 (initiated ordinance, allow ~90 existing medical stores to apply for retail licences): PASSED (secondary reporting: about 55% to 45%; one secondary count gives 54.64% to 45.36%, 129,979 to 107,888). Ballot Issue 2D (council-referred charter amendment to prohibit retail): FAILED (secondary reporting: about 49.5% to 50.5%). Do NOT quote the original report's 54.7% / 49.4% decimals as canvass figures. Early election-night reporting (8 Nov 2024) had both measures apparently passing at ~51–53%; the final result above supersedes it. Early "both passed" reports must not be quoted as the final result. 2025 litigation / re-vote attempt (secondary reporting — Verify in court record; no case name/number was given in the original report): City Council voted 7–2 in January 2025 to place a repeal question on the 1 April 2025 ballot. An El Paso County District Court judge blocked it, and the Colorado Supreme Court declined to weigh in (February 2025), allowing Question 300 to stand. NORML states licensed dispensaries could begin adult-use sales on 14 April (2025, by context) — Verify first-sale date and current store count against City Clerk / MED list. Current official licensing position (City of Colorado Springs marijuana licensing page — https://coloradosprings.gov/marijuana; corrected link — the original report's csfd.coloradosprings.gov/marijuana address is not the City's licensing page): allowed types listed: Medical — MMS (store), MMCF (cultivation), MMPM (products manufacturer), MM-TEST (testing); Retail — RMS (store), RMCF (cultivation), RMPM (products manufacturer), plus testing. Prohibited: "The City of Colorado Springs prohibits Hospitality, Hospitality and Sales, Transporter, and Delivery businesses." Cap: "The City of Colorado Springs has a cap on licensed marijuana business locations" under City Code §2.2.104 — corrected mechanism (City Code §2.2.104 — https://codelibrary.amlegal.com/codes/coloradospringsco/latest/coloradosprings_co/0-0-0-1845): the cap is CUMULATIVE — changes or additions cannot increase the number of licensed locations; surrender or revocation reduces the cap and creates no opportunity for new locations; testing licences are capped at one location per 100 capped locations (§2.2.104(H)). There is no single cap number in the code text. §2.2.104(D) is the separate rule that the Local Licensing Authority shall not receive or act upon any application for a new medical marijuana store licence (eff. 25 May 2017). New medical stores: "The City of Colorado Springs cannot accept any new Medical Marijuana Store applications." (https://coloradosprings.gov/marijuana). Modifications, ownership changes and transfers for existing types are accepted under current MED and City code. Zoning — corrected: City Code §2.2.104(I) (Ord. 25-08, eff. 10 Feb 2025) requires denial of an initial retail application if the business is within 1,000 feet of an operating public or private daycare facility, elementary or secondary school, or drug or alcohol treatment facility, measured by direct pedestrian access from the building to the facility's property line (https://codelibrary.amlegal.com/codes/coloradospringsco/latest/coloradosprings_co/0-0-0-1845). The September 2024 council zoning ordinance described in secondary reporting (CPR, 5 Nov 2024) as a 1-mile buffer must NOT be stated as the current governing buffer. A separate secondary summary states a 1,000-foot buffer already applied to medical dispensaries — the current code's 1,000-foot retail rule above is the figure to use for retail, subject to checking whether any separate 1-mile zoning provision survives. Tax: a 2022 pre-emptive tax measure to fund public safety, mental health and veteran PTSD programmes is referenced in CPR's 2024 reporting, but no rate was confirmed in an official source — Verify in City Code / 2022 ballot language. A secondary summary claims Question 300 included a 5% sales tax; that figure is NOT adopted as a confirmed Colorado Springs special rate. Do not assume a Colorado Springs special rate from CML, whose November 2024 row notes the charter-amendment / separate-ordinance history but gives no rate in the retrieved excerpt. Bottom line: the brief's parenthetical "(no retail)" must not be carried forward. Colorado Springs is now a retail-allowing jurisdiction with hospitality/delivery/transporter prohibitions and a cumulative location cap.

Aurora, CO (Arapahoe/Adams/Douglas counties — not Aurora, IL; an Aurora, OH code provision found in searches is irrelevant and is not used here). Status: allows retail stores (capped), retail cultivation, manufacturing and testing. Official cap (City of Aurora applicant page — https://www.auroragov.org/business_services/marijuana_and_hemp_licensing/applicant_information): "The city of Aurora's Code of Ordinances currently allows for licenses for four retail marijuana stores in each council ward, and all 24 have been awarded." Marijuana Licensing is accepting applications for retail and medical cultivation, manufacturing and testing on an ongoing basis, "and the number of such licenses that may be issued is not restricted" (same page). CONFLICT — Verify before stating Aurora's medical position: the applicant page's acceptance of medical cultivation/manufacturing applications conflicts with an older Aurora guide stating "Medical marijuana businesses, including medical marijuana centers or dispensaries, medical cultivation facilities and medical infused product manufacturers, are not permitted to operate within the city" (https://auroragov.org/UserFiles/Servers/Server_1881137/File/City%20Hall/Marijuana%20Regulations/Opening%20a%20New%20Retail%20Marijuana%20Establishment.pdf). The original report's claim that medical cultivation/manufacturing were authorised by voters in November 2018 (per Aurora's 2019 CAFR) does not resolve this conflict. Corrected position: medical marijuana centres/stores are described in a secondary summary as prohibited, citing Aurora Municipal Code §22.572 — that section citation was NOT confirmed in a code text opened in this audit, so it stays Verify; medical cultivation/manufacturing is UNRESOLVED (applicant page vs older guide) — Verify in current Aurora Code. Do not state either side as settled. Hospitality: Aurora is listed in the HB 26-1117 final fiscal note (February 2026) as one of three hospitality locations statewide (with Arvada and Denver) (https://leg.colorado.gov/bill_files/117143/download) — Verify current Aurora hospitality licences; hospitality allowance does not imply medical-store allowance. Tax: CML Nov 2024 (secondary): 5% excise, 4% sales (authority up to 10%). Reconciliation with Aurora's own historic documents: Aurora CAFR for year ended 31 Dec 2019 — 4 Nov 2014 voters passed a 2.0% sales tax (adjustable up to 10%) on retail marijuana plus a 5.0% excise on bulk wholesale; Council increased sales tax from 2.0% to 4.0% in 2017 to support homeless programmes; max 24 store licences, four per ward; as of 31 Dec 2019, 24 stores, 21 cultivations, 16 MIPs and 1 testing facility operating; 2019 marijuana tax revenue $11.7 million (historic, not current counts). Aurora Marijuana Tax Revenue Fund document states a 5.75% city sales tax in 2014, increased to 7.75% effective 1 July 2017. The 7.75% figure is best read as 4.0% special + ~3.75% general city sales tax, not as a 7.75% special rate — but that decomposition was not explicitly stated in the retrieved snippet (Verify current Aurora general + special split in Aurora Code / DR 1002 before publishing an Aurora total). Fees: not retrieved — Unavailable.

Boulder, CO (City of Boulder — not Boulder City, NV; distinct from Boulder County). Status: allows medical and retail stores, cultivation, manufacturing, testing (CML code links for both medical and recreational codes — secondary). Tax (official, current): City of Boulder, "Tax Rates & Types" (https://bouldercolorado.gov/tax-rates-types): general sales tax 3.86% (city) — applies to both medical and recreational; additional 3.50% on recreational marijuana sales, "in addition to the City of Boulder sales tax rate of 3.86%. The tax applies to all sales of any items containing marijuana"; 5.0% Recreational Marijuana Excise tax "due when marijuana is transferred from a recreational marijuana cultivation facility to a [MIP], testing facility or recreational marijuana dispensary," calculated on weight/number × value set (AMR values). City total on a recreational sale from city taxes alone: 3.86% + 3.50% = 7.36%, before state 15%, county and district taxes. Boulder County rate note on the same page: "Boulder County rates change from 1.185% to 1.335% as of January 1, 2026" (https://bouldercolorado.gov/tax-rates-types). That is the county layer at a Boulder address, not the city rate. City of Boulder December 2025 Revenue Report confirms the same structure and notes the state shareback reduction from 10% to 3.5% effective 1 July 2025 reduced city revenue from that source (https://bouldercolorado.gov/december-2025-revenue-report) (and, by extension, to zero from 1 July 2026 under HB 26-1409 — the report predates / does not discuss HB 26-1409, so that extension is this research's inference from §2.5, not a Boulder statement). Zoning/caps: Boulder County Land Use Code / City code setbacks referenced secondarily (1,000 feet from daycare/school/university/treatment facility for manufacturing in unincorporated Boulder County; max three manufacturing businesses within 500 feet of each other) — secondary, Verify in current Boulder / Boulder County codes. No city store cap figure retrieved — Unavailable.

Fort Collins (Larimer County). Status: allows retail and medical stores under Fort Collins Municipal Code Article XVII (secondary summary citing §15-608 for medical stores — Verify in current code). CML links to the Fort Collins marijuana page. History: a 1 November 2011 special election (Question 300 in Fort Collins — not Colorado Springs Question 300) put the future of medical centres to voters; the outcome of that 2011 vote was not retrieved — do not confuse the two Question 300s. Fort Collins' current allowance is confirmed by current code references above, not by the 2011 vote. Unincorporated Larimer County (distinct from the City of Fort Collins): secondary summary states only two Retail Marijuana Store Licences are to be granted in unincorporated Larimer County, cultivation must be fully indoors, and facilities must comply with the Larimer County Land Use Code zoning district — Verify the two-store cap in current Larimer County code (a county rule, not a Fort Collins city rule). Tax: CML notes a sales tax approved by voters in November 2020, but no rate retrieved — Unavailable. Fort Collins general sales-tax rate at a marijuana address must be taken from DR 1002 / Fort Collins Sales Tax office. Fees/buffers: not retrieved in official form — Unavailable. A historic (2011-era) 1,000-foot-from-schools / 500-foot-from-colleges/parks/places-of-worship description in secondary material must not be presented as current.

Pueblo — City of Pueblo AND Pueblo County (distinct jurisdictions; county governs unincorporated territory only). City of Pueblo: allows retail stores (Pueblo Code §11-11-302, cited secondarily) and medical stores (§11-10-302, cited secondarily) — Verify in current Pueblo Code. The City's licensing page confirms the Office of the City Clerk licenses and regulates the medical and retail marijuana industries in the City (https://www.pueblo.us/1849/Marijuana-Licensing) but does not confirm the cited section texts. Moratorium — secondary, Verify urgently: a secondary report (citing The Pueblo Chieftain) states Pueblo City Council passed a 24-month moratorium on new retail marijuana licences, effective 28 September 2026 (vote 28 September 2026), exempting renewals, ownership transfers and location changes, limited to retail stores (cultivation, testing, manufacturing and medical unaffected), expiring in 2028. This is not confirmed against a Pueblo ordinance in this run — Verify before stating the moratorium as law. If confirmed, it is the most recent local moratorium in the checklist and postdates CML November 2024. Secondary detail not adopted as confirmed: the Chieftain report states the city code allows eight retail stores (four north and four south of the Arkansas River), falling to six operating during the moratorium as two surrender — Verify that cap in the code as well; do not merge it with the older "eight stores" figure in the county paragraph below. Excise suspension — secondary, Verify: a secondary report states the City voted to suspend its 8% excise tax from 2024 to 2027 (8% → 0%) to attract jobs/growth — Verify in Pueblo ordinance/budget; the suspension end date (2027) means the rate may change again during the next research cycle. Historic scale (secondary, not a current count): "more than 200 cannabis businesses at peak" and a combined state+local tax burden "as high as 41%" are reported in a secondary industry history — do not use 41% as a current Pueblo total-tax figure. Pueblo County (unincorporated): Pueblo County Marijuana Code, Chapter 5.12 (official county page — https://county.pueblo.org/county-attorney-department/chapter-512-marijuana-licensing): adopted by Resolution No. 22-006 (replacing Chapter 5.12 adopted by Resolution No. 20-009), authority cited as Colo. Const. Art. XVIII, §§14 and 16; Title 44, Article 10; and CCR. Governs retail and medical establishments within unincorporated Pueblo County; local licensing authority is the Pueblo County Liquor and Marijuana Licensing Board. Caps: "There are no exceptions to the maximum cap on licenses" (Chapter 5.12 excerpt) — cap number itself not retrieved (Verify in Chapter 5.12, §5.12.060; secondary cap numbers found in non-official summaries are not adopted). Delivery ban (unincorporated): "There shall be no personal delivery of marijuana within unincorporated Pueblo County. This restriction shall apply to all licensees and to any stores that may be located outside of unincorporated Pueblo County." (Chapter 5.12 excerpt — https://county.pueblo.org/county-attorney-department/chapter-512-marijuana-licensing.) Tax compliance as licence condition: failure to comply with state or local tax collection/administration, "including the countywide sales and excise taxes proposed by Resolutions No. 13-186 and 15-203 and approved respectively by votes of the electors of Pueblo County," may result in sanctions including revocation. Countywide special tax: City of Pueblo 2024 Proposed Budget narrative (secondary) — voters of Pueblo County approved a ballot issue at the 2013 coordinated General Election, approving a three and one-half cent (3.5%) special tax on sale of retail marijuana and products in all portions of Pueblo County, plus a 2016 City ordinance noting eight (8) retail stores within the City, and a City–County Intergovernmental Agreement (IGA) sharing the county special-tax revenue generated in the City. The "eight stores" figure is a 2016 ordinance figure, not a current count.

Lakewood, CO (Jefferson County — not Lakewood, WA; MED's Lakewood office address does not imply Lakewood, CO licensing policy). Status — corrected wording: directory evidence suggests operating retail stores in Lakewood, CO (e.g. Star Buds Lakewood, 265 S. Wadsworth Blvd; Ascend Cannabis Co, 10712 W. Alameda Ave — search results, accessed 1 Nov 2026), and early-2010s reporting listed Lakewood, CO under a moratorium through 1 January 2015 (and a proposed extension). Directory listings are not licence proof, so the original report's "Lakewood, CO therefore allows retail stores as of this research" is softened to: directory evidence suggests retail stores operate there; the reversal ordinance/date and the full type scope (stores only vs cultivation/manufacturing/delivery/hospitality) are Verify in Lakewood, CO Municipal Code / MED list before stating full business-type scope. Tax / fees / caps / buffers: Unavailable in this run. No Lakewood, CO special-tax rate retrieved; do not import Lakewood, WA rates or the Lakewood, WA prohibition. Caution: MED's offices are in Lakewood, CO (1707 Cole Blvd, Suite 300, Lakewood, CO 80401 — MED application page — https://sbg.colorado.gov/med/new-regulated-marijuana-business-license-application). That is MED's mailing/drop-off location, not evidence about Lakewood, CO local licensing.

Thornton, CO (Adams/Weld counties). Status — corrected wording: directory evidence suggests operating retail stores in Thornton, CO (Rocky Road Thornton, 3901 E. 112th Ave, Unit G — "Rocky Road Thornton opened its doors in 2017"; Medicine Man Thornton, 130 W. 84th Ave; Skunked, 2683 E. 120th Ave — search results, accessed 1 Nov 2026), and 2013 reporting listed Thornton among cities barring retail stores. Directory listings are not licence proof: the reversal ordinance/vote and its date were not retrieved — Verify in Thornton Municipal Code / council records before stating Thornton "allows" retail as a code finding. Tax / delivery: CML Nov 2024 (secondary): 5% sales tax; "Approved delivery April 2021" (https://www.cml.org/docs/default-source/marijuana-resources/marijuana-(2024).pdf?Status=Temp&sfvrsn=779b27f2_6). Delivery approval is therefore separately noted in CML, unlike Colorado Springs / Pueblo County where delivery is prohibited. Fees / caps / buffers: Unavailable in this run.

Arvada, CO (Jefferson/Adams counties). Status — prohibits both, subject to code verification: secondary summaries citing Arvada City Code state: §53-42 (Article III) prohibits non-medical marijuana businesses including retail stores within city borders, and §53-22 (Chapter 53) prohibits medical marijuana businesses including medical dispensaries. Arvada therefore has no dispensaries within its borders on that secondary account; residents purchase in neighbouring jurisdictions. Verify current §§53-22 / 53-42 text on Municode / Arvada Code — the section texts were not opened in this audit, although §53-42 is corroborated as a real Arvada code section (a 2013 Arvada ordinance references §53-42 for medical cultivation limits). Hospitality exception — Verify: despite the store prohibition, the HB 26-1117 final fiscal note (February 2026, official — https://leg.colorado.gov/bill_files/117143/download) lists Arvada among hospitality locations (with Aurora and Denver). If accurate, Arvada allows hospitality (consumption) without allowing stores — a type-by-type distinction that must be verified in MED's hospitality list and Arvada code before republication. Do not infer from the fiscal note alone that Arvada allows retail sales. History: Arvada was under moratorium in 2013–2014 (with Lakewood and others "eventually allow" expectations in contemporary reporting that, for Arvada, did not materialise into store allowance). The moratorium history does not change the current prohibition finding above, subject to code verification. Tax: no special marijuana tax applies to (prohibited) stores.

Westminster, CO (Adams/Jefferson counties). Status — historic ban, current status Verify: Westminster banned retail businesses by council action in January 2013 (contemporary reporting) and was listed among banning cities in 2014 and 2018 compilations. No 2024–2026 official Westminster reversal or confirmation was retrieved in this run. CML's November 2024 table includes Westminster in its municipality list, but the retrieved excerpt does not give Westminster's current status/tax row. Do not state Westminster as currently prohibiting or currently allowing without checking the current Westminster Municipal Code. This is a priority follow-up, not a gap to fill by inference from the 2013 ban. Tax / fees / caps: Unavailable in this run.

Greeley, CO (Weld County — not Greeley, KS or elsewhere). Status — prohibits both medical and retail dispensaries, subject to code verification: secondary summary citing Greeley Municipal Code §24-1104(d) states §24-1104(d) "prohibits the establishment of recreational weed dispensaries in Greeley" and, by ordinance, medical dispensaries as well. Council voted in 2013 to ban commercial sales (contemporary reporting; a 2016 city report cited there concluded regulation costs could cancel out tax revenue). Verify current §24-1104(d) text; no Greeley reversal was retrieved. Enclave distinction — critical for Weld County research: Garden City, a separate town surrounded on three sides by Greeley, does allow dispensaries (four retailers in a town of under 300 residents, per the same secondary history) and is the de facto purchase point for Greeley residents. Garden City must not be reported as "Greeley allows dispensaries," and Greeley must not be reported as the location of Garden City's stores. Garden City's tax rates were not retrieved — Unavailable. Tax: no Greeley special marijuana tax applies to prohibited stores.

Longmont, CO (Boulder/Weld counties). Status: allows retail (and medical, per CML code links — secondary). Longmont is split between Boulder and Weld counties; the city code governs inside city limits, the counties govern enclaves until annexed (see below). Longmont Code Ch. 6.70's purpose clause confirms the city exercises its Art. XVIII §16(5)(f) authority to allow state-licensed establishments under local licensing requirements (https://longmont.primegov.com/api/compilemeetingattachmenthistory/historyattachment/?historyId=38997796-01cc-4443-8577-2f1aa6a66081). Tax (2026 council packet, as given; packet not re-opened in this audit — Verify): Longmont City Council Communication, 10 March 2026: annexed dispensaries "would need to collect and remit the City's 3.53% sales tax and the City's 3% special retail marijuana tax." Ballot language approved by voters (2017, per the same packet and a Longmont budget summary): 50% of the special retail marijuana tax to affordable housing, 50% allocated by Council for mental health services (2027 budget: $593,416 for the Special Retail Marijuana Tax, per that secondary budget summary — Verify in the adopted 2027 budget). CML conflict — UNRESOLVED: CML Nov 2024 older row: "3.5% sales tax; 3% excise tax with authority up to 15%." The 2026 packet's "3% special retail marijuana tax" and CML's "3% excise tax" may describe the same 3% levy under different labels, or two different levies. Verify in current Longmont Municipal Code Chapter 6.70 (Marijuana Stores) whether Longmont levies both a 3% special sales tax and a separate 3% excise tax, or one 3% levy. Do not add them together without that check. Annexation / cap (2026, in progress): 10 March 2026 packet: Council directed staff (2 Sept 2025 budget presentation, motion 6–1) to pursue annexing two dispensaries in Boulder County enclaves within city limits — JARS, 250 S. Main St., and (per the secondary budget summary) Native Roots, 19 S. Sunset St. — and to increase the marijuana store licence cap accordingly (secondary council reporting describes the proposal as raising the cap from four to six). Draft ordinance: 90-day temporary licence (no fee), then a conditional licence expiring on the same date as the current county licence, with MED notified to change the local authority of record. The secondary summary states the city "arrived at a solution in May" (2026) when it annexed the two dispensaries, to offset the loss of the state shareback. Verify annexation ordinance's effective date and new cap number — the March packet is a proposal, the May claim is secondary. State-shareback loss (context): the same secondary summary notes Longmont previously received roughly $500,000/year from three sources (3.53% city sales tax + 3% special tax + state shareback), with the shareback going 10% → 3.5% → 0% — consistent with §2.5. Longmont's marijuana revenue decline since a 2022 peak is reported there as part of a statewide sales decline — secondary, do not quote a Longmont peak figure without the city budget document.

Loveland, CO (Larimer County — not Loveland, OH or elsewhere). Status — newly allowing (2024 vote, 2025 ordinance, 2026 applications): "In 2024, City of Loveland voters approved local retail and medical marijuana sales, allowing a limited number of retail and medical marijuana businesses to operate in Loveland, and imposing an excise tax on sales." — City of Loveland, Marijuana Licenses page (https://www.lovgov.org/city-government/city-clerk/marijuana). Prior status: CML notes Loveland "Defeated by voters November 2019" (i.e. a prior sales proposal failed) and a 2024 CML excerpt notes "Sales and excise tax approved Nov 2024; 5% excise tax on retail sales." The 2024 approval therefore reverses the 2019 defeat — do not cite the 2019 result as current. Licensing timeline (official Loveland page — https://www.lovgov.org/city-government/city-clerk/marijuana): application consultation meetings for legacy applicants from Thursday, 5 February 2026 (first step); local applications may be submitted in person to the City Clerk starting 1 March 2026; non-legacy application period begins no earlier than Monday, 29 June 2026; state application must be submitted before the local application and a copy submitted with it (local applications without the state application will be denied). Legacy definition: evidence of at least 10% ownership over a prior legal retail or medical marijuana establishment in Loveland; legacy applicants have the first 120 days from 1 March 2026; only one application per legacy applicant reviewed at a time during that period; a pending-application locations list is published (example in snippet: 154 E. 15th St. — a pending location, not a guarantee of approval). Zoning / operating rules (Loveland council presentation, 16 Dec 2025, city site): business/industrial zones only; Adaptable Use Permit + pre-application consultation required; neighbourhood meeting required; 1,000-foot setback from schools, childcare centres and alcohol/drug treatment facilities; 1-mile distance requirement between licensees (functioning as a spacing cap — staff estimate 4–7 stores realistically, 4–11 by spacing arithmetic, per Reporter-Herald summary — an estimate, not a cap); hours 8:00 a.m.–10:00 p.m.; security plan and internal controls required; no alcohol/nicotine products or free giveaways; state-approved packaging/labelling. Loveland's council presentation cites CRS §44-10-311 for a minimum setback — corrected qualification: §44-10-311(1)(d) is a medical-licence rule that localities may vary (https://colorado.public.law/statutes/crs_44-10-311); Loveland's 1,000-foot setback stands as a local rule regardless. Tax (official): City of Loveland Finance page (http://LovGov.org/services/finance/sales-tax/marijuana-sales-excise-tax): "Each marijuana business shall collect and remit 3% city sales tax on all retail marijuana, retail marijuana products, paraphernalia, and other tangible personal property… Each marijuana business shall collect and remit 5% excise tax on all retail marijuana and retail marijuana products." Note: Loveland's "3% city sales tax" here is the general city sales tax applied to marijuana (not a special rate on top of a separate general rate) — do not double-count it. The 5% excise is the special levy. Fees (proposed — see §3.4): $7,500 / $7,500 / $10,000 / $2,500 — Verify final adopted schedule.

Grand Junction, CO (Mesa County). Status: allows retail (CML code/licensing-page links; sales/cultivation/manufacturing ticks in CML — secondary). Tax (CML Nov 2024, secondary): 5% sales tax, up to 15%; 3% excise tax, up to 10%; approved by voters April 2021 — Verify in Grand Junction code/ballot record. Zoning/caps/fees: Unavailable in this run — obtain from Grand Junction marijuana licensing page / Municipal Code. Regional note: Grand Junction is the Western Slope regional centre and the location of a MED regional office (200 Grand Ave., Suite 202, Grand Junction, CO 81501 — MED application page — https://sbg.colorado.gov/med/new-regulated-marijuana-business-license-application). The MED office location is not a licensing-policy fact about Grand Junction itself.

Durango, CO (La Plata County — not Durango, Mexico). Status: allows retail (CML Municipal Code link — secondary; Durango appears as a distribution recipient in historic state files). Tax (CML Nov 2024 excerpt, secondary): 3% sales tax. No excise figure in the retrieved excerpt — Verify whether Durango levies a separate excise tax. Zoning/caps/fees: Unavailable in this run.

Glenwood Springs, CO (Garfield County). Status: allows retail and medical (CML code links for both — secondary). Tax (CML Nov 2024, fragmented — Verify): Sales tax 5% up to 15%; excise tax 5%. The snippet breaks across rows; the base (on sales vs on transfer) and current rate must be verified in the Glenwood Springs Municipal Code before use. Zoning/caps/fees: Unavailable in this run.

Aspen, CO (Pitkin County). Status: allows retail and medical (CML code links for both — secondary; Aspen appears as a distribution recipient in historic state files, e.g. $15,807 for September 2017 sales — historic, not current). Tax: Unavailable in this run — CML excerpt gives no Aspen special-tax rate. Aspen's general sales tax and any special marijuana tax must be taken from the Aspen Municipal Code / Finance Department and DR 1002. Do not infer a rate from historic distribution shares. Zoning/caps/fees: Unavailable in this run.

Breckenridge, CO — Town of Breckenridge (Summit County) — spelling correction applied: Breckenridge, not Breckinridge. Status: allows medical and retail stores (CML code link and town licensing history — secondary). Contemporary 2013 reporting listed Breckenridge (with Telluride and Steamboat Springs) among resort communities expected to allow retail stores, and current directory listings show operating dispensaries in Breckenridge, CO (business names/addresses are not relied on here as licence proof — the CML code link and town licensing history are the status evidence). History (secondary, Verify in town records): voters in the Town of Breckenridge voted in 2009 to decriminalise possession of up to one ounce for persons 21+ (secondary timeline). That 2009 vote predates Amendment 64 and is not the retail-licensing authorisation; retail licensing followed the 2012/2013 state framework. The town's medical programme is described in the same secondary timeline as coming into effect in 2010 — Verify in Breckenridge Town Code. Tax (CML Nov 2024, secondary): 5% excise tax on all sales of marijuana (Breckenridge Municipal Code). Whether this is in addition to a town general sales tax, and how it interacts with any Summit County excise tax at a Breckenridge address, is Verify — see Summit County below. Zoning (secondary, Verify): a mountain-region regulatory summary states for Summit County (Breckenridge): no marijuana business within 50 feet of residential use/zoning, 1,000 feet of a licensed childcare facility, 1,000 feet of any elementary/middle/high school/college/university, or 500 feet of a halfway house/correctional facility. That summary is secondary and undated in the retrieved snippet — Verify in current Breckenridge Town Code / Summit County Land Use Code before quoting buffers. The same summary states there are no marijuana businesses licensed and operating in unincorporated Summit County, with businesses operating in the towns of Breckenridge, Frisco and Silverthorne — a county-vs-town distinction consistent with dual licensing, but Verify current unincorporated-county position (see Summit County entry). Fees/caps: Unavailable in this run.

Summit County, CO (unincorporated territory + countywide taxes — distinct from the Town of Breckenridge). Status (unincorporated): secondary mountain-region summary states no businesses operating in unincorporated Summit County. Verify in current Summit County code / MED local-authorities list — this is a material distinction: "Summit County allows" must never be stated without specifying town vs unincorporated. Tax: secondary 2013 report states "Summit County imposed an additional 5% excise tax" in 2013. Current countywide rate, base, and stacking with town taxes (Breckenridge 5%, Frisco, Silverthorne, Dillon) are Verify. CML's November 2024 table does not give a Summit County row in the retrieved excerpt. Towns in Summit County (for cross-reference, not full entries): Frisco and Silverthorne are stated (same secondary summary) to have operating businesses; Dillon appears in historic distribution lists. Their individual tax/zoning rules are out of the minimum checklist and Unavailable in this run.

Trinidad, CO (Las Animas County — not Trinidad, the island). Status: allows retail and medical (CML code links for both; CML ticks for sales/cultivation/manufacturing — secondary). Tax (CML Nov 2024, secondary): 5% sales tax — Verify. Border significance (New Mexico border): Trinidad lies 21 miles (34 km) north of Raton, New Mexico and 195 miles south of Denver (secondary geographic summary — geographic distance only; a Wikipedia entry is not a licensing source). It is the principal Colorado retail centre for New Mexico buyers, but no official out-of-state-buyer count for Trinidad was retrieved — do not quote a buyer-share figure. Historic secondary reporting: 2015 marijuana sales ~$44 million generating $4.4 million in tax revenue; 2018 High Times "Weed Town, USA" description of 23 licensed retail dispensaries for under 10,000 people. Both are dated secondary claims, not current licence counts — Verify current Trinidad licence count in MED's facilities list. Zoning/caps/fees: Unavailable in this run.

Steamboat Springs, CO (Routt County). Status: allows retail and medical (CML Municipal Code link — secondary; contemporary 2013 reporting listed Steamboat Springs among resort communities expected to allow retail stores). Tax: Unavailable in this run — CML excerpt gives a code link but no rate. A secondary note that "Steamboat Springs is the only area… reported to have lowered their marijuana tax" in a November-election roundup gives no rate or year with certainty in the retrieved snippet — do not attribute a lowered rate or a current rate without the Steamboat Springs Municipal Code. Zoning/caps/fees: Unavailable in this run.

Broomfield — City and County of Broomfield (consolidated city-and-county; distinct from Boulder County and from neighbouring Westminster/Thornton). Status — corrected: CML resources page links to Broomfield Municipal Code; CML November 2024 table notes a prohibition ordinance for cultivation/manufacturing (verbatim in CML PDF — https://www.cml.org/docs/default-source/marijuana-resources/marijuana-(2024).pdf?Status=Temp&sfvrsn=779b27f2_6). Method note: "border town" here means a Colorado municipality/county near a state line where cross-border purchase demand is a known local factor. No official origin-of-buyer data was retrieved for any border town in this run; entries below state allowance and tax only, not buyer shares. Interstate transport of marijuana remains unlawful (federal law; Colorado law does not authorise export) — that legal point is Part 10 territory and is noted here only to prevent misreading "border demand" as "lawful export".

3.6 Business concentration — ONLY what official sources say (no researcher ranking)

What was NOT retrieved — stated explicitly so absence is not mistaken for a finding: no current MED licence-count-by-jurisdiction table was opened in this run. MED licensed-facilities lists (by type) exist (see Part 5, https://sbg.colorado.gov/med/licensed-facilities — hub URL as given, not extracted in this audit), but their jurisdiction breakdown was not extracted here. No current DOR county-report breakdown was opened in this run (file linked from DOR Tax Reports page — https://cdor.colorado.gov/data-and-reports/marijuana-data/marijuana-tax-reports). Therefore this report does not rank, estimate or map clusters, and does not state that any city "has the most" licences/stores as a current fact.

What official sources do say, with dates — all items below are secondary-reported historic figures unless stated otherwise, and none is a current licence count: (1) Historic concentration (2014, state report via secondary reporting): at end of 2014, retail sales occurred in only 67 of Colorado's 321 local jurisdictions (secondary summary of DOR's first-year report). That is a 2014 fact about the early patchwork, not a current count, and the "321" denominator is itself secondary. (2) Historic distribution shares (state accounting files, not licence counts, via secondary summary): old 10% local distribution files show Denver as the largest single recipient by sales-tax share (e.g. Denver 33.34% for October 2015 sales; Denver $238,040 of the local distribution in that file). September 2017: Aspen $15,807 (1.04%), Durango $35,300 (2.31%), Glenwood Springs $7,553 (0.49%), Steamboat Springs $14,889 (0.98%), Trinidad $62,010 (4.06%), plus county recipients (Boulder County $989,362 in that file's county column — note: county column and city column are different distributions and must not be added). These are sales-tax shares in 2015/2017, under the old 10% regime, not licence counts and not current shares. (3) Boulder County, 2020 (state public-safety report via secondary summary): Colorado Department of Public Safety report (July 2021), as summarised secondarily, stated 227 licensed medical and recreational cannabis businesses in Boulder County as of 2020, out of 3,207 statewide. That is a 2020, county-level, secondary-reported figure — included only because it is the sole county licence-count figure retrieved, and it must not be updated or ranked without the underlying DPS report. (4) Modelled totals excluded: a Q3 2026 secondary market report models 2,106 licensed businesses at end-2025 (687 retail stores, 478 retail cultivations, 210 retail product manufacturers, 14 hospitality). Those are labelled "Modeled-Est." in that report itself and are not used here as official concentration evidence. If a current statewide total is needed, cite MED's 2025 Regulatory & Enforcement report / MED facilities lists (Part 5), not the modelled summary. (5) What official concentration evidence would look like for follow-up: (a) MED licensed-facilities lists filtered by local licensing authority; (b) DOR Marijuana Tax Revenue by County Report (state tax by county, not licence counts); (c) individual city licence registers (e.g. Denver's licensing portal, Aurora's store list — Aurora's applicant page links to "the list of retail marijuana stores in Aurora" — https://www.auroragov.org/business_services/marijuana_and_hemp_licensing/applicant_information). None of (a)–(c) was extracted by jurisdiction in this run.

No other concentration claim is made in this report. In particular, no claim is made that Denver, Pueblo, Trinidad, Breckenridge or any other jurisdiction is currently the "largest" or "most concentrated" market, because no current official jurisdiction table was retrieved to support such a claim.

Where this corrected text says "Verify," the item was not confirmed from a primary source in this audit and must be checked at the source named before publication or reliance. No current licence count by type/status is given in Part 4, because none was confirmed from an official source in this audit; use MED's licensed-facilities lists (Part 5) for counts. Part 4 contains no Schedule III / 280E analysis; for the federal baseline, medical licences only are Schedule III and only medical activity is outside 280E, retail activity remains Schedule I and fully subject to 280E — a business holding both medical and retail licences must split its activity accordingly.

PART 4 — LICENCE TYPES

Regulator in brief: The Marijuana Enforcement Division (MED), Colorado Department of Revenue, "is tasked with licensing and regulating the Medical and Retail Marijuana industries in Colorado" — MED home page, https://med.colorado.gov/ , accessed 1 Nov 2026. Current rules stated by MED: "Official Secretary of State publication of rules (Effective January 5, 2026)" — MED home page, accessed 1 Nov 2026. Governing statute: Colorado Marijuana Code, CRS Title 44, Article 10. Licence classes are in CRS §44-10-401 — https://law.justia.com/codes/colorado/title-44/marijuana-regulation/article-10/part-4/section-44-10-401/ , accessed 1 Nov 2026.

4.1 How Colorado licensing works — read this first

Two markets, parallel licences. Every business activity has a medical version and a retail (adult-use) version, and "Each facility is authorized to engage only in the type of activity for which it is licensed and as described in statute" — MED Licensed Facilities page, https://med.colorado.gov/licensee-information-and-lookup-tool/licensed-facilities , accessed 1 Nov 2026. A medical licence does not authorise retail sales, and vice versa. Many businesses hold both, at the same or different premises, under separate licences.

State + local dual licensing. A state licence alone does not authorise operation. MED's retail-licensee guidance states: "licensed does not mean operating. A marijuana business must be licensed by both the state and its local jurisdiction before being allowed to operate" — https://cannabis.colorado.gov/retail-cannabis-licensees , accessed 1 Nov 2026. The Hospitality application states the same rule in stronger form: "An applicant is prohibited from operating a Regulated Marijuana Business prior to obtaining all necessary approvals or licenses from both the State Licensing Authority and the local jurisdiction. A separate application is required for each license" — DR 8565, https://med.colorado.gov/sites/med/files/documents/DR%208565e%20Hospitality%201-2026.pdf , accessed 1 Nov 2026. MED will not even accept a new business application for a local jurisdiction that has not advised MED it is currently accepting new medical and/or retail applications — https://sbg.colorado.gov/med/new-regulated-marijuana-business-license-application . Local jurisdictions may cap, ban or limit types — that is Part 3 territory.

No statewide cap or lottery is stated on any MED page opened. That is a negative finding scoped to the pages opened, not proof that none exists — Verify before asserting it as a statewide rule, and verify any local cap before applying.

Licence term — 2 years at state level. SB 24-076 (2024) "extends initial license and license renewal periods from one year to 2 years. Local authorities may decide what licenses they will issue for one year or 2 years" — official bill summary, https://leg.colorado.gov/bills/sb24-076 , accessed 1 Nov 2026. SB 24-076 was APPROVED by the Governor on 5 June 2024 and EFFECTIVE 7 August 2024 (same page).

Unified application — from 1 July 2026. SB 24-076 required the State Licensing Authority to promulgate rules authorising multiple regulated marijuana business licensees with identical controlling beneficial owners to submit a single initial or renewal application — https://leg.colorado.gov/bills/sb24-076 . The 1 July 2026 introduction date comes from MED Industry Bulletin 26:06, listed on MED's home page as "Introduction of Unified Application Option on July 1, 2026, 06/22/26" — MED home page, accessed 1 Nov 2026. Secondary guides describe it as: applicants with identical controlling beneficial owners applying for multiple licences may file one unified application. The statute provides: "A UNIFIED APPLICATION IS SUBJECT TO A LOWER FEE FOR EACH APPLICATION THAN FOR APPLICATIONS FOR INDIVIDUAL LICENSES" — SB 24-076 bill text (PDF), https://leg.colorado.gov/bill_files/46031/download , accessed 1 Nov 2026. The dollar amount of the unified reduction is Verify — it was not in the fee table opened, and no secondary dollar figure is used here.

Fee structure — two payments, plus a local portion for retail. Under 1 CCR 212-3 Rule 2-115 (June 2025 reproduction): "The first payment must be submitted with the application" and "The second payment must be submitted at least twelve (12) months prior to the License expiration date" and failure to pay the second payment on time "shall result in disciplinary action, which may include an administrative action, fine, suspension, or revocation" — Justia — Rule 2-115, https://regulations.justia.com/states/colorado/200/212/rule-1-ccr-212-3/part-2/section-1-ccr-212-3-2-115/ , accessed 1 Nov 2026. For retail licences, "In addition to the fees in subparagraph (1) of this Rule, an Applicant must submit a separate check made out to the local jurisdiction" — same source. That local portion is not a local licence fee; the local jurisdiction charges its own licence fees separately (see Part 3 / Part 5, local records).

Ownership levels drive most business fees. Rule 2-115 levels, for businesses "with direct Controlling Beneficial Owners": Level 1 = 1–4; Level 2 = 5–9; Level 3 = 10 or more — same Justia source. Indirect controlling beneficial owners are excluded from the level count per Rules 2-235(A)(2)(a) and 2-235(B)(1)(b), as cited in Rule 2-115.

MED application forms hub. All current business, owner, employee, permit and modification forms are listed at MED — Applications and Forms, https://sbg.colorado.gov/med/applications-and-forms , accessed 1 Nov 2026 (form dates as listed there in the original run; re-check the live forms page before filing — form versions may have changed for the 5 January 2026 rules). Key forms as listed in the original run: DR 8548e Regulated Marijuana Business (RMB) License Application (8/7/25); DR 8529 RMB License Renewal Application (9/07/22); DR 8520 Natural Person Finding of Suitability; DR 8557e Business Owner Entity Finding of Suitability; DR 8517 Employee License Application; DR 8523 Social Equity Program – RMB License Application (2/08/23); DR 8514 Accelerator Endorsement Application (5/26/22); DR 8565e Hospitality Marijuana Business Application (5/7/2025); DR 8569 Delivery Permit (10/26/21); DR 8540e Centralized Distribution Permit Application (6/23/2025); DR 8518e Off-Premises Storage Permit Application (6/18/2025); DR 8542 R&D Co-Location Permit; DR 8561 Transition Permit; DR 8535e Change of Controlling Beneficial Owner Application (5/7/2025); DR 8563 Changes Exempt of Change of Ownership (2/10/22); DR 8545e Report of Changes (4/11/25).

MED business-licence hub. MED — Licenses and Fees, https://med.colorado.gov/licenses-and-fees , accessed 1 Nov 2026.

4.2 Licence-by-licence table — CRS §44-10-401 classes + MED descriptions

MED Licensed Facilities page quotations are verbatim from that page — https://med.colorado.gov/licensee-information-and-lookup-tool/licensed-facilities , accessed 1 Nov 2026 — unless otherwise noted. State fees are Rule 2-115, June 2025 reproduction (see version warning at the top of Part 4). "1st + 2nd" = first payment with application + second payment at least 12 months before expiry; totals are the sum of both. All fees below must be re-checked against the 5 January 2026 schedule before budgeting or quoting to an applicant.

A. Medical licences — CRS §44-10-401(2)(a) — https://law.justia.com/codes/colorado/title-44/marijuana-regulation/article-10/part-4/section-44-10-401/

  • Medical Marijuana Store (§44-10-501): "operate a business that sells Medical Marijuana to Colorado Medical Marijuana Registry Patients and Transporting Caregivers." 1st + 2nd, each: L1 $8,460; L2 $12,710; L3 $16,910. Totals: L1 $16,920; L2 $25,420; L3 $33,820. No separate local portion is shown for medical licences in Rule 2-115(C)(2), which applies to retail licences only.
  • Medical Marijuana Cultivation Facility (§44-10-502): "operate a cultivation business to grow and harvest Medical Marijuana." Class 1 (1–500 plants) 1st + 2nd, each: L1 $3,210; L2 $4,835; L3 $6,410. Totals: L1 $6,420; L2 $9,670; L3 $12,820. Class 2 and Class 3 fee rows were not legible in the June 2025 reproduction — Verify Class 2/3 fees in the 5 Jan 2026 schedule.
  • Medical Marijuana Products Manufacturer (§44-10-503): "operate a business that produces Medical Marijuana Products such as edibles, concentrates or tinctures. These licensees are only authorized to wholesale their products to MED licensed Medical Marijuana Centers." 1st + 2nd, each: L1 $3,210; L2 $4,835; L3 $6,410. Totals: L1 $6,420; L2 $9,670; L3 $12,820. ("Centers" is MED's wording in the quotation; the statute says "stores.")
  • Medical Marijuana Testing Facility (§44-10-504): "operate a facility that conducts potency and contaminants testing and research for MED Medical Marijuana business licenses." Same fees as the manufacturer above.
  • Medical Marijuana Transporter (§44-10-505): "provide transportation and temporary storage services to MED Licensed Medical Marijuana Businesses." $3,625 + $3,625 = $7,250 total. No ownership levels shown.
  • Medical Marijuana Business Operator (§44-10-506): "provide professional operational services to one or more MED Licensed Medical Marijuana Businesses." 1st + 2nd, each: L1 $4,200; L2 $6,300; L3 $8,400. Totals: L1 $8,400; L2 $12,600; L3 $16,800.
  • Marijuana Research and Development (facility) (§44-10-507): "grow, cultivate possess and transfer marijuana for use in research only." 1st + 2nd, each: L1 $3,210; L2 $4,835; L3 $6,410. Totals: L1 $6,420; L2 $9,670; L3 $12,820. Note: this is the only R&D licence in §44-10-401(2)(a); it is not split medical/retail in that list.

B. Retail licences — CRS §44-10-401(2)(b) — same §44-10-401 source. Fees below are state fees (June 2025) PLUS the local portion at application shown for each row.

  • Retail Marijuana Store (§44-10-601): "operate a business that sells Retail Marijuana to an individual twenty-one years of age or older." 1st / 2nd: L1 $3,120 / $5,620; L2 $5,960 / $8,460; L3 $8,740 / $11,240. State totals: L1 $8,740; L2 $14,420; L3 $19,980. Plus local portion $2,500 at application (separate cheque to local jurisdiction).
  • Retail Marijuana Cultivation Facility (§44-10-602): "operate a facility to grow and harvest Retail Marijuana plants." Tier 1 (1–1,800 plants) 1st / 2nd: L1 $2,440 / $4,940; L2 $4,910 / $7,410; L3 $7,370 / $9,870. State totals: L1 $7,380; L2 $12,320; L3 $17,240. Plus local portion $2,500. Tier 2–5 and Expanded Production Management fee rows were not legible — Verify in the 5 Jan 2026 schedule.
  • Retail Marijuana Products Manufacturer (§44-10-603): "operate a facility that manufactures retail marijuana-infused products such as edibles, concentrates or tinctures." Same 1st/2nd figures and totals as Retail Cultivation Tier 1 above. Plus local portion $2,500.
  • Retail Marijuana Testing Facility (§44-10-604): "operate a facility that conducts potency and contaminants testing for other MED Licensed Retail Marijuana businesses." 1st / 2nd: L1 $2,100 / $3,150; L2 $3,415 / $4,465; L3 $4,725 / $5,775. State totals: L1 $5,250; L2 $7,880; L3 $10,500. Plus local portion $1,050.
  • Retail Marijuana Transporter (§44-10-605): "provide transportation and temporary storage services to Retail Marijuana Businesses." $3,075 + $3,600 = $6,675 state total. Plus local portion $525. No ownership levels shown.
  • Retail Marijuana Business Operator ("Operator") (§44-10-606): "provide professional operational services to one or more Retail Marijuana Businesses." 1st / 2nd: L1 $3,100 / $4,150; L2 $4,935 / $5,985; L3 $6,720 / $7,770. State totals: L1 $7,250; L2 $10,920; L3 $14,490. Plus local portion $1,050.
  • Accelerator Cultivator (§44-10-607): CORRECTED DEFINITION (statute prevails over the MED-page sentence quoted in the original run): a social equity licensee qualified to participate in the accelerator programme, authorised by rule to exercise the privileges of a retail marijuana cultivation facility on the premises of an accelerator-endorsed retail marijuana cultivation facility licensee — CRS §44-10-103(1), https://law.justia.com/codes/colorado/title-44/marijuana-regulation/article-10/part-1/section-44-10-103/ . The MED Licensed Facilities page sentence that described this licence as a "manufacturing operation" is WRONG and must not be relied on. Plus local portion $2,500.
