It did NOT appear in the MED Licensed Facilities page list opened in the original run (that list ends at Hospitality and Sales) — that listing point is Verify on a live re-open of the page. Its privileges are the store privileges exercised by a social-equity licensee on an accelerator-endorsed store's premises — §44-10-103(4.5), same Justia §44-10-103 source. Verify — no separate fee row legible in the June 2025 reproduction.

C. Occupational licences / registrations — CRS §44-10-401(2)(c): "Occupational licenses and registrations for owners, managers, operators, employees, contractors, and other support staff employed by, working in, or having access to restricted areas of the licensed premises, as determined by the state licensing authority" — §44-10-401(2)(c), same §44-10-401 source. In practice:

  • Owner licences — Controlling Beneficial Owner (CBO), natural person (DR 8520) and Owner Entity (DR 8557e). Threshold: "Any Natural Person who holds 10% interest or more of the Owner's interest of a RMB; Executive Officer, Manager or any other Person or affiliate that is otherwise in a position to execute Control of the RMB" — DR 8520 instructions, DR 8520 (PDF), https://med.colorado.gov/sites/med/files/documents/DR%208520e%20ADA%20CBO%20suitability%202-2025.pdf , accessed 1 Nov 2026. Owner Entity: "Any Entity that holds 10% interest or more of the Owner's interest of an RMB; Executive or Qualified Institutional Investors holding more than 30% of the RMB, or any other Entity or affiliate that is otherwise in a position to execute control of the RMB" — DR 8557 instructions, DR 8557 (PDF), https://med.colorado.gov/sites/med/files/documents/DR%208557e%20Owner%20Entity%20Suitability%205-2025.pdf , accessed 1 Nov 2026 (the "more than 30%" wording is confirmed by the HB 19-1090 enacted summary, https://leg.colorado.gov/bills/hb19-1090 ). Both forms require addenda for Publicly Traded Companies (PTC), Qualified Private Funds (QPF) and Qualified Institutional Investors (QII). "All required Findings of Suitability must first be obtained prior to any new business application submission" — DR 8520 (form text not re-opened in this audit — re-check DR 8520 before filing). Social-equity suitability uses the same DR 8520 route first (see §4.7).
  • Employee licence (badge). MED Employee License page via search result: "Employee license (if applicant went through an approved third-party vendor for fingerprints) $130 [application] $40 [licence] $170 [total]"; "if applicant needs MED to do fingerprints $209.50"; "Employee license renewal $90 + $30 = $120"; "Conditional employee license $150 + $70 = $220" — MED — Replace an Employee or Owner License Badge, https://sbg.colorado.gov/med/replace-an-employee-or-owner-license-badge , accessed 1 Nov 2026. Submit via the ML1 web portal. "You can live anywhere in the U.S. and apply" and "the MED License/Badge is only valid in Colorado" — same page. CAUTION — 2026 CHANGE: those fingerprint-route fees describe the pre-5 January 2026 position. HB 25-1209 (enacted; applies to conduct on or after 5 January 2026) requires fingerprint-based criminal-history checks only for controlling beneficial owners and passive beneficial owners; other employees need only a name-based judicial record check — enacted summary, https://leg.colorado.gov/bills/hb25-1209 . The renewal $120 figure is NOT confirmed for 2026 (secondary reporting says biennial occupational renewal/fees were eliminated — secondary-only, so renewal is Verify for 2026). A February 2026 MED compliance tip is listed on MED's home page as "Discontinuation of Physical Employee Badges 2/18/2026" — MED home page, accessed 1 Nov 2026 — but the tip text itself was not opened in this audit, so physical-badge vs digital-credential mechanics are Verify. The current employee fingerprint / digital-credential position is Verify — the MED employee page text fetch predates the 5 January 2026 change and still describes fingerprint routes and a badge.
  • Court appointee / temporary appointee registration. CRS §44-10-401(3) (2025), same §44-10-401 source: prior to accepting a court appointment as receiver, personal representative, executor, administrator, guardian, conservator, trustee or similarly situated person to take possession of, operate, manage or control a licensed medical or retail marijuana business, the proposed appointee shall certify TO THE COURT that it is not prohibited from being issued a licence under §44-10-307(1); within the rule-established time frame the appointee shall notify the state and local licensing authorities and apply to the State Licensing Authority for a finding of suitability; on notification the Authority issues a temporary appointee registration effective as of the date of appointment. From 5 January 2026 (HB 25-1209 amendments to §44-10-401(3)(a), (b) and (d)) this scheme expressly covers retail businesses as well as medical businesses. Forms DR 8570e (Court Appointee Application, 7/28/2025) and DR 8571 (Court Appointee Operator) are on the MED forms page.
  • Responsible Vendor Provider registration. Form DR 8554 (1/30/19) on the MED forms page — a provider registration, not a business licence. Details Verify; no fee was shown in the forms list.

4.3 Cultivation tiers and classes — full plant-count structure

Medical — 3 classes (Class 1 confirmed; Classes 2–3 secondary-only): Class 1: 1–500 plants — confirmed in the June 2025 Rule 2-115 table. Class 2: 501–1,500 plants; Class 3: 1,501–3,000 plants. Source for class bands: secondary cultivation guide, accessed 1 Nov 2026 (bands are also the standard MED class definitions, but official rule text for Classes 2–3 was not legible in the fee table opened — Verify Class 2/3 bands against 1 CCR 212-3 Part 5 cultivation rules before publishing).

Retail — 5 tiers + Expanded Production Management: Tier 1: 1–1,800 plants — confirmed in Rule 2-115 June 2025 table; Tier 2: 1,801–3,600; Tier 3: 3,601–6,000; Tier 4: 6,001–10,200; Tier 5: 10,201–13,800; Expanded Production Management: each additional tier of 3,600 plants over Tier 5, at an additional fee per tier — described in November 2023 fee-rule revisions, Nov 2023 Fee Rule Revisions (PDF), https://sbg.colorado.gov/sites/sbg/files/documents/231109%201%20CCR%20212-3%20Final%20Fee%20Rule%20Revisions.pdf , accessed 1 Nov 2026, and secondary cultivation guide. Tier 2–5 dollar fees are Verify in the 5 Jan 2026 schedule.

Older schedules conflict and must not be mixed: e.g. an August 2024 emergency schedule reproduced in secondary reporting gave Tier 1 renewal $4,840 up to Tier 5 $18,700, while a 2023 schedule gave different application/licence splits. Do not quote either as current.

What a cultivation licence does NOT allow: a cultivator may sell wholesale only to the buyers listed in its statute — retail: licensed retail stores, retail products manufacturers, retail hospitality-and-sales businesses, or other retail cultivation facilities (§44-10-602(1), https://law.justia.com/codes/colorado/title-44/marijuana-regulation/article-10/part-6/section-44-10-602/ ); medical: licensed medical stores, medical products manufacturers, or other medical cultivation facilities (§44-10-502(1)). In particular a retail cultivator may NOT sell to a hospitality-only business (§44-10-609) — only to a hospitality-and-sales business (§44-10-610). It may not sell directly to consumers. Verify exact wholesale counterpart rules in §§44-10-502/602 and the Part 5/6 rules before relying on this paragraph for a transaction.

4.4 Other business licences in detail

Products Manufacturer (medical §44-10-503 / retail §44-10-603): manufactures edibles, concentrates, tinctures and other infused products. Medical manufacturers "are only authorized to wholesale their products to MED licensed Medical Marijuana Centers" (MED wording, §4.2). No separate packaging/labelling licence exists in §44-10-401; packaging and labelling are rule requirements on the manufacturer/store, not a licence class — that negative point is Verify before transactional reliance (it rests on the absence of such a class in §44-10-401).

Testing Facility (medical §44-10-504 / retail §44-10-604): potency and contaminants testing (and research for medical). MED's Licensed Facilities page states testing-facility lists "are updated as testing certifications are renewed" rather than monthly — see Part 5. Testing facilities must also hold relevant accreditation/certification — the accrediting body and certificate requirement are Part 11 territory and are not detailed here; Verify against 1 CCR 212-3 Part 4.

Transporter (medical §44-10-505 / retail §44-10-605): transport + temporary storage between licensed businesses. A transporter is not authorised to sell. (The original run's qualifier about a social-equity independent-delivery conversion is DELETED: there is no independent-delivery licence in §44-10-401 (2025) to convert to — see §4.5.)

Business Operator (medical §44-10-506 / retail §44-10-606): provides professional operational services to one or more licensed businesses. This is the "management company" licence; it does not itself authorise cultivation, manufacture or sale except through the businesses it operates, and the operator's own suitability/ownership rules apply.

Research and Development (§44-10-507): "grow, cultivate possess and transfer marijuana for use in research only." There is also an R&D Co-Location Permit (DR 8542) — see §4.6. A university or commercial R&D project needs to be matched to the correct instrument (licence vs co-location permit) — Verify which instrument applies to a given research site in 1 CCR 212-3 Part 2/3.

4.5 Hospitality, delivery and related privileges

Hospitality Business (§44-10-609, DR 8565e): consumption on the premises; no sales. The application form lists licence-type checkboxes including "Hospitality Business," "Retail Marijuana Hospitality and Sales Business," "Mobile Hospitality Business," and "Within a Retail Food Establishment" — DR 8565e, accessed 1 Nov 2026 (form text not re-opened in this audit — re-check DR 8565e before relying on the mobile / food-establishment checkboxes). A "separate application is required for each mobile licensed premises" — same form. Local opt-in for hospitality is a separate local decision (Part 3).

Hospitality and Sales Business (§44-10-610): sale and consumption on the same licensed premises. Fee in §4.2. By statute this facility cannot be mobile (see §4.2).

Delivery Permit (not a standalone business licence): a permit attached to a store or transporter licence, authorising delivery to consumers. Form DR 8569 "Delivery Permit (10/26/21)" is on the MED forms page. Fees are in conflict across versions and are Verify for the 5 Jan 2026 schedule: June 2023 fee rules show "Delivery Permit: $5,250.00" and "Delivery Permit Renewal: $2,650.00" — June 2023 Fee Rules (PDF), https://sbg.colorado.gov/sites/sbg/files/documents/230629%201%20CCR%20212-3%20Fee%20Rules_Final.pdf , accessed 1 Nov 2026; August 2024 emergency schedule shows "Delivery Permit $11,030.00 / Delivery Permit Renewal $5,570.00" — Aug 2024 Emergency Fee Schedule (PDF), https://med.colorado.gov/sites/med/files/documents/EmergencyRulesFeeSchedule_08082024.pdf , accessed 1 Nov 2026; a secondary 2025 summary shows $5,515 / $2,785. Do not quote any one of these as the current delivery-permit fee. Delivery is also subject to local opt-in and to delivery rules in §§44-10-501(11), 44-10-505(5), 44-10-601(13) and 44-10-605(5) — Verify current delivery-area, vehicle and $1-surcharge position: a 2023 bill summary states the $1 delivery surcharge was to be eliminated, but that was a bill summary, not a confirmed current-rule statement.

Independent Delivery Licence — NOT A CURRENT LICENCE TYPE. DO NOT PRESENT IT AS ONE. HB 23-1020 as introduced and as reengrossed in the House proposed: an Independent Delivery Licence for social-equity licensees, an Accelerator Independent Delivery Licence, an Accelerator Transporter Licence and an Accelerator Hospitality Business Licence — see reengrossed bill text at HB23-1020 reengrossed text (PDF), http://leg.colorado.gov/bill_files/93256/download , accessed 1 Nov 2026, and the reengrossed summary at https://leg.colorado.gov/bills/hb23-1020 . However: (a) current CRS §44-10-401 (2025) contains none of those four classes — https://law.justia.com/codes/colorado/title-44/marijuana-regulation/article-10/part-4/section-44-10-401/ ; (b) MED's Accelerator page lists only three participating retail types (cultivation, manufacturer, store). HB 23-1020's final enacted status could not be confirmed from the leg.colorado.gov crawl in this audit (the page shows the reengrossed summary with no Signed Act / Became Law footer) — that status is Verify on leg.colorado.gov bill history — but it does not affect the conclusion: whatever happened to HB 23-1020, its four proposed classes are NOT in current statute and must not be presented as current licence classes. The same applies to any claim that an independent-delivery licence is "repealed 1 Jan 2028" — that repeal date appears in the 2023 bill text, not in confirmed current statute, and is deleted as a current date. (The original run's "applications from 1 Mar 2024 / before 1 Jan 2028" dates were likewise proposal text only and are deleted.)

4.6 Permits attached to licences (permit-rule numbering Verify for 2026)

All are permits, not standalone business licences, each with a MED form. CORRECTED LINEAGE: the fee rule formerly numbered 2-205 (2023) is now Rule 2-115; what Rule 2-120 covers was not confirmed in this audit — numbering stays Verify against the 1 CCR 212-3 Part 2 table of contents.

  • Delivery Permit — DR 8569: See §4.5 conflict: $5,250 / $2,650 renewal (2023) vs $11,030 / $5,570 renewal (Aug 2024) vs $5,515 / $2,785 (secondary summary). Verify current fee in the 5 Jan 2026 schedule.
  • Centralized Distribution Permit — DR 8540e (6/23/2025): $50 (2023) vs $60 (Aug 2024). Allows a licensed business to use a central distribution point — exact privileges Verify in 1 CCR 212-3. (Note: §44-10-602 also references a centralized distribution permit, including a 90-day storage limit for concentrate/products held under it — that statutory reference does not confirm the fee.)
  • Off-Premises Storage Facility Permit — DR 8518e (6/18/2025): $2,000 (2023) vs $2,100 (Aug 2024). A separate "Transporter Off Premises Storage Permit" figure of $2,684 / $2,648 also appears in older material — Verify which, if either, is current.
  • R&D Co-Location Permit — DR 8542: $100 (2023) vs $110 (Aug 2024). Verify current fee.
  • Transition Permit — DR 8561: Fee not shown in material opened — Verify.
  • Plant Count Increase Request — DR 8504 (1/14/21): Not a licence; a cultivation plant-count change request. Fee Verify.
  • Outdoor Cultivation Contingency Plan Review Request — DR 8512 (12/23/21): Fee Verify.

4.7 Social equity programme — MED + OEDIT

Enabling legislation (MED page): HB 20-1424 "Established a 'Social Equity License' [and] Expanded the Accelerator Program" and SB 19-224 "Established the Accelerator Program" — MED Social Equity page, https://med.colorado.gov/social-equity , accessed 1 Nov 2026. The statute source notes confirm the lineage: article added by SB 19-224 (ch. 315, eff. 1 Jan 2020); social-equity subsections added by HB 20-1424 (ch. 184, eff. 14 Sept 2020) — §44-10-308 source note, https://law.justia.com/codes/colorado/title-44/marijuana-regulation/article-10/part-3/section-44-10-308/ . MED states: "A person who meets the eligibility criteria for a Social Equity Licensee can participate in the Division's 'Accelerator Program' or may apply to independently own and operate a Regulated Marijuana Business license" — same MED page (sentence re-confirmed on the page opened in this audit).

Eligibility — READ THE DATE FIRST. There are TWO tracks in §44-10-308, divided by the date of the application for a finding of suitability, and the original run's single list mixed them up:

  • OLD track — §44-10-308(4), for suitability applications on or before 1 February 2025 ONLY (§44-10-308(4)(b)). A natural person qualifies if, in addition to any rule criteria: (I) is a Colorado resident; (II) has not been the beneficial owner of a licence subject to disciplinary or legal action from the state resulting in revocation of a licence under Article 10; (III) has demonstrated at least one of: (A) resided for at least 15 years between 1980 and 2010 in a census tract designated by OEDIT as an Opportunity Zone or designated as a "Disproportionate Impacted Area"; (B) the applicant or the applicant's parent, legal guardian, sibling, spouse, child, or minor in their guardianship was arrested for a marijuana offence, convicted of a marijuana offence, or was subject to civil asset forfeiture related to a marijuana investigation; or (C) household income in the year prior to application did not exceed an amount determined by rule; and (IV) the social equity licensee, or collectively one or more social equity licensees, holds at least 51% of the beneficial ownership of the regulated marijuana business licence. This is the list the OEDIT page still shows (OEDIT Cannabis Business Office, https://oedit.colorado.gov/cannabis-business-office , crawl 30 Apr 2026) — the OEDIT page is STALE against the statute and must not be quoted as the current criteria.
  • CURRENT track — §44-10-308(6), for suitability applications on or after 1 February 2025 (§44-10-308(8)(a)), added by SB 24-076 (ch. 410, eff. 7 Aug 2024). A natural person qualifies if, in addition to any rule criteria: (a) has not been the beneficial owner of a licence subject to disciplinary or civil action from the State Licensing Authority resulting in revocation of a licence under Article 10; (b) has demonstrated at least one of: (I) resided (A) for at least any five years of the thirty-year period prior to application (and for which data is available) in a census tract designated by OEDIT as an Opportunity Zone or designated as a Disproportionate Impacted Area; or (B) for at least any five of the thirty years prior to application, in housing with funding under §8 or §9 of the federal United States Housing Act of 1937; or (C) for at least any five years between 1980 and 2021, in housing with funding from federal low-income housing tax credits, Colorado affordable housing tax credits, or any federal/state/local programme restricting maximum rents for low- or moderate-income natural persons under a monitored use restriction; (II) the applicant or the applicant's spouse, parent, or legal guardian was arrested for AND convicted of a marijuana offence; (III) the applicant's sibling or child or a minor in the applicant's guardianship was arrested for or convicted of a marijuana offence, AND (A) that person resided in a Disproportionate Impacted Area for five years between 1980 and 2021, OR (B) that person received assistance from at least one of the programmes in (IV) for at least five years between 1980 and 2021; (IV) the applicant received assistance from at least one of the following for at least five of the ten years prior to application: (A) the low-income energy assistance programme (Title 40, Art. 8.7); (B) SNAP (Title 26, Art. 2, Part 3); (C) TANF (§26-2-703(19)); (D) WIC (42 U.S.C. §1786); or (E) the Colorado Medical Assistance Act (Title 25.5, Arts. 4–6); and (c) holds at least 51% of the beneficial ownership of a regulated marijuana business licence alone or collectively with at least one other social equity licensee. NOTE: the current track does NOT list Colorado residency as a criterion, and does NOT contain a standalone "50% of state median income" test — both belonged to the old track (and the income test in the old track was "an amount determined by rule," with 50% of median income being the OEDIT-page formulation). The secondary "1 April 2025" effective date reported in the original run is WRONG and is deleted: the statutory dividing line is 1 February 2025, keyed to the suitability-application date.

Licence-count cap (RESOLVED — the original run's truncated sentence). Under §44-10-308(7), for purposes of subsection (6), an applicant is not eligible to be a social equity licensee if the applicant is a controlling beneficial owner of MORE THAN THREE retail marijuana store licences, medical marijuana store licences, retail marijuana cultivation facility licences, or medical marijuana cultivation facility licences, unless each listed licence for which the applicant is a CBO is itself a social equity licence. Co-located retail + medical store licences, or co-located retail + medical cultivation licences, constitute ONE licence for this count. This is a social-equity eligibility cap, not a general statewide ownership cap (see §4.9).

Revocation bar (narrowed). The bar is on having been the BENEFICIAL OWNER of a licence subject to disciplinary or legal/civil action from the state/SLA resulting in revocation — not on merely having "had a licence revoked" in any capacity. See (4)(a)(II) and (6)(a) above.

Additional eligibility conditions in MED forms: the State Licensing Authority "will not deny an application for a Social Equity License or a related request for a Finding of Suitability on the sole basis of a marijuana conviction" — MED Social Equity page and Accelerator page, both accessed 1 Nov 2026; confirmed in statute at §44-10-401(6), same §44-10-401 source. DR 8520's social-equity affirmation requires that "the applicant, or collectively one or more proposed Social Equity Licensees, will hold at least fifty-one percent (51%) ownership of a Regulated Marijuana Business" — DR 8520, accessed 1 Nov 2026 (consistent with §44-10-308(4)(a)(IV) and (6)(c)).

MED also provides a Disproportionate Impacted Area tool built with the Department of Public Safety and the Department of Local Affairs' State Demography Office (MED social-equity material, search result) — tool URL was not exposed in the text fetch; Verify from the MED social-equity page.

How to apply (MED, current pages): (1) FIRST submit a Natural Person Finding of Suitability Application (DR 8520), with fingerprints via in-person appointment ("Regulated Business License Social Equity Program Applicant") or a Colorado State-Approved Third-Party Fingerprint Provider — MED Accelerator Program — Social Equity Licensee, https://med.colorado.gov/social-equity/accelerator-program-social-equity-licensee , accessed 1 Nov 2026. (Note: CBO suitability fingerprints are fingerprint-based; the HB 25-1209 name-based change in §4.9 applies to other employees, not to CBO suitability.) (2) On approval, MED sends an approval letter. "You have two years from the date of the letter to apply for a Regulated Marijuana Business License by submitting the Regulated Marijuana Business - Social Equity Program Application (DR 8523)" — same page. (An older MED presentation said suitability expired after one year — the two-year figure on the current Accelerator page prevails; the one-year figure is superseded and must not be used. NOTE: the two-year window was NOT re-verified from the page text opened in this audit — Verify it on a live re-open of the Accelerator page before relying on it.) (3) Then choose: Independent Operator or Accelerator Licensee — MED Social Equity page. (4) Online payment of reduced fees is, per MED, "available only for the Finding of Suitability Request for a Controlling Beneficial Owner – Natural Person – Social Equity application. For all other Social Equity applications, please use the hard copy applications" submitted to MED, 1707 Cole Blvd. Suite 300, Lakewood, CO 80401 — MED Social Equity page (address + online-payment limit re-confirmed on the page opened in this audit; this is a published office address, not a personal contact).

Accelerator Programme — what it is: "The Accelerator Program allows individuals who may have faced barriers to entry in Colorado's retail (adult-use) regulated marijuana industry to own and operate a marijuana business license as part of an agreed-upon partnership with an existing marijuana business that has been endorsed by the MED as an 'Accelerator-Endorsed Licensee.'" "The Accelerator-Endorsed Licensee provides capital and/or technical support." "The Social Equity Licensee may apply to operate as a Store, Manufacturer or Cultivation on the same Licensed Premises or on a separate Licensed Premises provided by the Accelerator-Endorsed Licensee." — MED social-equity material, via MED Social Equity page, accessed 1 Nov 2026, and Accelerator page. Participating types (MED Accelerator page, current): exactly three — "Retail Marijuana Cultivation, Retail Marijuana Product Manufacturers and Retail Marijuana Stores" — under MED Rule series 3-1105 to 3-1115 (rule-series numbers not re-verified in this audit — Verify). Accelerator Endorsement Application: DR 8514. Finding an endorsed host: MED directs applicants to the Licensee Look-Up Tool, Facility Search page, choosing "Accelerator Store," "Accelerator Cultivations," or "Accelerator Mfg." — Accelerator page (tool labels not re-verified — Verify). See Part 5 for that tool.

Accelerator-endorsed tax credit — secondary only, Verify: up to $50,000 for an accelerator-endorsed licensee hosting and supporting a social-equity licensee for at least 12 consecutive months, reported in secondary 2026 guides. No official DOR/OEDIT figure was opened in this run; do not publish as an official amount.

Reduced fees — secondary August 2024 schedule, Verify for 2026: MED's current page confirms only that "Social Equity Applicants and Licensees may be eligible for reduced fees" — MED Social Equity page, accessed 1 Nov 2026 (sentence re-confirmed on the page opened in this audit), with no amounts on the page text opened. Secondary reporting of the August 2024 schedule gives reduced licence fees (no application fee) of: store $2,840; products manufacturer $2,520; cultivation Tier 1 $2,520; testing $1,370; transporter $1,680; operator $1,790 — secondary, accessed 1 Nov 2026 (that source itself notes MED lists a newer schedule effective 5 Jan 2026 that it could not read). Treat all six figures as Verify for 2026. Accelerator and Accelerator-Endorsement Holder applications carried no fee in a 2023 MED fee-setting presentation — MED Fee-Setting Presentation (PDF, June 2023), https://med.colorado.gov/sites/med/files/documents/230605_DOR_MED_Fee_Setting_Stakeholder_Presentation.pdf , accessed 1 Nov 2026 — also Verify for 2026.

Social-equity counts — secondary, dated, NO current count confirmed: "99 approved [social equity licensees] as of April 1, 2025" and "84 active social equity licensees and 119 pending" as of January 2023 (HB 23-1020 fiscal note) — secondary reporting, accessed 1 Nov 2026. No official MED social-equity count for late 2026 was opened; Verify. Do not present either figure as a current count. The original run's note that "MED is required to report annually to the legislature" rested on the HB 23-1020 bill summary (proposal text) and is NOT cited here as current law — check the current statute for any reporting duty before asserting it.

4.9 Ownership, transfer, renewal, suitability — cross-cutting rules

Licences are not freely transferable. CRS §44-10-312(1) (2025): "A state or local license granted under the provisions of this article 10 is not transferable except as provided in this section, but this section does not prevent a change of location as provided in section 44-10-313 (13)" — Justia — §44-10-312, https://law.justia.com/codes/colorado/title-44/marijuana-regulation/article-10/part-3/section-44-10-312/ , accessed 1 Nov 2026 (verbatim, re-confirmed).

CBO transfer: "For a transfer of ownership involving a controlling beneficial owner, a license holder shall apply to the state and local licensing authorities on forms prepared and furnished by the state licensing authority" and the authorities "shall consider only the requirements of this article 10, any rules … and any other local restrictions" — same source. Form: DR 8535e Change of Controlling Beneficial Owner Application.

PBO change: "For a transfer of ownership involving a passive beneficial owner, the license holder shall notify the state licensing authority on forms … within forty-five days to the extent disclosure is required by section 44-10-309" — same source. Form DR 8563 covers changes exempt from a full change of ownership.

Publicly traded / 10% rule: a person that becomes a controlling beneficial owner of a publicly traded marijuana business, or that becomes a beneficial owner (directly or indirectly through a controlling beneficial owner) of 10% or more of a publicly traded marijuana business, "must disclose the information required by section 44-10-309 and apply … for a finding of suitability or exemption … within forty-five days" after becoming such a controlling beneficial owner — §44-10-312(4), same source. QII threshold is MORE THAN 30% (DR 8557 / Rule 1-115 definitions, see §4.2; confirmed by HB 19-1090 summary, https://leg.colorado.gov/bills/hb19-1090 ).

Ownership caps — corrected. No GENERAL statewide cap on the number of licences per owner, and no general statewide ban on vertical integration, was confirmed in official material opened — but that negative finding is Verify against §§44-10-307/309/310 and 1 CCR 212-3 Part 2 before publishing a cap claim, and it must now be stated alongside the cap that DOES exist: the social-equity eligibility cap in §44-10-308(7) (more than three store/cultivation licences, with the co-location and social-equity exceptions — see §4.7). Denver-specific limits are Part 3.

Residency — RESOLVED, do not assert the old rule. The former rule in §44-10-308(3)(a)(I) — "All natural persons with day-to-day operational control over the business must be Colorado residents" — was REPEALED effective 5 January 2026 by HB 25-1209 (§44-10-308(3)(a)(II); HB 25-1209 §21(1) applies the act to conduct on or after 5 January 2026) — §44-10-308 (2025), same §44-10-308 source. The HB 25-1209 enacted summary likewise states the act "repeals provisions that prohibit a person from … [h]aving day-to-day operational control over the business if the person isn't a Colorado resident" — https://leg.colorado.gov/bills/hb25-1209 . Older secondary hospitality guides stating a two-year Colorado residency requirement are therefore superseded. The MED employee page still states "You can live anywhere in the U.S. and apply" for employees — consistent with the repeal. (HB 25-1209's signing date in June 2025, reported secondarily, was not confirmed from the leg.colorado.gov crawl in this audit and is not asserted here; the 5 January 2026 effective date IS confirmed.)

Employee background checks — RESOLVED in the same way. HB 25-1209 (enacted summary, same leg.colorado.gov source): "Current law requires all applicants for an employee identification card to obtain a fingerprint-based criminal history check. The act requires only controlling beneficial owners and passive beneficial owners to obtain a fingerprint-based criminal history record check, and other employees must merely obtain a name-based judicial record check." The secondary claim that "from 5 Jan 2026 fingerprints are no longer required for employee licences" is therefore confirmed in substance as enacted law (for non-CBO/PBO employees); badge/digital-credential mechanics remain Verify (see §4.2).

Federal immigration warning (MED, on every application hub): "holding a Marijuana Business or Occupational License may have adverse Federal immigration consequences" — MED Licenses and Fees page, https://med.colorado.gov/licenses-and-fees , accessed 1 Nov 2026 (re-confirmed on the page opened in this audit).

Renewal: RMB Renewal Application DR 8529; CBO Renewal DR 8516 / DR 8581e (Owner Equity variant); Employee Renewal DR 8527e. Renewal term is 2 years at state level per SB 24-076 (§4.1). Exact renewal windows, late-renewal and reinstatement rules are Verify — a "Request for Regulated Business License Reinstatement Form" exists on the MED forms page but its conditions were not opened. Employee renewal fees for 2026 are separately Verify (see §4.2).

Change of location, surrender, revocation: governed by §§44-10-313/314 and MED rules; not detailed here because no official text for those sections was opened in this run — follow-up, not a gap to fill by inference.

4.10 Whether applications are open — answer

Yes, on the evidence opened, with the local-approval qualifier: MED's forms page lists current business, owner, employee, hospitality, delivery, storage and distribution applications with 2025 form dates, and MED's home page lists a July 2026 unified-application bulletin — i.e. the state intake is operating, not closed or lottery-gated at state level. Qualifier that must travel with the answer: MED will not accept a new business application for a jurisdiction that has not advised MED it is accepting applications, and MED will not make a state licence usable without local approval; many jurisdictions ban or cap types. An application is not permission to operate (DR 8565 wording, §4.1). No application window, deadline or lottery is stated on any MED page opened (negative finding scoped to pages opened). If a local jurisdiction runs a competitive / lottery process (e.g. Denver's former processes), that is a local rule, not a MED statewide window — Part 3.

Social-equity suitability intake: open via DR 8520 first, then DR 8523 — with the two-year window from the suitability approval letter flagged Verify (see §4.7). CORRECTED: the original run's open question — whether MED is issuing new social-equity licences without interruption, on the basis of a 2023 bill summary mentioning a temporary bar — is RESOLVED and deleted. The bar in HB 23-1020's introduced text ran only "beginning on the effective date of House Bill 23-1020 through February 29, 2024," and §44-10-308 (2025) contains no bar on issuing new social-equity licences. The bar is long expired on its own terms and is not a current restriction.

4.11 Intoxicating hemp and hemp products — MED / CDPHE licences (cross-reference to Part 7; full detail belongs in Part 7)

This is a summary only, to avoid duplicating Part 7. Do not treat hemp as a MED marijuana licence.

Split jurisdiction (official): "The Colorado Department of Agriculture's Hemp Program regulates only the cultivation of hemp. The Department also administers a certified seed program. The Hemp Program does not have jurisdiction over the processing, sale or distribution of hemp" — CDA — Hemp, https://ag.colorado.gov/plants/hemp , accessed 1 Nov 2026 (re-confirmed on the page opened in this audit). "Hemp farms are licensed and regulated by the Colorado Department of Agriculture, once the crop leaves the farm it is [CDPHE's] responsibility to oversee the manufacturing, packaging, warehousing, and distribution of hemp products" — CDPHE — Hemp Food, https://cdphe.colorado.gov/dehs/hemp-food , accessed 1 Nov 2026 (re-confirmed). "CDPHE does not register operations that are producing marijuana infused products. You need to contact the Department of Revenue, Marijuana Enforcement Division" — same CDPHE page (re-confirmed).

CDPHE hemp registrations (not MED licences): Hemp Product Registration (Not Safe Harbor) and Safe Harbor Hemp Registration, for manufacturers and warehouses of hemp foods, dietary supplements and cosmetics. "All applications require a non-refundable $100.00 application fee, payable by check or money order" and the department then invoices "the remaining registration fee" before issuing the registration; "Registration is specific to the owner and location. It is not transferable or prorated" — CDPHE hemp page (all re-confirmed on the page opened in this audit). New nuance from the same page, flagged for Part 7 (not over-interpreted here): the CDPHE page states "Due to the change in legislation renewals will no longer be possible" and that safe-harbor applications need an attestation plus a third-party audit mailed with the application — Verify what legislation/change this refers to before relying on it.

Governing rules: "Colorado Hemp Products and Safe Harbor Hemp Products Regulations, 6 CCR 1010-24, Adopted by the Board of Health on November 15, 2023; effective, January 14, 2024" — same page (re-confirmed).

The remaining registration fee amount(s) were not on the page opened — Verify in CDPHE registration guidance (secondary summaries give $60 / $300 by gross sales for non-Safe-Harbor and $1,500 for Safe Harbor; do not publish those as official until CDPHE confirms).

CDA hemp registrations (not MED licences): Commercial and R&D cultivation registrations via the Hemp Online Portal (HOP), CDA Hemp Online Portal — https://cda.state.co.us/HOP — accessed via search 1 Nov 2026. Fee figures in secondary material ($500 base + $5/acre outdoor or $3 per 1,000 sq ft indoor; older rule text $200 + $1/acre) conflict and are Verify — the CDA hemp page opened states only "Application Fees are Non-Refundable" with no amounts (re-confirmed). Colorado runs its own USDA-approved state plan (see Part 5, USDA entry), not the USDA direct programme — this Part 4 audit did NOT open the USDA/CDA plan document, so this sentence is a cross-reference only and stays flagged: confirm from the Part 5/Part 7 plan source before relying on it here.

MED intoxicating-hemp licence — no such standalone licence confirmed. SB 23-271 (2023) created a framework under which CDPHE regulates hemp products and MED regulates intoxicating / potentially intoxicating cannabinoid compounds, with products containing potentially intoxicating compounds or intoxicating cannabinoids to be produced/distributed/sold only by a person licensed by MED for that compound — bill summary, leg.colorado.gov — SB23-271, https://leg.colorado.gov/bills/sb23-271 , accessed 1 Nov 2026. SB 23-271 was APPROVED by the Governor on 7 June 2023 and EFFECTIVE 7 June 2023 (same page). No MED "intoxicating hemp licence" class appears in CRS §44-10-401 or on MED's Licensed Facilities list opened in the original run. Whether MED has since created such a licence by rule, or whether intoxicating cannabinoids are handled solely inside existing marijuana licences, is Verify — Part 7 must resolve this from current 1 CCR 212-3 and any MED intoxicating-cannabinoid rule, and must not assume a new licence class exists.

Federal hemp dates: the federal dates in the commission (PL 119-37 §781 effective 12 Nov 2026, limited by PL 119-103 §2019 until 11 Dec 2026; USDA DEA-lab enforcement delayed to 31 Dec 2026) interact with Colorado's SB 23-271 framework, but no Colorado agency response to those specific 2026 federal dates was located in this run — Verify / Part 7 follow-up. Note these federal dates fall after this audit's 1 November 2026 date, so no pre-date Colorado response could resolve the interaction. Part 4 states no Colorado response and must not invent one.

Hemp definition (CDA, official): "Hemp means the plant species Cannabis sativa L. and any part of the plant, whether growing or not, containing a delta-9 tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) concentration of no more than three-tenths of one percent (0.3%) on a dry weight basis. Under State and Federal law, the CDA tests for total THC through the process of post-decarboxylation" — CDA Hemp page, accessed 1 Nov 2026 (re-confirmed).

4.12 Estimated startup costs — NON-OFFICIAL ESTIMATES ONLY, clearly marked

No Colorado agency publishes an official startup-cost estimate. Everything in this section is secondary / non-official and must be labelled as such in any publication.

Dispensary (non-official, conflicting ranges): $150,000 to ~$2,000,000 — secondary 2025 guide, accessed 1 Nov 2026 (says the range "covers the annual advertising fee, renting fee, license application fees, yearly staffing, and security"). A second non-official 2026 guide gives a narrower Colorado range of $150,000–$500,000 — secondary, accessed 1 Nov 2026. The $1.5m spread between sources is itself the finding: do not publish a single "cost to open" figure.

Components inside those non-official ranges (same sources, non-official): annual payroll $100,000–$250,000; professional/legal ~$50,000/year (first guide); rent $5,000–$30,000/month and equipment $50,000–$100,000 in older secondary material (stale — do not use without re-checking). Wholesale flower $750–$850/lb in the 2025 guide — a market price, not a fee, and already dated.

What IS official and must be used instead of an estimate for budgeting: state fees in §4.2 (June 2025 table, Verify for 2026), local portion in §4.2, plus the applicant's own local licence fees (Part 3 / Part 5 local records — e.g. Fort Collins publishes its own fee schedule, see Part 5), Metrc/tag costs, testing, security, premises, insurance and working capital — none of which has an official statewide total.

Cultivation / manufacturing startup totals: No credible non-official Colorado-specific total was found that is worth quoting. Do not invent one. The only usable official anchors are the tier/class fees in §4.2–4.3 and the statement that a cultivation licence fee rises with plant count.

End of corrected Part 4.

Last audited: 1 November 2026.

5.2 MED Licensed Facilities lists — detail

URL: MED Licensed Facilities — accessed 1 Nov 2026 (page crawl 5 Mar 2026). Holder type: MED-licensed medical and retail facilities, by licence type (the 17 classes in §4.2 — 7 medical, §§44-10-501–507, and 10 retail, §§44-10-601–610, as listed on the page itself). Format / access: a web page that states "All lists are updated monthly, except the testing facilities which are updated as testing certifications are renewed" and links an "Archived Licensee List". The text fetch does not expose the underlying list files — their file names, formats (PDF vs spreadsheet) and direct URLs cannot be stated from the fetch and are not guessed here. This is the single most important Part 5 gap: a live-browser pass over this page is needed to capture each list's direct link and file name. The page's own licence-type descriptions are quoted in §4.2. Fields available: not stated on the page text opened. The data.colorado.gov MED dataset (§5.4) is described as containing "license information and addresses," which suggests name, licence type, address and status are the core fields — Verify field list from the actual list file once its link is captured. Limitations: (1) monthly, so intra-month openings/closures/suspensions are missed; (2) testing facilities on a different cycle; (3) licensed ≠ operating (local licence still required); (4) archived list exists but its coverage dates were not stated in the fetch.

Note (MED's own wording, retained as a flag, not silently corrected): the MED page's Accelerator Cultivator description says the holder operates "a retail marijuana product manufacturing operation" — see §5.15 gap (14). Flag to MED / note in publication; do not silently correct it.

5.3 MED Licensee Lookup Tool — detail

Access route: via the Licensed Facilities page ("Licensee Information and Lookup Tool") and directly referenced on MED's Accelerator page and Employee Renewal page ("the status of a MED license can also be verified by using the Licensee Lookup Tool"). How it works (MED Accelerator page instructions, accessed 1 Nov 2026; page crawl 22 Feb 2026): "To obtain a list of Accelerator Endorsed Licensees, visit the MED Licensee Look-Up Tool" — go to the Facility Search page; in the Search Criteria box choose the licence type (e.g. Accelerator Store / Accelerator Cultivations / Accelerator Mfg.); complete the "I am not a robot" check; click Search. Format: interactive search by name, address or licence number (per older MED guidance — Verify: the older guidance was not opened in this audit). No bulk download, no export button is stated anywhere in material opened. Treat as search-only. Fields / limitations: record-level verification only; it does not give a statewide count, and a search that returns nothing does not prove a business is unlicensed (name-variant / trade-name vs legal-name mismatch is a known trap — search by legal business name, not trade name, per secondary testing-lab guidance; Verify that advice against MED's own search help).

5.5 MED enforcement, discipline and advisories — detail

There is no single published MED disciplinary-action database in material opened. What exists is fragmented across three channels, and that fragmentation must be stated:

2025 Regulatory & Enforcement Activity report (annual aggregate). MED press release 19 Feb 2026: "The Colorado Marijuana Enforcement Division (MED) conducted 469 underage compliance checks in 2025 … The compliance rate on those checks was 99%"; "the 26-person MED field investigations team investigated 2,829 licenses, or about 235 licenses per month"; "846 licenses were subject to an administrative action … and about $1.08 million in fines were assessed"; "issuing 17 Health & Safety Advisories in 2025"; "more than 160 product safety investigations in 2025"; "18 industry bulletins, three compliance tips, and one position statement" — all confirmed verbatim in the press release. The release states: "The 2025 MED Regulatory & Enforcement Activity report can be found on the MED website's home page under Helpful Links." The report PDF's exact file name/URL was not exposed in the text fetch — Verify from the MED home page. Secondary reporting of the same report (for cross-check only, not as the primary source) adds: "338 notices of denial, 45 orders to show cause, 27 orders of summary suspension and 57 stipulations, agreements and orders in 2025" and "total fines reaching $1,082,000" — secondary, 23 Mar 2026, accessed 1 Nov 2026. Use the MED press-release figures as official; use the Herald's breakdown only as "reported from the MED report" until the report PDF itself is opened. (Audit note: 338+45+27+57=467 orders vs 846 licences subject to action is not a contradiction — different units, orders vs licences.)

Health & Safety Advisories (product recalls in substance). Two URLs must be given because the archive moved: (a) current 2026 list on MED's home page (to 13 Oct 2026, confirmed on the home page crawled 20 Oct 2026): Staycon LLC dba Craft (pesticides) 13 Oct 2026; expanded Staycon/Craft 8 Oct 2026; StayCon update — adverse health events 1 Oct 2026; StayCon 25 Sept 2026; CC Brands LLC 15 Sept 2026; Navajo Management LLC 10 Sept 2026; Sofa King Medicinal Wellness Products (updated 21 Aug 2026, expanded 31 July 2026, 2 July 2026); Colorado Medical Processing dba Colorado's Best Dabs (expanded 31 July 2026, 15 July 2026); Workhorse Global / WH Acoma 1 June 2026; and others back to Jan 2026 (Natural Alternatives for Health Corp. 12 May 2026; Arkansas Valley Organics 5 May 2026; Levels IV Inc 14 Apr 2026; J&C Corp dba Juicy Concentrates 1 Apr 2026; David Jackson LLC dba Timberline Extracts 20 Mar 2026; Double C Farms LLC 26 Feb 2026; RMRC LTD dba High Octane 26 Feb 2026; HG LTD dba Higher Grade 13 Feb 2026; Sweetwater Group LLC 6 Feb 2026; Karing Kind LLC 22 Jan 2026; Dutch Botanicals dba Morganic Concentrates 22 Jan 2026; MBF Labs dba My brothers flower 22 Jan 2026; HG LTD dba Higher Grade 22 Jan 2026; Egozi Ventures LLC 9 Jan 2026; Rotation LLC 8 Jan 2026). (b) Archived list: sbg.colorado.gov — Health and Safety Advisories, accessed 1 Nov 2026 (crawl 26 Oct 2024; lists 2024 advisories to July 2024, then 2023, 2022, 2021, 2020, 2019, 2018, 2017, 2016). Its stated purpose: "In the instance the marijuana or marijuana products have tested positive for contaminants (such as unauthorized pesticides), the MED issues a Health and Safety Advisory … in order to warn the public not to consume any product they may have purchased." Format: web list; each advisory is an individual document. No bulk CSV, no closure/withdrawal list found. Individual discipline (stipulations / orders to show cause / summary suspensions): no consolidated public list was located. "Monthly updated list of approved sources for hemp manufacturing and storage facilities that are active." The list's file format and direct URL were not exposed in the text fetch — Verify from the CDPHE hemp page (live-browser pass). This list is the closest thing to a public CDPHE hemp-facility register, but it is an approved-source list for manufacturers, not a full register of every hemp product or every registrant, and Safe Harbor vs non-Safe-Harbor status must be checked per facility.

CDPHE registration applications (for Part 7, noted here as data sources): "Hemp Product Registration (Not Safe Harbor)," "Safe Harbor Hemp Registration," "Safe Harbor Attestation Form," "Commissary Agreement," "Hemp registration application guidance" — all linked from the CDPHE hemp page (confirmed verbatim on the page). These are application forms, not a public list.

CDA Hemp Online Portal (HOP): CDA Hemp Online Portal — accessed via search 1 Nov 2026; portal fetch 1 Nov 2026 confirms the structure. The portal home page lists "Qualified Hemp testing facilities" (maintained by CDPHE certification), "Apply to be an Authorized Sampler," and "Find Authorized Hemp Samplers — Get a list of authorized samplers who are certified to sample hemp and deliver samples to a qualified lab" (with a "List of Authorized Hemp Samplers" link). The portal itself is an application/payment system for growers, not a public grower list. No public CDA grower-registration list was located — that absence must be stated, not filled by the voluntary Networking Directory.

CDA Hemp Networking Directory: CDA Hemp Networking Directory, accessed 1 Nov 2026 (crawl Mar 2026). "The Hemp Networking Directory is where Colorado growers, manufacturers, processors, and consumers connect … The Colorado Hemp Directory is currently accepting listings. Would you like to have your business listed? Add your information below!" Voluntary, opt-in, self-submitted — it is not a registry, not complete, and must never be cited as a registrant count.

CDA hemp programme contact (for records requests): hemp@state.co.us; Hemp Program Manager 303-869-9082; Registration and Records Coordinator 303-869-9055 — CDA — Hemp, accessed 1 Nov 2026 (agency programme contacts as published; role titles only — the CDA page also names the post-holders, and those personal names are not reproduced here). Records requests are the practical route to a grower list if one is disclosable — Verify disclosability; grower location data may be restricted for law-enforcement / security reasons and that restriction, if any, should be recorded rather than assumed. CDA scope note (confirmed on the same page): the Hemp Program "regulates only the cultivation of hemp" and "does not have jurisdiction over the processing, sale or distribution of hemp."

5.10 Local licence records — detail (examples only; no statewide list)

No statewide local-licence list was found. MED's Licensed Facilities page is state licences only. Each city/county is its own source. Two verified examples show the pattern: Denver: Department of Licensing and Consumer Protection, Online Permitting and Licensing Center. Denver's marijuana page lists the licences/permits the city issues (including medical and retail delivery permits, hospitality business licences including mobile premises, and retail hospitality and sales licences) and states most applications must be submitted online, with testing facilities and medical R&D facilities still on paper — Denver — New Marijuana Application, accessed 1 Nov 2026 (page fetch 1 Nov 2026 confirms department, portal, paper exceptions, and the licence/permit list). Denver's "Licensed establishment" record system (record IDs in YEAR-LE-####### format, e.g. 2020-LE-1234567) is a separate establishment record, not the licence itself — Denver — Licensed Establishment, accessed 1 Nov 2026 (format confirmed verbatim on the page). Fort Collins: City Clerk's marijuana licence application-fee page, with 2025 and 2026 fees by type (e.g. medical store application fee 2026 $2,253; medical store licence fee 2026 $1,126; social-equity fees shown as "Email" — rate not published on the page, Verify with the Clerk; transfer fees) — Fort Collins — Marijuana License Application Fees, accessed 1 Nov 2026 (page fetch 1 Nov 2026 confirms the $2,253 / $1,126 figures and the "Email" social-equity entries). Fort Collins fees are Fort Collins only and must not be generalised. General rule for Part 3 / Part 5 cross-reference: for every other jurisdiction, the source is that jurisdiction's clerk / licensing office and its code/ordinance — there is no MED-published "jurisdictions allowing each business type" list in material opened. If Part 3 claims such a MED list exists, that claim is Verify — the MED pages opened here do not contain it.

5.11 Secretary of State business entity search — detail

What it is: the Colorado Secretary of State's Business Database Search — a filing registry for all Colorado business entities (LLCs, corporations, partnerships, nonprofits, trade names, trademarks). It is not a marijuana-licence search and a filing proves nothing about marijuana licensure or lawful operation. URLs — conflict, Verify current: secondary guides give two URLs: https://www.coloradosos.gov/ucc/pages/biz/bizSearch.xhtml and coloradosos.gov/biz/BusinessEntityCriteriaExt.do — both via secondary sources accessed 1 Nov 2026. The official SOS search page itself was not opened in this run; do not publish either URL as verified until it is opened. Secondary descriptions agree on: free, no login, search by business name, trademark, trade name, ID number or document number; results show ID number, business name, filing event, current status, entity type and formation date; entity records show status, principal office and registered agent. All field claims in this paragraph are secondary until the SOS page is opened. Limitations: does not cover sole proprietors without a trade name; does not cover local licences; does not certify lawful operation (SOS's own disclaimer as reported in secondary sources).

5.12 Tribal records — detail

Finding (corrected in this audit): the USDA AMS plan table (updated 17 Feb 2026) DOES list a Colorado-tribe hemp plan — "Ute Mountain Ute | Approved Plan (pdf)" ( = approved under the final rule effective 22 Mar 2021) — USDA AMS — State and Tribal Plan Review. No Southern Ute plan appears in the full tribal table. That resolves the original's "snippet did not list a Colorado-tribe plan, but the full table was not opened" — the full table has now been opened. LIMIT: a USDA-approved tribal hemp plan is not a cannabis/marijuana licence list. No public tribal cannabis/marijuana licence list was located in this run for the Southern Ute Indian Tribe or the Ute Mountain Ute Tribe, and no tribal regulator's licence database was opened. Status for marijuana licences: Unavailable / Verify. This must be carried into Part 10, not filled by inference. Do not cite the MED lists as covering tribal licences: MED licences are state licences; a tribal licence, if one exists, would be a separate instrument.

5.13 USDA hemp records for Colorado — detail

Colorado's plan status (official): USDA AMS "List of USDA-approved Hemp Plans" table: "Colorado | CO Approved Plan (pdf)" with " Plan approved under the final rule which took effect March 22, 2021" and "Updated February 17, 2026" — USDA AMS — State and Tribal Plan Review, accessed 1 Nov 2026 (table fetch 1 Nov 2026 confirms all three items verbatim). Consequence: Colorado growers are licensed under the state plan, NOT under a USDA Hemp Producer License. USDA producer licences are, per AMS FAQ, "invalid once the State or Tribe begins to issue licenses under their own jurisdiction."

Plan PDF: linked from the AMS table as "CO Approved Plan (pdf)." The direct PDF URL was not exposed in the search snippet and is not guessed — access via the AMS table link.

Hemp Public Search Tool / HeMP Law Enforcement Search Tool: AMS FAQ states "Information on licensees in your area can be obtained through the Hemp Public Search Tool" (confirmed verbatim). The public tool's coverage of state-plan producers and its field list were not verified in this run — Verify before citing it as a Colorado grower source. The law-enforcement tool access route (via farmbill.hemp@usda.gov and Login.gov/eAuthentication) was not found in the fetched FAQ text — Verify against AMS documentation before citing access steps; do not conflate it with the grower-contact page's separate use of Farmbill.Hemp@usda.gov for tribal/USDA-managed enquiries. The law-enforcement tool is restricted and is not a public data source.

AMS FOIA Reading Room — USDA licensees PDF: "USDA Hemp Producer Licensees (pdf) – Updated April 14, 2026" — USDA AMS FOIA Reading Room, accessed 1 Nov 2026 (confirmed verbatim; direct PDF URL not exposed in text fetch — link label only). Limitation: this lists USDA-managed producers only. Because Colorado has its own approved plan, Colorado state-plan growers will not be in this PDF (except any legacy USDA licence, if any). Do not use it as a Colorado grower count.

Colorado contact on AMS grower list: ag.colorado.gov/plants/hemp; hemp@state.co.us; (303) 869-9050 — USDA AMS Grower Contact List, accessed 1 Nov 2026 (page fetch 1 Nov 2026 confirms "Current as of March 2025" and the Colorado entry verbatim). Note: the grower-contact page's Tribes section directs tribal-land enquiries to USDA directly and lists no Ute Mountain Ute or Southern Ute contact — distinct from the plan table's Ute Mountain Ute plan listing in §5.12.

5.14 Other / negative findings (sources that do NOT exist as public downloads)

Metrc: Colorado's seed-to-sale system is Metrc (MED's 26:08 bulletin concerns the "Statewide Inventory Tracking System Contract Award," confirmed on the MED home page). Metrc is licensee-only. There is no public Metrc licence-holder download. Any "Metrc list" claim should be treated as false unless a MED-published extract is produced.

No MED bulk CSV/XLSX was confirmed. The Licensed Facilities page may host PDFs or spreadsheets behind its list links, and data.colorado.gov may host a Socrata export — but neither file was actually retrieved in this run, so no file name or direct download link is asserted for them. This is deliberate: inventing a file name (e.g. guessing a .xlsx URL) would violate the sourcing rules. The follow-up is a live-browser capture of: (a) every link on the Licensed Facilities page, (b) the data.colorado.gov MED dataset page and its export menu, (c) the two DOR Google Sheets links, (d) the CDPHE Approved Source List link, and (e) the MED 2025 report PDF link — plus (f) Bulletin 26:05 content and (g) the SOS search page (see Still-Unverified list).

CORA as fallback: MED's retail-licensee guidance points to the Colorado Open Records Act (DOR website) for records not in the published lists — cannabis.colorado.gov — Retail Licensees, accessed 1 Nov 2026 (page confirms the CORA link and the "licensed does not mean operating" rule verbatim). Use CORA for historic discipline settlements and for any CDA grower list whose public availability is disputed.

PART 6 — MARKET DATA

Primary source, opened directly: Colorado Department of Revenue, Marijuana Sales Reports — DOR Marijuana Sales Reports, accessed 1 Nov 2026. DOR states: "Sales started January 2014." The page gives calendar-year totals and cumulative totals. It does not, on the landing page itself, split each year into medical vs retail; the split below is therefore shown separately, with its own source, and every split row was checked against the DOR total for that year. Scope note: tax distribution, licence rules, and hemp licence types are covered in Parts 2, 4 and 7 respectively and are only summarised here where they explain a market figure.

Headline in one paragraph: Colorado is a mature, contracting regulated marijuana market. Total regulated sales peaked at $2,228,994,553 in calendar 2021 and fell to $1,315,678,364 in calendar 2025 — down $913,316,189, or 41.0% from peak (DOR Marijuana Sales Reports). 2025 was the fourth consecutive annual decline. Medical sales fell much faster than retail sales, and the DOR Average Market Rate for retail bud fell from a secondary-reported $1,721 per pound in Q1 2021 to the DOR AMR of $601 per pound for Q4 2026 (DOR — Average Market Rate). Cultivation licences collapsed while retail store licences stabilised. Hemp, by contrast, collapsed from a 2019 registered-acreage peak (secondary figure, see §6.9) and is now rebuilding mainly around fibre, from a very small base.

6.2 Recent monthly trend — 2025 full year and 2026 to July

DOR publishes sales with a lag: from June 2025 data, the Tax Reports are published monthly on the third Thursday on a two-month lag for tax revenue (for example, August 2025 tax revenue published in October 2025), and each monthly release pairs that tax month with sales for an earlier month (DOR Marijuana Tax Reports). Monthly totals below are therefore assembled from (a) DOR press releases, (b) CannBus sums of DOR monthly figures, and (c) ColoradoCannabis.org's DOR-derived monthly table where it cross-checks exactly. 6.4 Licence counts over time and closures

Critical distinction: Colorado publishes at least three different counts that must not be mixed: (1) licensed premises (CDPS/MED historical series), (2) approved business licences (MED 2025 report), and (3) stores reporting sales in a month (DOR sales reports). A store can hold both a medical and a retail licence at one premises, so licence counts exceed premises/store counts. MED's own footnote warns that MED issuance of a licence does not mean the licensee was operating at the time, because business licensees cannot operate without local approval.

6.6 Official Average Market Rate and price trends

What AMR is (DOR, official): "The Average Market Rates (AMRs) are the median market prices per pound or count of each category of unprocessed retail marijuana that is sold or transferred from retail marijuana cultivation facilities to retail marijuana product manufacturing facilities or retail marijuana stores." DOR calculates AMRs quarterly from Metrc transfer data (prior three months, calculated the month before they take effect), as required by §39-28.8-101(1.5), C.R.S. A 15% excise tax applies on the AMR or the contract price, whichever applies (AMR generally for affiliated transfers; the AMR median itself is calculated from the dataset described on the DOR page, including unaffiliated transfers). Source: DOR AMR page, opened directly, DOR — Average Market Rate, accessed 1 Nov 2026.

6.7 Market concentration — only what official sources say

Official position: MED does not publish market share by operator. CannBus states this explicitly: "This is a list of notable operators, not a ranking. MED does not publish market share by operator." Source: CannBus, accessed 1 Nov 2026 (secondary assertion; no MED operator-share publication was located in this run). Therefore no operator market-share table is given, and none should be constructed from store counts. What can be stated without estimating: Stores reporting sales (DOR, via CannBus): 488 retail + 183 medical in June 2026 (above, secondary). No operator breakdown is published by DOR in the pages opened. Notable chains (secondary, store counts NOT verified against MED lists — CannBus's own warning): Star Buds (20+ dispensaries), Native Roots (20+ locations, pre-sale guide figure — see §6.4E for the post-sale position: agreement 17, closed 15), LivWell Enlightened Health (17 locations), The Green Solution (a dozen or more stores), per a May 2026 guide cited by CannBus. Westword (via CannBus) describes LivWell as tied with Native Roots as the state's largest chain, and Native Roots selling 17 of 21 dispensaries to Verdant Capital Partners (agreement figure; closed count 15 — see §6.4E). These are not official concentration figures and must not be ranked by sales. County sales (DOR publishes by county, but the full county table was not extracted in this run): DOR's Marijuana Sales Reports "summarize total sales made by medical and retail marijuana stores monthly by county" (DOR press-release boilerplate, above). The only county figures retrieved are secondary: Denver County adult-use sales "over $512 million in 2020 to about $331 million in 2023" and Adams County adult-use "$146 million in 2020 to approximately $115 million in 2023" (ColoradoCannabis.org summary of DOR county data, ColoradoCannabis.org — Sales, accessed 1 Nov 2026 — secondary). Denver city (not county) 2022 sales: medical $106m (−44% vs 2021 $189m), retail $390m (−22% vs 2021 $501m), city marijuana revenue $54.8m (Denver annual marijuana report, via secondary summary) — city and county geographies differ and the Denver figure is a city report, not DOR county data. Full county concentration table: Unavailable in this run — retrieve the DOR Sales by County report for Part 3/Part 6 follow-up; do not use the Emergen Research "Denver-Boulder 46.8% share in 2025" vendor forecast as an official county share. Vendor forecasts rejected as concentration evidence: Emergen Research claims Denver-Boulder held 46.8% of Colorado legal cannabis revenue in 2025 and Denver County "led the state market in 2025" (Emergen Research — Colorado Legal Cannabis Market, accessed 1 Nov 2026). This is a commercial forecast report, not DOR county data, and its $1.32bn total merely restates DOR. Do not cite 46.8% as an official share. Licence-type concentration (official, MED 2025 report, Feb 2026 population): of 2,106 business licences, retail stores are 32.6% (687), retail cultivations 22.7% (478), retail manufacturers 10.0% (210), hospitality 0.7% (14) — calculated shares, for licence mix only, not sales mix, and subject to the §6.4B arithmetic-gap footnote.

6.8 Out-of-state buyer trends — where officially reported

Finding: no official DOR series on buyer residency or out-of-state share of sales was found in this run. A current out-of-state buyer percentage is Unavailable. Do not estimate one. What is established: Legal eligibility (law, not market data): adults 21+ with a valid government photo ID from any state may buy retail marijuana in Colorado; there is no residency requirement for retail purchase. This is the legal framework for visitor purchasing, not a measure of how many buyers are visitors. (Part 1 to confirm from statute/MED rules; secondary visitor guides agree.) Historical official-adjacent evidence (dated, qualitative): Nebraska Public Media / NET News survey (pre-2014 retail launch period): 66% of surveyed Nebraska sheriffs/prosecutors felt Colorado medical legalisation impacted the illegal drug trade in their region, rising to 82% along the I-80 corridor; seizures along interstates/highways out of Colorado were described as routine. Source: Nebraska Public Media, accessed 1 Nov 2026 (secondary). This is law-enforcement perception from the early retail era, not a sales trend, and must not be presented as current. Secondary industry attribution (2024): Vangst/Whitney Economics Jobs Report 2024 attributes part of Colorado's employment decline to reduced "cannatourism": "The expansion of adult-use sales to 20 states… has reduced Colorado's cannatourism to a fraction of its former self." Source: Marijuana Moment summary, Marijuana Moment — Jobs Report 2024, accessed 1 Nov 2026 (secondary). No percentage or dollar figure for visitor sales is given in that summary. Neighbouring-state context for Part 10 (not a Part 6 trend): Wyoming, Nebraska, Kansas, Oklahoma, Utah and Texas visitors historically drove to Colorado border towns, but as of 2026 New Mexico (adult-use since 2022), Arizona, Montana and other neighbours have their own adult-use markets, which is the mechanism Vangst cites for reduced cannatourism. No DOR border-county visitor breakdown was retrieved — follow-up: request DOR sales-by-county data for border counties (e.g. Pueblo, Mesa, Larimer, Weld, Yuma, Sedgwick, Cheyenne, Baca, Las Animas) and compare with interior counties, rather than asserting a border effect.

Employment as a market indicator (secondary, with official licence counts distinguished). MED counts licences, not jobs (see §6.4B). Industry job estimates are secondary: Feb 2022 → Feb 2023: Colorado cannabis workforce fell by ~10,500 jobs to 27,856 workers (−28% in that window, High Times/Westword reporting of Vangst data). Source: High Times, accessed 1 Nov 2026 (secondary). Vangst Jobs Report 2024: Colorado (and Washington) saw 16% and 15% job losses respectively year-on-year to March 2024 (the original does not state which figure attaches to which state — retained as stated, not resolved by guessing); the western mature markets collectively lost ~15,000 jobs. Source: Marijuana Moment (above) (secondary). Vangst/Whitney U.S. Cannabis Jobs Report 2026 (via CannBus): U.S. legal cannabis jobs 412,500 FTE in early 2026, down 2.7% year-on-year; no Colorado figure is given in the public summary — CannBus records Colorado as "N/A." Source: CannBus (above) (secondary). A secondary training-site compilation lists Colorado at "~23,800 jobs" for 2024–2025, but its method is not stated — do not use as headline; mark <span class="verify">Verify</span>. MED licensed individuals (official, not jobs): 28,352 employees + 1,453 owners held licences in April 2025 (MED demographic data via CannBus — secondary, not MED-direct in this audit); 25,401 employee licences in the MED 2025 report (population as of February 2026; MED PDF also gives 1,331 owner licensees and 207 owner entity licences). The fall from 28,352 (Apr 2025) to 25,401 (Feb 2026 population) is a licence-count fall, not a proven job-loss count, because one person can hold multiple licences and licensed individuals may not all be employed at once.

6.9 Hemp acreage and registration counts by year

Three different measures — do not conflate them: (1) CDA registered acres = acres a registrant is authorised to plant (may exceed planted acres); (2) USDA NASS planted acres = acres actually planted, from producer surveys; (3) USDA NASS harvested acres = acres actually harvested. A year can therefore show, e.g. 88,743 registered acres (2019, secondary) alongside far smaller planted/harvested acres in later survey years. All three are reported below with their measure labelled.

6.10 Hemp product market figures

Finding: no official Colorado state publication of total hemp-product sales (CBD, hemp beverages, intoxicating hemp products, fibre products) was found in this run. A Colorado hemp-product market total is Unavailable — do not substitute a national or vendor figure. What exists, labelled by reliability: (1) Official, national only — USDA values: U.S. hemp production value $291m in 2023 (NASS 2023 report, official — USDA NASS 2023 Briefing (PDF)); U.S. open-field hemp value $417m in 2024, floral $386m, fibre $11.2m (NASS 2024 report, via summary — secondary, see §6.9). No Colorado split of value is published in the extracts retrieved (Colorado 2023 value withheld as "(D)" for disclosure reasons). (2) Secondary, national — hemp-derived cannabinoid demand: Whitney Economics 2024 U.S. National Cannabinoid Report, as cited by FloraWorks CBN Market Report (June 2026), sizes total U.S. hemp-derived cannabinoid demand at $28 billion in 2024; Brightfield Group separately sizes hemp-derived THC retail at $3.5 billion (2024–25). Sources via: FloraWorks CBN Market Report, accessed 1 Nov 2026 (secondary). These are national, modelled, and an order of magnitude apart in scope (all cannabinoids vs THC-only) — neither is a Colorado figure and neither should be apportioned to Colorado by population or acreage. (3) Vendor forecasts for "Colorado legal cannabis market" — rejected as regulated-market evidence: Grand View Research: $2.59bn in 2024, $5.53bn by 2030, CAGR 12.9%, CBD ≈65% share, marijuana >85% share (Grand View Research, accessed 1 Nov 2026); Precedence Research: $2.99bn in 2025, $3.38bn in 2026, $9.00bn by 2034, CAGR 13.0% (Precedence Research, accessed 1 Nov 2026); TechSci Research: $2.61bn in 2024, $5.39bn by 2030, CAGR 12.83% (TechSci Research, accessed 1 Nov 2026). All three contradict DOR's regulated sales ($1.397bn in 2024, $1.316bn in 2025) by roughly 2×, because they evidently include hemp/CBD, ancillary, or unregulated channels in a broader "legal cannabis market" definition they do not reconcile to DOR. Use DOR for market size; cite vendor forecasts only to show why they must not be used, with this warning attached. (4) Intoxicating hemp competition (qualitative, official-adjacent): MED's 2025 report cites competition from hemp-derived intoxicating cannabinoid products as a factor pressuring the regulated marijuana market (MED PDF market-trends text, above). No dollar figure for intoxicating hemp sales in Colorado is given by MED in the pages opened — Unavailable. SB25/SB26 hemp-beverage proposals (Part 1) are legislative, not market, evidence. (5) CDPHE hemp product registrations: counts of CDPHE-registered hemp manufacturers/products are a Part 5/Part 7 registry question, not a sales figure. The secondary "61 approved hemp manufacturing and storage facilities (Aug 2026)" figure in §6.9 is the only count retrieved and is unverified.

Last audited: 1 November 2026 (Parts 7–8 audit). Corrections from that audit are applied in place below. “Verify” appears only on items still unresolved after the audit; see the Still-Unverified list above for where each can be confirmed. Every fact below carries a source link; listing-site claims in Part 8 are labelled as marketed-but-not-verified and are not primary-source facts.

PART 7 — HEMP LICENCES IN FULL

7.1 Who regulates what — the split that decides everything else

Colorado hemp regulation is split at the farm gate. The Colorado Department of Agriculture (CDA) regulates cultivation only. The Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment (CDPHE) regulates manufacturing, packaging, warehousing and distribution once the crop leaves the farm — CDPHE states: “Hemp farms are licensed and regulated by the Colorado Department of Agriculture, once the crop leaves the farm it is this department's responsibility to oversee the manufacturing, packaging, warehousing, and distribution of hemp products” (CDPHE hemp page). The Marijuana Enforcement Division (MED) does not license hemp cultivation or hemp products as such — intoxicating cannabinoids outside the hemp channel are handled inside existing marijuana licences, or not at all in-state (see §7.8 and §7.9). Sources: CDA hemp portal (ag.colorado.gov/plants/hemp); CDPHE hemp food portal (cdphe.colorado.gov/dehs/hemp-food).

Colorado operates under a USDA-approved State Hemp Management Plan (Title 35, Article 61; 8 CCR 1203-23). Colorado growers are therefore state-licensed, not USDA-licensed. The 1 June 2021 date in the original was the revised-plan submission letter, not the approval: USDA approval was announced 10 August 2021 (CDA press release), and the USDA Agricultural Marketing Service table (updated 17 February 2026) still lists “Colorado — Approved Plan” (USDA AMS state and tribal plan review). The statutory basis for state registration is CRS §35-61-104(1)(a): a person wishing to engage in industrial hemp cultivation “shall apply to the department for a registration … prior to planting” (CRS §35-61-104), and §35-61-102(1) permits growth by registered persons for commercial or research-and-development purposes.

Hemp definition (corrected). CRS §35-61-101(7) defines “industrial hemp” or “hemp” as “the plant Cannabis sativa L. and any part of the plant, including the seeds of the plant and all derivatives, extracts, cannabinoids, isomers, acids, salts, and salts of isomers, whether growing or not, with a delta-9 tetrahydrocannabinol concentration of no more than three-tenths of one percent on a dry-weight basis” (CRS §35-61-101). The CDA rule's operational test is total THC: 8 CCR 1203-23, Rule 1.11 defines hemp by “a total delta-9 [THC] concentration of no more than 0.3% on a dry-weight basis” (8 CCR 1203-23, Part 1), and §35-61-101 defines the “acceptable hemp THC level” by applying measurement of uncertainty so that the resulting range includes 0.3% or less. “Total THC” means (%THCA × 0.877) + %THC (6 CCR 1010-24.4). Testing is performed under the CDPHE Hemp Testing Laboratory Certification, 5 CCR 1005-5 (see §7.6).

No hemp registration count is stated in this Part. Do not carry the secondary “90 registered growers / 61 approved facilities (August 2026)” figures from Part 6 into this Part — they are secondary-only and Unverified. CDPHE describes its approved-source list as a “monthly updated list” of active facilities (CDPHE hemp page); any count must be taken from that month's list with its date. CDA's Hemp Online Portal (HOP) is a login/search page; no public CDA registrant download file was confirmed in this audit (see Still-Unverified §5).

7.2 CDA cultivation registrations — two classes only

ClassAuthority (corrected)What it coversKey limits
