Research & Development (R&D)8 CCR 1203-23, Rule 1.28 (Part 1)Cultivation for research only, by an institution of higher education or other entity approved by the Department for agricultural or academic researchR&D plants cannot move into a commercial registration or enter commerce (Rules 2.17, 4.7.9)

Correction: the original cited Rules 1.3/1.4 for these classes. Those numbers are wrong in the current rule; Commercial is Rule 1.5 and R&D is Rule 1.28. R&D still exists in current rule text — SB 20-197 did not abolish it: SB 20-197 (ch. 194) retains §35-61-102(1)(b), growth “for research and development purposes” (SB 20-197 session law). No current 10-acre R&D cap was found in the current rule text — the 10-acre limit appeared on a 2014 application form only. Do not publish any 10-acre cap.

Statute mirrors the structure: CRS §35-61-104 (CRS §35-61-104).

Application is via the CDA Hemp Online Portal (HOP), signed and complete, with registration notification received prior to planting (Rule 2.1, Part 2). Required (Rule 2.1.1–2.1.7): Key Participants list (full name, title and email for each Key Participant), entity type and employee identification number, principal business location address, telephone and email, Secretary of State ID, legal description (Section/Township/Range), GPS coordinates taken at the approximate centre of the Registered Land Area, map showing boundaries and dimensions in acres or square feet, and statement of intended use and varieties. R&D adds (Rule 2.2.7–2.2.9): the registrant's URL for publishing its research, scope and standard operating procedures including a narrative of the planned project, and a disposal plan. Each noncontiguous land area needs its own registration (Rule 2.7). No person may cultivate in a proposed area until the Commissioner has approved and issued a registration (Rule 2.3).

The older “30 days prior” filing deadline does not appear in current Rule 2.1 text — current Rule 2.1 requires notification of registration prior to planting, with no 30-day rule. Processing-time advice (secondary sources suggest allowing about 30 days) is Verify — it is not a rule and is not adopted here.

7.3 Key Participants and criminal-history checks

“Key Participants” are defined in CRS §35-61-101: a sole proprietor, a partner in a partnership, a person with executive managerial control in a corporation, or faculty at an institution of higher education; executive managerial control includes persons such as a chief executive officer, chief operating officer, or chief financial officer; the definition does not include nonexecutive managers such as farm, field, or shift managers (CRS §35-61-101).

Each Key Participant must submit a complete set of fingerprints to the Colorado Bureau of Investigation or the department for an FBI check, with the submission of the application (CRS §35-61-104(1)(c), CRS §35-61-104). An arrest without disposition triggers a name-based judicial record check as defined in §22-2-119.3(6)(d). The Key Participant pays the costs of the fingerprint-based check. A secondary “fingerprints within 60 days of application” window was not confirmed — Verify (confirm from the current CDA application form/guidance; do not publish a 60-day window).

A controlled-substance felony makes a person ineligible for 10 years from the date of conviction (Rule 5.2.1, Part 5), with the pre-20 December 2018 exception as written in Rule 5.2.2: a person lawfully growing under a department registration before 20 December 2018 whose felony also occurred before that date shall not be denied under Rule 5.2.1. See §7.6.

7.5 CDA term, transfer, amendments and reporting

Term: registrations are valid one year from issuance (Rule 2.11; CRS §35-61-104(3)(a)). There is no true renewal — re-apply yearly. Plant material not harvested in the registration period in which it was planted, and volunteer plants not destroyed, must be declared for inclusion in a subsequent registration (Rule 2.12). Transfer: registrations are non-transferable (Rule 2.4). Amendments: limited to changes within the original land area with an updated legal description/GPS/map (Rule 2.13); contact changes within 10 days (Rule 2.15). All citations in this paragraph are to Part 2.

Planting Report: within 10 days after planting (and within 10 days after emergence of volunteer plants kept), with varieties and intended use, GPS coordinates and map showing location and actual acreage/square footage (Rules 3.1/3.3, Part 3). A Planting Report must be submitted any time hemp is planted in, moved into, or (for R&D) moved within a Registered Land Area, subject to the container-replanting exceptions in Rules 3.1.3 and 3.3.3. Harvest Report: at least 30 days prior to harvest (Rules 3.2/3.4). Harvest-date changes of more than 5 days need an immediate Amended Harvest Report (Rules 3.2.2/3.4.2); the Commissioner may require additional testing on such a change. Other changes: each registrant shall report any change to registration or previously submitted reports, including intended disposition, within 10 days of the change (Rule 3.5) — this is a general 10-day duty, not only a harvest-change duty. Records: records of plants acquired/grown/produced/handled/disposed including THC results (Rule 3.6); report acreage to USDA Farm Service Agency (Rule 3.7); retain records 3 years (Rule 3.8); records open to department/USDA inspectors, auditors or representatives during reasonable business hours (Rule 3.9).

7.6 CDA inspection, sampling, remediation, disposal and discipline

All registrations are subject to routine inspection/sampling to verify total THC does not exceed the acceptable hemp THC level (Rule 4.1, Part 4), plus additional compliance inspections, with a subset randomly selected yearly for records audit, premises inspection and sampling (Rule 4.4). The registrant or authorised representative shall be present at the growing operation if possible; the department has complete unrestricted access to all hemp plants, parts and seeds, land, buildings and structures used for cultivation and storage (Rule 4.6). Samples are collected within 30 days prior to anticipated harvest (Rule 4.3); each variety/lot is sampled individually, not commingled (Rules 4.7.1, 4.7.8). Testing is for total THC under protocols / standard operating procedures in the CDPHE Hemp Testing Lab Certification, 5 CCR 1005-5 (Rules 4.7.2–4.7.3). A representative result above the acceptable level is conclusive (Rule 4.7.4). No harvest before sample collection (Rule 4.7.6). Harvested material may not leave the Registered Land Area before results except to off-site storage to prevent crop loss, with the registrant retaining control and ownership and reporting the storage location (Rule 4.7.7). Authorised Samplers need registration/certification, yearly training and an exam (Rules 4.10.1–4.10.2, including Rule 4.10.1.2: yearly department-approved training course and passing an examination). Performance-based sampling petitions exist for certified-seed/clone, R&D, 3-consecutive-year same-variety, microgreen/transplant, and grain/industrial producers (Rule 4.8).

Remediation is allowed only for lots above the acceptable level but below 1.0% total THC — separate/destroy flowers retaining stalks/leaves/seeds, or blend the whole lot into biomass (Rule 4.7.10). It requires prior department permission via a Remediation and Disposal form (Rule 4.7.11). Correction: Rule 4.7.12 requires that request within 10 days of the registrant receiving the Remediation and Disposal form from the Department (not within 10 days of the test result). Department verification/sampling occurs within 10 days of the reported remediation date (Rule 4.7.13; note the rule text's cross-reference to “rule 4.7.9” in Rule 4.7.13 is an error in the rule itself — the duty is tied to the date reported under Rule 4.7.11). No remediation at or above 1.0% (Rule 4.7.14) — dispose via a DEA-registered reverse distributor or law enforcement, or on-site at the farm or hemp production facility per USDA AMS Hemp Remediation and Disposal Guidelines (15 January 2021, incorporated by reference) (Rule 4.7.15).

Violations: civil penalties up to $2,500 per violation, denial, summary suspension or revocation (CRS §§35-61-107, 24-4-104; Rule 5.1, Part 5); growing above 0.3% total THC is a listed violation (Rule 5.1.5). Negligent violations draw corrective action including a correction date, periodic reporting of not less than 2 years, and inspections (Rules 5.1.8.1–5.1.8.3); 3 negligent violations in 5 years → 5-year ineligibility (Rule 5.1.9); reasonable efforts plus ≤1.0% is not a negligent violation (Rule 5.1.7.3); material falsification → ineligibility (Rule 5.1.10.1); culpable-state violations are reported to the US and Colorado Attorneys General (Rule 5.1.10.2). Numbering caution: the 2021 State Plan letter cites this discipline structure as Part 6; current text numbers it Part 5 — the discrepancy is recorded here, the rule is not renumbered. A 3-year denial look-back after suspension/revocation/relinquishment appears in the plan letter only — Verify against the current rule.

7.8 CDPHE definitions, Safe Harbor, package/serving rules and labelling — with a Run 1 correction

Definitions (6 CCR 1010-24; CRS §25-5-427). A “hemp product” is a cosmetic, dietary supplement, food, food additive or herb for human use, at ≤1.75 mg THC/serving with CBD:THC ≥15:1 — the Run 1 / SB 23-271 rule, unchanged (CRS §25-5-427 §(2)(d); Rule 24.4(12)). Safe Harbor is permitted only for export, not for sale or distribution in Colorado (CRS §25-5-427 §(2)(l); Rule 24.4(25)). Broad spectrum (rule): ≤0.05 mg total THC/gram and ≤6.0 mg total THC/container (Rule 24.4(2)). Full spectrum (rule): ≤1.75 mg THC/serving, ratio ≥15:1 (Rule 24.4(8)).

The nonintoxicating list includes full-spectrum extract (≤1.75 mg/serving, ≥15:1), broad-spectrum extract, CBD, delta-9 THCV, CBC, CBT, CBL, CBE, CBG, CBDV and CBN (CRS §25-5-427 §(4)(b)(I); Rule 24.4(18)). Qualifier added by this audit: delta-8 THCV is not in that list — it is listed as intoxicating (see below).

Potentially intoxicating and intoxicating cannabinoids are prohibited in-state as hemp products except as safe-harbor exports, and may not be marketed as containing THC (or, for potentially intoxicating cannabinoids, as containing any potentially intoxicating cannabinoid) (CRS §25-5-427 §§(4)(c)(I), (4)(d)(II)). The intoxicating list, in an amount exceeding any amount established by rule (or in any amount if no rule establishes one), is (CRS §25-5-427 §(4)(d)(I)): delta-10, delta-9, delta-8, delta-7 and delta-6a,10a THC and their isomers; exo-THC; THC metabolites (11-hydroxy-, 3-hydroxy-, 7-hydroxy-THC); hydrogenated forms (HHC, HHCP, HHCH); synthetic forms including dronabinol; ester forms (delta-8 THC-O-acetate, delta-9 THC-O-acetate, HHC-O-acetate); tetrahydrocannabivarins including delta-8 THCV but excluding delta-9 THCV; analogues with an alkyl chain of four or more carbon atoms including THCP, THC-octyl, THC-hexyl and THC-butyl; and combinations including HHCP-O-ester. Synthetic cannabinoids also may not be manufactured, produced, sold or offered for sale unless authorised by rule (CRS §25-5-427 §(4)(e)(I)); Rule 24.9(A) prohibits manufacture, production or distribution of a hemp or safe-harbor product that is also a synthetic cannabinoid (Rule 24.9).

Safe-harbor facilities must show federal cGMP compliance via CDPHE-approved third-party audit evidence by 1 July each year plus an annual attestation by 1 July each year (Rule 24.5(B); CRS §25-5-427 §(5)(c)). The attestation includes: no export to a state where the product is prohibited by state law; no manufacture, production or distribution of a synthetic cannabinoid; and either (i) the facility is not registered as a hemp or wholesale-food manufacturer/storage facility, or (ii) if it is, each safe-harbor product is physically separated or made, produced, stored and distributed under department-approved procedures ensuring no cross-contamination (Rule 24.5(B)(2)(d)). Safe-harbor records are kept at least 2 years (Rule 24.8(A)) including purchaser, the state of sale and documentation the product is not prohibited there, that state's THC limits per serving and/or per container, and that state's labelling requirements differing from Rule 24.7(E).

Package caps — RESOLVED against the secondary figures. The secondary ≤5 mg/package (non-safe-harbor), ≤2.5 mg/serving and ≤10 mg/package (safe-harbor) figures do NOT appear in 6 CCR 1010-24.7 or 24.9 as opened — do NOT publish them as Colorado rule caps. This corrects Run 1, which carried them as secondary summaries.

The rule's actual package mechanism — manufacture vs sale must not be collapsed (correction to the original's single-mechanism presentation).

Manufacture — Rule 24.9(H)–(I) (Rule 24.9): a package with more than 5 servings is prohibited if it has >1.25 mg total THC/serving with a ratio <15:1; a package with more than 30 servings is prohibited if >1.25 mg/serving with a ratio <20:1; both exempt broad-spectrum products, tinctures, cosmetics and FDA-GRAS products. Rule 24.9 also prohibits: manufacture of a hemp product with >1.75 mg total THC per serving (24.9(F)) or a CBD:THC ratio <15:1 (24.9(G)); manufacture of a hemp product containing potentially intoxicating cannabinoids unless specifically allowed by regulation (24.9(B)); manufacture of a hemp product containing intoxicating cannabinoids other than THC within allowed limits (24.9(C)); and chemical modification, conversion or synthetic derivation of cannabinoids/hemp-derived compounds for use as a hemp product or ingredient, except for nonintoxicating cannabinoids (24.9(D)).

Sale — statute §25-5-427(8)(f)–(g) (CRS §25-5-427), different pairings: selling a hemp product in a package with more than 5 servings is unlawful if it has >1.25 mg THC/serving AND a ratio <20:1 (§(8)(f)); selling a hemp product in a package with more than 30 servings is unlawful if it has >1.25 mg THC/serving AND a ratio of 20:1 or more (§(8)(g)). Exemptions for both sales bans: products with no THC, tinctures, cosmetics, and FDA-GRAS products. Reconciliation note: the manufacture and sales pairings differ, and together they do not reduce to a single “5-serving / 30-serving” rule. Reconciliation against the official session law / leg.colorado.gov CRS text stays Verify (see Still-Unverified §6) — the corrected text states both provisions separately rather than choosing one.

Minimum age — labelling vs sales are different tests (correction; the original's sales-clause Verify is resolved). Labelling trigger (Rule 24.7, conjunctive “and”): if a serving contains more than 1.25 mg of total THC, AND less than a 20:1 CBD to THC ratio, labelling indicating individuals must be 21 or older to purchase is required on the principal display panel (Rule 24.7(E)(3)(e)(1)). Sales prohibition (statute, disjunctive “or”): it is unlawful to sell a hemp product to an individual under 21 if the product has more than 1.25 mg THC per serving OR has a ratio <20:1 (CRS §25-5-427 §(8)(e)(I)), except for products with no THC, tinctures, cosmetics, and FDA-GRAS products (§(8)(e)(II)). Do not present the labelling trigger as the sales test.

Labelling (Rule 24.7). State total THC per serving, total THC per package, and CBD:THC ratio per serving, in or directly below the ingredient list in bold (Rule 24.7(E)(3)(e)). With the exception of broad-spectrum products and cosmetics, labels of products containing THC, potentially intoxicating or intoxicating cannabinoids must include a consumer-notice statement disclosing their presence, including potential positive drug-test result, potential impairment, not evaluated for safety/efficacy, pregnancy/breastfeeding physician-consultation advice, and keep-out-of-reach-of-children (Rule 24.7(E)(7)); CBD labels must include the Rule 24.7(E)(8) notice (pregnancy/breastfeeding advice; potential liver injury, male reproductive harm, and sedative effects impairing driving/operating machinery). Labels/packaging must not appeal to children or target individuals under 21 (Rule 24.7(E)(11)).

Testing (Rule 24.7). Certified lab under 5 CCR 1005-5; products must test as broad-spectrum or as full-spectrum ≤1.75 mg total THC with ratio ≥15:1 under the statute (Rule 24.7(D)(5)(b) phrases the test as “greater than 15 to one” — the statute's “greater than or equal to” controls the definition); an unidentified peak >1.0% of total peak area is investigated and fails if it is an unlabelled cannabinoid (Rule 24.7(D)(5)(a), Rule 24.7). Safe-harbor products must have test results listing THC and other intoxicating/potentially intoxicating cannabinoid levels (Rule 24.7(D)(5)(c)).

Transport (Rule 24.7). Products must be protected from adulteration, allergen cross-contact, environmental contamination and other hazards (Rule 24.7(H)); transfer must comply with all applicable transportation laws (Rule 24.7(H)(1)). Waste: waste THC diluted to <0.3%, converted, or disposed of per CDPHE waste rules (Rule 24.7(I)(1)); the facility owner/operator must secure and limit access to hemp-derived THC >0.3% (Rule 24.7(I)(2)) (Rule 24.7).

Enforcement (Rule 24.10). Incomplete application/fees = not an approved source (Rule 24.10(A)–(B)); adulterated/misbranded products may be embargoed (CRS §25-5-406, Rule 24.10(C)); CDPHE may require recall (CRS §25-1.5-102(1)(c), Rule 24.10(D) — framed as investigating/controlling epidemic and communicable diseases affecting public health), issue a cease-and-desist (Rule 24.10(E), citing §§25-5-420 and 25-5-427(9)) or admonition, or deny, suspend, refuse to renew, restrict or revoke (Rule 24.10(F)). Added by this audit: a person violating §25-5-427, its rules, or a final cease-and-desist/clean-up order is subject to a civil penalty of not more than $10,000 per day per violation (§25-5-427(9), CRS §25-5-427).

CBD and hemp beverages — no separate beverage regime. There is no separate Colorado hemp-beverage licence and no higher beverage cap in current law. A hemp beverage sold as a hemp product (a food) must meet the same hemp-product definition (≤1.75 mg THC/serving, ≥15:1) and the serving-count rules above. CBD itself is a nonintoxicating cannabinoid; §25-5-427 creates no separate “CBD licence”. The only beverage-specific proposal in this Part, SB 26-164, did not pass (see §7.9).

7.9 Seed, handler/processor, MED intoxicating hemp, transport and retail — findings, not assumptions

Seed — rule citations corrected/removed. A separate CDA registration exists under the Colorado Seed Act (labels, germination/purity; applications via the CDA portal) as a matter outside 8 CCR 1203-23, but the original's citations to 8 CCR 1203-23 Rules 7.1–7.3 must not be used as current law: Part 7 of 8 CCR 1203-23 is “Reserved” in the current rule (history eff. 31 December 2021) (Part 7 — Reserved). The original's statements that certified-seed variety approval “requires testing below 0.3% delta-9 THC in multiple Colorado trials (Rule 7.1)” and that registrants “pay an additional Committee-set fee plus variety-testing costs (Rules 7.2–7.3)” are therefore removed as current-rule claims. Current seed-labeler registration, any certified-seed list, and any fee must be confirmed from the current CDA seed programme — Verify (see Still-Unverified §8). Do not publish the secondary “$75–$700/year” seed-fee range or the dated 2020 certification fees ($500 CSGA + $1,500 CDA). “No state certified hemp seed” is dated material — Verify.

Handler/processor: NO standalone Colorado hemp handler or processor licence was identified. The model is exactly two registrations (CDA cultivation + CDPHE manufacturer/storage). CDA's direction to its Farm Products Program for commodity handlers is not a hemp handler licence; whether a commodity-handler licence applies to any hemp dealer is Verify (confirm from CDA Farm Products Program / CRS Title 35, Article 36). State this as a current finding, not a proven universal negative.

MED intoxicating hemp — RESOLVED: no standalone MED intoxicating-hemp licence class exists in CRS §44-10-401 (full medical and retail class lists checked) (CRS §44-10-401). Intoxicating cannabinoids are prohibited in-state in the hemp channel (except safe-harbor export) or handled inside existing marijuana licences: a medical store may transfer a hemp product to a patient only after verifying required testing at a medical testing facility and that the transferor is CDPHE-registered under §25-5-427 (Rule 5-105, Rule 5-105; statute §44-10-501(1)(e), CRS §44-10-501 — note some reproductions still cite the superseded §25-5-426; the current citation is §25-5-427). Retail-store sentence corrected: a retail store is not limited to selling only retail marijuana products and hemp products as consumables — §44-10-601 permits a retail store to sell retail marijuana, retail marijuana products, marijuana accessories, nonconsumable products, hemp products, and food including food not infused with marijuana or hemp, and bars giving away or selling cigarettes or alcohol (CRS §44-10-601). A retail store that sells a hemp product must ensure it passed all testing required for retail marijuana products at a licensed retail testing facility and verify the transferor is CDPHE-registered under §25-5-427 (§44-10-601). Caveat retained: the full current 1 CCR 212-3 (effective 5 January 2026) intoxicating-cannabinoid provisions were not opened end-to-end — Verify beyond the two store rules above.

Transport/retail. CDA “recommends” carrying a Certificate of Analysis (≤0.3% THC) plus a travel manifest/bill of lading with any shipment — the full recommended list was truncated, Verify the complete list; that is a recommendation, not a cited transport-permit rule. No Colorado hemp transport permit/licence was identified (finding, not proven universal negative). There is no state hemp store licence (registration falls on the manufacturer/storage facility) — but local licences can still apply: for example, Aurora's May 2026 handbook (summarising Ordinance 2026-05, approved 9 March 2026, effective 11 April 2026, $500 annual fee) requires an annual city Tobacco and Age-Restricted Psychoactive Products Retailer Licence for retailers selling hemp products with 1.25–1.75 mg THC/serving (Aurora handbook, Revised May 2026; Ordinance 2026-05). The original's further claim that Aurora “prohibits loose hemp bud sales” is removed — it was not confirmed in the handbook excerpt opened and stays Verify. Aurora is a local example only — do not generalise it statewide. SB 26-164 is not law: it was Postponed Indefinitely by the Senate Finance Committee on 28 April 2026 (final fiscal note 4 June 2026: “this bill was postponed indefinitely … therefore, the impacts … do not take effect”) (SB 26-164 fiscal note). As introduced it would have created “lawful THC beverages” (nonalcoholic hemp-derived beverages ≤10 mg THC/serving) — that 10 mg beverage framework does not exist in current law.

7.10 Federal-response follow-ups still open after Part 7 — with the federal-baseline interaction now stated

MED Bulletin 26:05 contents were NOT obtained (listing on med.colorado.gov confirmed; text not opened — do not summarise it from secondary sources). It is the single most important outstanding Colorado Schedule III document.

No Colorado agency response (CDPHE/CDA/MED/Governor) to the 12 November / 11 December 2026 federal hemp dates was located — status remains Unavailable / Verify after 11 December 2026, recorded as “none located,” not as a proven negative. This also corrects Part 11's cross-reference: Part 11's statement that CDPHE hemp fees were “Verify” is superseded by §7.7 above.

How the federal dates interact with Colorado's intoxicating hemp law (added by this audit, on the federal baseline as given). Until 11 December 2026, PL 119-103 §2019 limits PL 119-37 §781 to only the provisions excluding cannabinoids that are not naturally produced or are synthesised. In that window, Colorado's existing ban on synthetic/converted cannabinoids in the hemp channel (see §7.8) points in the same direction as the federal exclusion, but Colorado's 1.75 mg/serving + 15:1 hemp-product definition is not yet displaced by the federal total-THC definition or container cap. After 11 December 2026, the full federal total-THC definition and the 0.4 mg total THC per container cap apply (baseline as given). On those terms, a Colorado hemp product at 1.75 mg per serving — and any multi-serving container totalling more than 0.4 mg — would exceed the federal container cap if Colorado's rule is unchanged, and hemp status would be governed by total THC (including THCA). Whether Colorado amends §25-5-427 / 6 CCR 1010-24, enforces its existing rule, or takes another position after 11 December 2026 is Verify after 11 December 2026 — no Colorado response was located as of 1 November 2026. Separately, USDA enforcement of the DEA-registered-laboratory hemp testing requirement is delayed until 31 December 2026 (baseline as given), so that testing change does not bite before year-end. For the avoidance of doubt: the federal Schedule III / 280E changes concern medical marijuana licences only and create no hemp licence, no MED intoxicating-hemp licence, and no change to CDA/CDPHE hemp registration by themselves; all retail (adult-use) activity remains Schedule I and fully subject to 280E. No statement in Part 7 decides whether any tribal programme counts as “state-licensed” — that question belongs to Part 10 and stays Verify unless supported by the text of the federal rule.

PART 8 — CANNABIS-ZONED PROPERTIES (strict verified standard)

8.1 The standard — and why it was not lowered

A property counts as strict-verified only if all four tests are met: (a) currently listed for sale/lease (or recently sold/leased with a dated source); (b) address/jurisdiction stated; (c) positive evidence of zoning/permission for a named cannabis use (official zoning, licence, or a listing stating cannabis use — not merely “warehouse in Denver”); (d) price/size/terms from the listing itself. Snippet, index and brochure evidence was not counted as verification. The standard was not lowered to fill a table.

HEADLINE: ZERO properties meet the strict verified standard on the evidence opened in Run 2. That is the honest result, not a missing table. It is a finding on the evidence opened, not proof that no qualifying property exists anywhere in Colorado. Everything below the headline is either zoning mechanics (how a parcel could qualify) or a clearly separated list of marketed-but-not-verified candidates. Never add a candidate to a verified count.

8.3 Zoning mechanics — how a parcel could qualify (official sources, accessed 1 Nov 2026, as corrected)

Denver. Marijuana Facility Location Guide (revised 3 June 2026) (Denver guide PDF — note: returned via Denver's qa.denvergov.org file host; confirm the live PDF location on denvergov.org) — the zoning code controls over the guide; a zone use permit is required. Cultivation districts in the guide extract, as sets (column pairing garbled — Verify the complete paired list against the full guide table before publishing a closed list): Denver Zoning Code I-A, I-1, I-B, I-2; Former Chapter 59 OS-B, I-0, OS-1, O-2. Correction: the original's additional reference to “OS-2” is removed — the extract shows O-2, not OS-2, and OS-2 is most plausibly a misreading of O-2. No cultivation within 1,000 ft of specified locations (schools and residential districts are the legible limbs — the complete protected-location list stays Verify, the guide table was not fully opened); stores, hospitality and cultivation cannot be within 1,000 ft of a school; Denver's proximity check tool draws the 1,000-ft buffer; maximum one medical + one retail cultivation licence per licensed premises (confirmed in the guide extract). Denver FAQ (official, Denver marijuana FAQ): social-equity reservation of store/transporter/cultivation/manufacturing/hospitality until 1 July 2027; Denver no longer issues new medical store or medical cultivation licences. Secondary Denver claims NOT adopted (2016 medical-cultivation stop; $5,000/$1,830 fees; 8am–midnight store hours) — Verify against the current fee schedule / Denver Revised Municipal Code Chapter 6, Article V.

Boulder — dated material only, not current law. City material found is a 2013 council handout (recreational centre as “convenience retail <2,000 sq ft,” cultivation as “greenhouse/nursery” or “manufacturing <15,000 sq ft,” no business in a building containing a residence or in a residential district) and county material is a 2014 DRAFT (Medical Marijuana Center Establishment permitted by right in T, B, C, LI, GI with 500-ft separation except in LI/GI) — both must be re-verified against current Boulder city and Boulder County codes before being stated as current. They are retained here only as dated historical material with that warning; they are Unverified as current law.

Pueblo (city). City code (Title XVII) permits multiple medical/retail uses by right subject to use-specific and licensing requirements (§17-4-51(c), the permitted-use table); four medical uses (§17-2-2(87): center, home cultivation, infused-product manufacturing, optional cultivation) and four retail uses (§17-2-2(131): cultivation facility, product manufacturing facility, store, testing facility) are defined; use-specific standards at §§17-15-5–7 (Pueblo ordinance material). Two items stay flagged: “conditional use permits for marijuana uses expire after one year” is Unverified (not confirmed in the material opened), and the district-by-district use table was not fully extracted — Verify before naming districts.

Pueblo County A-1/A-2 districts (secondary-hosted code extract — Verify vs official county code): Hemp Establishment, medical non-contiguous optional-premises cultivation, medical MIP (on-site cultivation only, no open-blast butane), retail non-contiguous cultivation, retail MIP (same limits) as uses by right subject to cited subsections. This paragraph rests on a secondary-hosted extract only and is Unverified against the official county code. Do not merge it with Pueblo city provisions — city ordinance material describes discontiguous optional cultivation premises differently (prohibited uses in one version).

Colorado Springs (corrected). Retail cultivation in MX-M is evidenced as sought by conditional use, not as an exhaustive list, and not as proven approvals: the 11 June 2025 Planning Commission agenda lists CUDP-25-0010 as “A Conditional Use to allow the addition of retail marijuana cultivation facility use and an expanded marijuana cultivation area from 1,800 to 5,700 square feet in the [MX-M] zone district … at 1105 South Chelton Road” (Planning Commission agenda, 11 June 2025). An agenda listing is not proof of approval — final approval/minutes stay Verify. The second item cited in the original, 2926 Wood Avenue, CUDP-25-0009 (May 2026), is Unverified — no confirming official record was located in this audit. Verify the full Unified Development Code use table. UDC §7.3.303 (MMJ facility prohibited in a residential district/dwelling except home cultivation; local + state licences and sales-tax licences; no on-premises consumption; odour filtration) was not opened in this audit — its content stays Verify and is not presented as confirmed. UDC §7.3.304 home cultivation is confirmed (UDC §7.3.304): maximum 12 plants / 150 sq ft per all single- and two-family dwellings regardless of the number of persons residing in the unit, enclosed locked space limited to 150 sq ft, no outdoor cultivation, specified districts only (R-E, R-1 9, R-1 6, R-2, single-/two-family PDZs, and R-Flex districts). Retail-allowed status (Question 300) does not by itself zone any parcel: voters approved Ballot Question 300 on 5 November 2024, and Ordinance No. 25-10 (finally passed 28 January 2025) amended Chapter 7 (UDC) to identify zones and use-specific standards for retail marijuana, including a 1,000-ft buffer from daycare/school/treatment facilities in the ordinance summary (Ordinance No. 25-10, Legistar).

PART 9 — REGULATORS AND HISTORY

9.1 Regulator map — who does what, and what each does NOT do

State Licensing Authority / MED, Department of Revenue (DOR). The State Licensing Authority is, by statute, the Executive Director of DOR (or the Deputy Director if so designated); the Executive Director is its chief administrative officer (CRS §44-10-201 — Verify against the official CRS on leg.colorado.gov; the original cited the unofficial reproduction at colorado.public.law). Its mandate is “for the purpose of regulating and controlling the licensing of the cultivation, manufacture, distribution, sale, and testing of regulated marijuana in this state” (CRS §44-10-201(1)(a)). Powers (CRS §44-10-202 — Verify against official CRS as above) include developing and maintaining the seed-to-sale tracking system, granting or refusing state licences and suspending, fining, restricting or revoking them, promulgating rules, and hearing contested denials and complaints. MED does not fix prices (CRS §44-10-202(2)), does not limit law-enforcement investigation (CRS §44-10-202(3)), does not license a business by itself (a local licence is also required — Run 1, Part 3), does not run the patient registry (CDPHE) and does not regulate hemp cultivation (CDA). MED's mission statement: “The Marijuana Enforcement Division is tasked with licensing and regulating the Medical and Retail Marijuana industries in Colorado” (med.colorado.gov). MED's home page states official Secretary of State publication of rules effective 5 January 2026, and lists 2026 Industry Bulletins including 26:06 (Unified Application Option, 1 July 2026) and 26:05 “Attorney General Rescheduling Order, 05/04/26” — whose full text was not opened in Run 2 (see §7.10) and must be opened before any Colorado Schedule III implementation claim or any tribal “state-licensed” claim is drawn from it — Verify. DOR's Taxation Division (separate from MED within DOR) administers excise and sales tax (Run 1, Part 2). Current leadership names are not stated here: no current MED director / DOR Executive Director name was confirmed from an official page opened in Run 2, and a secondary “interim” name was deliberately not used — Verify from med.colorado.gov / cdor.colorado.gov before naming any individual. MED portal: med.colorado.gov; fees: med.colorado.gov/licenses-and-fees; Licensed Facilities lists: med.colorado.gov — Licensed Facilities — the underlying list is an interactive lookup/list page; direct download file names/formats/URLs remain Unavailable (Run 1 gap unchanged). Do not cite a file name that was not opened.

CDPHE — medical registry + hemp products. Article XVIII, §14 and CRS §25-1.5-106 authorise qualified physicians and advanced practice practitioners with prescriptive authority to recommend medical marijuana; the recommendation is submitted to the Medical Marijuana Registry with the rest of the application, and if complete the patient is issued a registry identification card. A recommendation “cannot be 'filled' as a prescription at a pharmacy” (CDPHE provider page, cdphe.colorado.gov — registry providers). Registry information is confidential (see §12.2). Provider qualifications on the same page: to recommend for all debilitating and disabling conditions — M.D. or D.O., in good standing, Colorado-licensed, with valid unrestricted DEA certification; for disabling conditions only, advanced practice practitioners with prescriptive authority (and dentists, per the same page — Verify) may recommend. Recommendations must be made during an in-person encounter in a clinical setting; telemedicine recommendations are prohibited (Verify against current CDPHE/Medical Board rules). A card for a debilitating condition is valid one year (Verify). Registry statistics portal: cdphe.colorado.gov — registry data (latest PDF opened in Run 1: March 2026 — 52,617 patients / 896 caregivers; April–October 2026 PDFs not opened — do not update the count without opening the CDPHE monthly PDF for the month cited). CDPHE hemp portal: cdphe.colorado.gov/dehs/hemp-food. CDPHE does not license hemp cultivation (CDA), does not license marijuana businesses (MED), and does not issue “prescriptions.” A secondary Q3 2026 summary stating CDPHE “would assume testing/safety oversight from MED if SB 26-161 is enacted as introduced” is not law — SB 26-161 was postponed indefinitely 28 April 2026 (Run 1; status Verify on leg.colorado.gov).

CDA — hemp cultivation only. CRS Title 35, Article 61; application before planting with Key Participants and land details (CRS §35-61-104); annual reporting including pre-planting verification of ≤0.3% delta-9 THC, and an inspection programme for THC concentration (CRS §35-61-105 — FindLaw reproduction; Verify against the official CRS on leg.colorado.gov). CDA does not regulate hemp products after the farm gate (CDPHE), does not license marijuana businesses (MED), and its Hemp Online Portal is an application portal, not a public grower list — no public CDA grower-registration list was located in searches tried (Run 1, unchanged). Colorado has its own USDA-approved state plan (AMS state-and-tribal plan review page); the AMS table “updated 17 Feb 2026” stamp Verify against the current AMS table.

OEDIT — Cannabis Business Office (social equity / business support, not licensing). Created by SB 21-111 (status Verify on leg.colorado.gov), funded by the Marijuana Tax Cash Fund (Run 1, Part 4); portal oedit.colorado.gov — Cannabis Business Office. Programmes (all amounts/statuses secondary-only in Run 1 — do not publish as official OEDIT figures): CannaBusiness Foundations and Growth technical assistance, Cannabis Business Grant, Cannabis Business Loan, Access to Experts, banking/pro bono legal resources; resources are “substantially limited for businesses that work directly with THC.” Eligibility (Run 1, OEDIT page): (1) resided at least 15 years between 1980 and 2010 in a census tract designated as an Opportunity Zone or “Disproportionate Impacted Area”; OR (2) applicant or parent/legal guardian/sibling/spouse/child/minor in guardianship was arrested/convicted for a marijuana offence or subject to civil asset forfeiture related to a marijuana investigation; OR (3) household income in a year prior to application did not exceed 50% of state median income. Eligibility effective date conflict unchanged: 1 Feb 2025 (older MED page) vs 1 Apr 2025 (secondary 2026) — Verify. OEDIT does not issue licences, run the registry, or set tax rates.

Governor. Signs/vetoes bills, issues executive orders, holds clemency power for state convictions, and appoints the DOR Executive Director. Official Governor's office summary: “In 2020, Governor Polis took Executive action to pardon 2,732 Coloradans who had previous marijuana possession convictions of one ounce or less. In 2021, Gov. Polis signed a law increasing the amount of marijuana that adults 21 and older in Colorado can legally possess from one ounce to two ounces and signed an Executive Order granting an additional 1,351 pardons for convictions of possession of two ounces or less of marijuana” (governorsoffice.colorado.gov — rescheduling statement). Total: 2,732 + 1,351 = 4,083. Detail (secondary, consistent — Verify against the executive orders themselves): the 1 Oct 2020 order pardoned 2,732 convictions for possession of 1 oz or less, state-court convictions only, 1978–2012, automatic (no application), not applying to municipal-court or out-of-state convictions, and not expunging/sealing records. The enabling bill was HB 20-1424 (signed June 2020, effective September 2020 — Verify on leg.colorado.gov). Advocacy is not law: Polis called on Congress to pass the Safe Banking Act (April and August 2021), led fellow governors calling on the FDA to reschedule (late 2023), and in September 2024 requested the state appear as a witness in the rescheduling matter; the same Governor's office page calls rescheduling “smart policy, long overdue.” No federal cannabis banking law has been enacted (given baseline). No Colorado statute or rule implementing Schedule III was located in Run 2 beyond MED Bulletin 26:05's title. The Governor does not license businesses, set AMR or tax rates, or run the registry, and a pardon does not expunge/seal a record (see §12.4).

General Assembly. Enacts the Colorado Marijuana Code (Title 44, Article 10), tax statutes (Title 39, Article 28.8), hemp statutes (Title 35, Article 61; Title 25, Article 5), and refers ballot measures (e.g. HB 15-1367 referring Proposition BB — Verify on leg.colorado.gov). Bill pages: leg.colorado.gov. A secondary tracker states the 2026 session adjourned 13 May 2026 — Verify against leg.colorado.gov before stating any 2027 pre-file or special-session position. Run 1's “fresh sweep including 2027 pre-files and any special session” is still outstanding — do not print “nothing pending” without it. The Assembly does not issue licences, administer the registry, or change federal scheduling or federal tax (280E) treatment. Under the given baseline, 280E relief on rescheduling applies to medical activity only; adult-use activity remains fully subject to 280E.

Secretary of State. Administers statewide elections and publishes results; the Colorado Legislative Council's Ballot History pages reproduce official ballot titles and results (see §9.3). The Secretary of State business search is a filing registry, not a marijuana-licence record; two secondary URLs conflict and the official page was not opened — Verify before publishing either URL. The Secretary of State does not license marijuana or hemp businesses, set marijuana tax policy, or decide local opt-in.

Colorado courts. The Colorado Supreme Court and Court of Appeals decide state constitutional/statutory questions (Coats, Cox, Clendenin — §9.4); district courts hear local matters (e.g. the El Paso County District Court judge who blocked Colorado Springs' January 2025 repeal attempt, and the Colorado Supreme Court's February 2025 decision declining to intervene — Run 1, Part 3, secondary-reported, Verify with City Clerk / court records); the U.S. District Court for the District of Colorado and the Tenth Circuit decide federal questions affecting Colorado (Serna, Green Room — §9.4). Courts do not license, tax or regulate prospectively; a holding is limited to its case and jurisdiction (Green Room is a Wyoming case, binding in the Tenth Circuit on its §1983 point but not a Colorado licensing decision).

Department of Public Safety (CDPS) — research and enforcement data, not licensing. CDPS's Division of Criminal Justice, Office of Research and Statistics, publishes Impacts of Marijuana Legalization in Colorado pursuant to CRS §24-33.4-516. The 2025 report (data spanning 2008–2023) is dated December 2025, revised February 2026 (CDPS 2025 Impacts report (PDF) — URL corrected: the ?ref=restoremag.com parameter in the original citation is not part of the official document URL; PDF not re-opened in this audit). Its framing: “2013: Amendment 64 takes effect. Personal possession and grow limits for recreational marijuana are in place but sales are not commercialized. Medical continues as a regulated, commercial market. 2014 to present: Recreational and medical marijuana fully regulated and commercialized. Licensed retail stores opened January 1, 2014.” Its February 2026 revision corrected the executive summary's traffic-fatality figures to: “The number of fatalities with cannabinoid-only or cannabinoid-in-combination positive drivers increased 240%, from 55 in 2013 to 187 in 2022. The number of drivers who had cannabinoids present increased by 39% from 2019 to 2022. Additionally, there were 130 fatalities in 2022 where at least one driver tested positive for a cannabinoid and an additional substance.” Do not quote the pre-correction figures. CDPS does not license businesses or run the registry, and its report is a research publication, not a licence list or tax table. Licence-count-by-premises figures in Run 1 Part 6 citing the CDPS 2025 report (Table 5.1: 2,249 in 2014, peak 3,051 in 2017, 2,580 in 2023) are premises counts, distinct from MED's 2,106 approved business licences end-2025 — do not mix the two series. Neither series was re-opened in this audit.

Department of Law / Attorney General. Colorado's chief legal officer; led a 12-state attorneys-general letter to the DEA urging rescheduling to Schedule III (January 2024, secondary report — Verify against the letter itself / Colorado AG release before quoting). Quote attributed to Attorney General Phil Weiser: “Colorado is committed to protecting the integrity of its first-in-the-nation regulated cannabis market… this action of rescheduling cannabis will better enable that market to function.” Signatories listed: Colorado, Illinois, California, Maryland, Connecticut, Massachusetts, Delaware, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Nevada, New Jersey and Rhode Island (Hemp Gazette — AG rescheduling letter — secondary source, not a primary source). The AG does not license businesses or set Colorado marijuana tax, and no post-28 April 2026 Colorado AG opinion or guidance on Schedule III / the tribal “state-licensed” question was located — Verify before attributing any such position to the AG. MED Bulletin 26:05 is titled “Attorney General Rescheduling Order” (federal Attorney General, by title) — do not confuse it with a Colorado AG opinion.

Local licensing authorities. Every business needs a state MED licence and a local licence from the Local Licensing Authority where the premises sit; MED will not accept a new application unless the local authority has advised MED it allows that business type and is currently accepting applications (Run 1, Part 3). A county governs only unincorporated territory; a city inside it has its own authority. Denver and Broomfield are consolidated city-and-counties — keep them distinct from neighbours. Same-name traps throughout: Aurora CO (not IL), Boulder CO (not Boulder City, NV), Pueblo CO (not Puebla, Mexico), Frisco CO (not TX), Durango CO (not Mexico), Lamar CO, Golden CO, Louisville CO (not KY), Englewood CO (not NJ), Lafayette CO (not LA/IN).

9.4 Key court cases

9.4.1 Coats v. Dish Network, LLC, 2015 CO 44 — brief summary only (full treatment is Run 1, §1.8; do not contradict it)

Brandon Coats, quadriplegic Dish Network customer-service representative 2007–2010, Colorado medical licence for painful muscle spasms, off-duty medical use in accordance with state law, never used at work, terminated after a May 2010 random drug test positive for a marijuana component. Statute: CRS §24-34-402.5 (lawful off-duty activities). Holding: “lawful” under §24-34-402.5 means lawful under both state and federal law; because marijuana was Schedule I federally, off-duty medical use was not protected “lawful activity.” DOJ non-prosecution policy and December 2014 appropriations rider arguments rejected. Claim dismissed; termination lawful under Colorado law as it stood in 2015. Verify against the opinion itself (2015 CO 44) — Run 1 summary only in this audit. Whether Schedule III changes Coats for state-licensed medical use is Verify / unresolved — no post-28 April 2026 Colorado decision was located (Run 1 flag, unchanged). Under the given baseline, Schedule III covers state-licensed medical marijuana and FDA-approved products only; all adult-use remains Schedule I, and the federal medical-marijuana appropriations rider is in force through 11 December 2026. Source: Run 1.

9.4.2 People v. Cox, 2021 COA 68, 493 P.3d 914; interlocutory People v. Cox, 2018 CO 88, 429 P.3d 75

Court of Appeals No. 19CA2085, Mesa County District Court No. 17CR1974, Judge Brian J. Flynn, opinion by Judge Berger, Dailey and Tow, JJ., concurring, announced 13 May 2021. Appeal by the district attorney under §16-12-102(1), C.R.S. 2020, after a jury acquitted defendant David Lawrence Cox of marijuana offences. Source: Justia — People v. Cox, 2021 COA 68 (unofficial reproduction — cite the opinion itself, not the summary). Holdings (as a matter of first impression): (1) the elements of the medical marijuana affirmative defence are prescribed by Colo. Const. Art. XVIII, §14(2)(a) and cannot be supplemented by additional elements purportedly added in later-enacted Colorado statutes; (2) marijuana does not include industrial hemp — bound by the Colorado Supreme Court's interlocutory decision in the same case, People v. Cox, 2018 CO 88, 429 P.3d 75, relying on Art. XVIII, §16(2)(f): “Amendment 64 makes clear that the definition of marijuana 'does not include industrial hemp.'” The trial court expressly did not declare §§18-18-406(3.5), 18-18-406(3)(b)(I), or 18-18-102(18)(a) unconstitutional, contrary to the district attorney's framing. Cox was charged with unlawful cultivation under §18-18-406(3)(a)(I) and asserted the §14(2)(a)(I)–(III) affirmative defence. Citation caution: the Justia header warns division summaries “constitute no part of the opinion” and “may not be cited or relied upon as they are not the official language” — cite the opinion itself, not the summary. A separate People v. Cox (2023) entry in a secondary index concerns jury-deliberation instructions, not the 2021 affirmative-defence holding — do not conflate the two Cox decisions.

9.4.3 People v. Clendenin (2009), Colorado Court of Appeals No. 08CA0624

Holding as summarised in Run 1 and a secondary index: a person does not qualify as a “primary caregiver” under Colorado law simply by supplying marijuana to a patient; they must have significant responsibility for managing the patient's overall well-being. Merely supplying marijuana is not, by itself, “significant responsibility.” Source: Justia — People v. Clendenin (unofficial reproduction). Flag (Run 1, unchanged): current precedential value after Coats is Verify. The full opinion text was not re-opened line-by-line in Run 2; open it before quoting any passage verbatim.

9.4.4 Federal cases affecting Colorado — Serna and Green Room (through-transport / private right of action)

Serna v. Denver Police Department, 58 F.4th 1167 (10th Cir. 2023), No. 21-1446, decided 24 January 2023, opinion by Judge Moritz. Facts (as pleaded, taken as true on a Rule 12(b)(6) dismissal): Francisco Serna, a Texas-licensed hemp farmer, arrived at Denver International Airport in March 2021 for a return flight to Texas travelling with 32 hemp plant clones/rooted clippings and certificates stating he could transport them; Denver police allegedly prevented him from transporting them. He asserted a single claim under §10114(b) of the Agriculture Improvement Act of 2018 (2018 Farm Bill), which authorises states to legalise hemp and regulate production but generally precludes states from interfering with interstate transportation of hemp. District court dismissed for failure to state a claim because §10114(b) did not create a private cause of action. Tenth Circuit affirmed: §10114(b) language did not suggest Congress intended to grant hemp farmers a right to freely transport their product from one jurisdiction to another with no interference from state officials, and courts could not read a private cause of action into a statute lacking rights-creating language; the district court also properly declined to allow amendment. Source: Justia — Serna v. Denver Police Department (unofficial reproduction — verify against the slip opinion). What Serna does NOT decide: it does not decide whether a state ban on through-transport is itself pre-empted in a suit brought by the proper plaintiff or by the United States. Do not over-read Serna as holding that states may freely ban through-transport.

Green Room LLC v. Wyoming, 157 F.4th 1196 (10th Cir. 2025), Nos. 24-8053 & 24-8054, published opinion 27 October 2025. Plaintiffs: Green Room LLC; JB Development Inc. d/b/a Polyxtracts; Cind's CBD and Vape LLC; Up N Smoke II LLC d/b/a Up N Smoke, et al. v. State of Wyoming. The opinion recites the 2018 Farm Bill history (CSA did not distinguish hemp from marijuana before 2018; Farm Bill excluded hemp from the CSA definition of marihuana/marijuana, 21 U.S.C. §802(16)(B)(i), defining hemp as Cannabis sativa L. with delta-9 THC not more than 0.3% dry weight — the pre-11 December 2026 federal definition; the total-THC definition applies after 11 December 2026 per the given baseline) and cites Serna for the proposition that the Farm Bill “authorizes states to legalize hemp and regulate its production within their borders but generally preclude[s] states from interfering with the interstate transportation of hemp” (Serna, 58 F.4th at 1168). The National Agricultural Law Center index summarises its holding as: the Farm Bill's transportation-through provision does not create individual federal rights enforceable under 42 U.S.C. §1983. Sources: govinfo — Green Room opinion (PDF); National Agricultural Law Center — hemp case index. Jurisdiction warning: Green Room is a Wyoming case, not a Colorado case. Include it only as binding Tenth Circuit authority that also governs Colorado federal courts on the §1983 point, and as the through-transport companion to Serna. It is not a Colorado licensing or tax decision.

Other federal material — not verified, do not cite as authority: a secondary federal-hemp litigation tracker summarises four circuits (Seventh in C.Y. Wholesale 2020, Fourth in Northern Virginia Hemp 2025, Eighth in Bio Gen 2025, Tenth in Green Room 2025) as holding the 2018 Farm Bill does not pre-empt state restrictions on hemp-derived THC, while the Ninth Circuit in AK Futures (delta-8) and Fourth Circuit in Anderson (THC-O) hold those cannabinoids federally lawful hemp — and notes PL 119-103's redefinition and a claimed DEA HHC Schedule I listing/drug code (4 May 2026). Source (research lead only, do not cite as authority): federal-hemp-litigation-tracker. Verify each circuit holding from the opinions themselves, and verify the HHC listing against the Federal Register / DEA, before including either. Also listed in the National Agricultural Law Center index, not verified: Brown v. United States, 144 S.Ct. 1195 (2024) (2018 Farm Bill reclassification of “hemp” does not apply retroactively to marijuana convictions) — general federal law, not a Colorado holding. No Colorado-specific federal district-court hemp/marijuana injunction was located in Run 2 — Verify before claiming none exists.

9.4.5 Additional Colorado Supreme Court cases touching the registry (research-notes material, not headline cases)

Doe v. Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment, 2019 (Colorado Supreme Court — citation number Verify), and companion Boland cases: CDPHE's Medical Marijuana Policy No. 2014-01 (Referral Policy) — CDPHE would use statistical reviews of physician recommendations (caseload ≥3,521 recommendations/year; increased plant counts for >30% of caseload; >one-third of caseload under age 30) to decide reasonable-cause referrals to the Colorado Medical Board. The Supreme Court concluded: (1) an entire state agency could not be a “state public body” under the Open Meetings Law, so the Doctors did not establish CDPHE violated the OML; (2) the Referral Policy was interpretive rather than legislative, so it fell within an APA exception and was not subject to APA rulemaking requirements; (3) referring the Doctors to the Board did not constitute final agency action and was not reviewable under the APA. Governor Bill Owens designated CDPHE as the “state health agency” by Executive Order No. D 001 01 (5 February 2001). Sources: Justia — Doe v. CDPHE (2019); FindLaw — Boland v. Colorado Medical Board (2019) (both unofficial reproductions). Caution: the 3,521 threshold and referral policy are 2014-era material — do not present them as the current CDPHE referral policy without a current CDPHE/Medical Board source.
