PART 10 — TRIBAL AND INTERSTATE

10.1 The two Colorado tribes — government and location

Colorado has two federally recognised tribes, both in southwestern Colorado: the Southern Ute Indian Tribe and the Ute Mountain Ute Tribe. Source (secondary for the count): 500 Nations — Colorado Cannabis — Verify the count against the Bureau of Indian Affairs tribal list; tribal government structure below is from official tribal/USDA sources where stated.

Southern Ute Indian Tribe: headquarters Ignacio; reservation predominantly within La Plata County, southwestern Colorado. The governing body is the Southern Ute Tribal Council (the 2024 Criminal Code is enacted “pursuant to its Constitution, Article VII, Section 1(e),” authorising the Tribal Council to govern administration of justice through tribal courts). Sources: Southern Ute Title 5 Criminal Code (PDF, eff. 1 Mar 2024); Southern Ute Drum, 23 Feb 2023 (tribal newspaper).

Ute Mountain Ute Tribe: headquarters Towaoc (pronounced TOW-ay-ock); reservation near Towaoc in the Four Corners region, primarily in Colorado, extending into Utah and New Mexico; borders Mesa Verde National Park, the Navajo Reservation and the Southern Ute Reservation (geography secondary — Verify against the Tribe's official site). The governing body is the Ute Mountain Ute Tribal Council (Constitution and By-Laws adopted 8 May 1940 in the Act's recital; 6 June 1940 in the Resolution's recital — note the two dates differ between the two documents in the same USDA file; do not print either as settled without a tribal constitution source). The Tribe's regulator under its cannabis/hemp instruments is the Cannabis Regulatory Commission. Sources: USDA — Ute Mountain Ute Cannabis Control Act / Hemp Plan (PDF); Free Dictionary encyclopedia entry (secondary, geography only).

Current tribal leadership names are not stated here. Manuel Heart is named as Chairman in the 17 August 2022 Ute Mountain resolution, and Marilynn House as Recording Secretary — those are 2022 document signatories, not a verified current-leadership statement for 2026. Do not carry them forward as current leaders.

10.2 Southern Ute Indian Tribe — cannabis and hemp position (official tribal law controls)

Criminal Code (effective 1 March 2024), Title 5, §5-7-102 “Unlawful Possession or Use of Marijuana”: “(1) It is unlawful to possess or consume marijuana, so long as it remains illegal under federal law. (2) Any person who violates this Section is subject to penalties, dependent on amount, in accordance with the criminal penalty schedule.” Source: Southern Ute Title 5 Criminal Code (above). Penalty schedule (March 2024): §5-7-102 unlawful possession/use of marijuana — fine limit up to $100 for amounts under one ounce; §5-7-108 (underage possession/consumption, under 18 / 18–20) is a Class 6 offence with fine, community service and rehabilitative sentencing options. Source: Southern Ute Criminal Penalty Schedule (1 March 2024, Res. 2023-119 — Verify against the schedule document itself; it is not separately linked in Part 10).

What this means, carefully: the Southern Ute offence is expressly tied to federal illegality, not to Colorado state law. Adult-use marijuana remains Schedule I federally, so the tribal prohibition plainly still covers adult-use possession on the Southern Ute Reservation. The Schedule III move for state-licensed medical marijuana does not by itself make tribal possession lawful: Schedule III substances remain federally controlled, possession outside a lawful (e.g. prescription/registration) channel remains federally unlawful, and the Tribe has no medical programme that could supply such a channel (see below). Do not read §5-7-102 as automatically switching off for medical marijuana after 28 April 2026 — that inference is Verify, and the safer reading on the text alone is that the prohibition remains in force for any federally unlawful possession.

No Southern Ute cannabis or hemp programme found: no Southern Ute medical marijuana programme, retail dispensary, marijuana licence, or hemp cultivation licence was located in any official tribal or state source in Run 2. No Southern Ute USDA-approved tribal hemp plan appears on the USDA AMS list (see §10.4) — phrased as none located in searches tried, not absolute proof; a full AMS-list check is still required (see Still-Unverified list).

Texas hemp-processing investment — not a Colorado programme: “The Southern Ute Indian Tribe recently partnered with Panda Biotech to process hemp in a facility located in Wichita Falls, Texas. Members of Tribal Council and the Southern Ute Growth Fund toured the processing facility in person, which is slated to begin production later this year.” The article discusses fibre/stalk/herd before seed, industrial hemp, and uses in textiles, plastic, paper & pulp, construction, protein and feed. Source: Southern Ute Drum, 23 February 2023 (above). Do not present this as a Southern Ute Reservation cultivation licence, dispensary, or Colorado programme — it is a Texas processing investment/partnership.

Historical interest, not a programme: Southern Ute Councilman Adam Red, Tri-Ute Council meeting, Towaoc, 7 June 2019: “The Southern Ute Indian Tribe is open to all aspects of hemp,” the 2014 Farm Bill opened all aspects of hemp production to tribes without a university/academic stipulation, only one hemp-processing plant in Colorado at that time (in Montrose, CO), “We need to partner in some way, on the hemp side, the non-THC product,” and concern that big companies would flood the market with infused products. Source: Southern Ute Drum, 7 June 2019 (via prior research). Historical federal-funding concern, unresolved in that document: Colorado Commission of Indian Affairs, 2nd Quarterly Meeting Minutes, 8 December 2018 (History Colorado, Denver): Councilman Adam Red “expressed concern that if the SUIT institutes a retail hemp or marijuana outlet, federal funding might be taken away.” The question was referred for follow-up (CCIA, DOR, UMUT, SUIT listed) and Jim Burack stated he did not know the answer. Source: CCIA minutes (via prior research). This is 2018 concern, not a programme, and the federal-funding consequence was not resolved in that document.

Old secondary “ban” claim — do not use as current law: Simplifya, “Tribes and Cannabis: Federalism is Messy” (last updated ~2,789 days before the prior search — an old page, not current evidence) states: “In Colorado, none of the Ute tribal governments have expressed interest in the industry, and the Southern Utes actively enforce a ban on cannabis in their territory,” and asserts PL-280 gives states criminal jurisdiction over reservations. Source: Simplifya (via prior research). Do not present this as current official tribal law: the operative current evidence is the Tribe's own 2024 Criminal Code (§5-7-102 above), and Colorado's PL-280 status and its application to the two Ute reservations is itself Verify — do not assert it from Simplifya alone. Note also that the Simplifya blanket “no Ute interest” reading is already contradicted for Ute Mountain Ute by its 2022 Act/Plan and AMS approval (§10.3).

10.3 Ute Mountain Ute Tribe — hemp YES, marijuana NO (the Act's title misleads; its operative text decides)

USDA-approved tribal hemp plan — confirmed current in substance: USDA AMS List of USDA-approved Hemp Plans lists “Ute Mountain Ute | Approved Plan (pdf) ” (“Approved ” = plan approved under the final rule which took effect 22 March 2021 — AMS table update stamp “17 February 2026” Verify against the current AMS table). Once approved, a plan remains in effect unless withdrawn by the Tribal government or revoked by USDA, or unless substantive revisions require re-submission. Source: USDA AMS plan review.

The 2022 instruments: Tribal Council Resolution No. 2022-107, dated 17 August 2022 (adopted 6 for, 0 against, quorum of 7), formally approving the Hemp Program Plan for submission to USDA and the Cannabis Control Act; the Plan and Act had first been approved 20 April 2022 by Resolution No. 2022-067, then edited after USDA review. Source: USDA Ute Mountain Ute PDF (above).

Hemp Program Plan — scope and licences: the Tribal Council establishes the Plan regulating all activities related to hemp cultivation, manufacture, possession, import, transport and distribution under Tribal Constitution Art. V, §§2(b), (d), (g), (n) and (p) and §2; it applies to all hemp operations on the Tribe's Lands, including fee lands whether within the exterior boundaries of the reservation or not; no person may cultivate, possess, distribute, transport or import hemp of any kind on or onto Tribal Lands without first obtaining a licence under the Plan and complying with relevant regulations (transport through Tribal Lands is not regulated so long as the product is not unloaded onto Tribal Lands). Licences that may be issued: Hemp Industry Licence; Hemp Import Licence; Hemp Cultivation Licence; Hemp Distribution Licence; Hemp Product Manufacturing Licence; Hemp Transport Licence (not required for through-transport not delivered/deposited on Tribal Lands). USDA licence numbering: DOI Tribal Government Identification Code for Ute Mountain Ute is M45754, so licences are numbered M45754_####. Regulatory activities are administered by the Tribe's Cannabis Regulatory Commission under the Cannabis Control Act. Same USDA PDF source.

The decisive marijuana exclusion — read this before citing the Act's title: the Hemp Program Plan states (Title I, §1.07): “The Tribe's Cannabis Control Act allows the issuance of various licenses related to hemp and does not authorize any licenses related to marijuana.” And the Cannabis Control Act itself states (§1.04.01(a)): “Possession, cultivation, distribution, import, transport, and manufacture of marijuana and marijuana products on Tribal Lands is not authorized by this Act and remains illegal.” The Act's §1.01 purpose language (“authorizes the possession, cultivation, distribution, and manufacture of cannabis”) is expressly qualified by “Nothing in this Act is intended to authorize activities which are prohibited by federal law,” and §1.04 limits authorised activity to hemp “only to the extent such activities are authorized by the Agricultural Improvement Act of 2018” and “not prohibited by the United States.” No licence may be issued under the Act until the Tribal Hemp Program Plan is approved by USDA and remains in effect; if the Plan is suspended or terminated, the Act is simultaneously suspended or terminated. Same USDA PDF source.

Consequence — state it plainly: despite its name, the Ute Mountain Ute Cannabis Control Act does not create a marijuana programme, a medical marijuana programme, or any marijuana licence. It creates a hemp-only regulatory regime. No operating Ute Mountain Ute marijuana dispensary, medical programme, or marijuana licence was located in any official source in Run 2, and no count of hemp licences actually issued under the Plan was located — licences issued: Unavailable (the Plan authorises licences; authorisation is not proof of issuance).

Superseded history (show the change, do not present as current): as of January 2020 / July 2021 summaries, Ute Mountain Ute was “Drafting a Plan for USDA Review” (USDA January 2020 table via Triage Health Law Blog; PMC content analysis adapting USDA AMS 2021 status as of 14 July 2021). That is superseded by the 17 February 2026 AMS Approved Plan entry (update stamp Verify, above). Sources: PMC article PMC10245984; Stratis Hemp state/tribal plans page (both secondary). Old secondary list entry (superseded in part): The Emerald Magazine's “100+ Indigenous-Owned Cannabis Businesses” states “Ute Mountain Ute Tribe (Towaoc, Colo.) … it appears the Tribe is only in the preliminary discussion phase with several entities regarding their for…” (truncated in extract). Do not use as current status — it predates/is superseded by the 2022 Plan/Act and AMS approval for hemp, and it does not establish a marijuana programme in any event.

10.4 Tribal compact / IGA law — no Colorado cannabis compact statute was found

Answer to the commission's question (“cite CRS §26-2C-41 equivalent if any”): No Colorado statute equivalent to New Mexico's §26-2C-41 tribal cannabis IGA regime was located in searches tried. State that absence plainly and do not import New Mexico's Picuris/Pojoaque IGA model into Colorado. (For the avoidance of doubt: §26-2C-41 is a New Mexico citation; Colorado has no section of that number creating cannabis IGAs, and no Colorado cannabis compact with either Ute tribe was located.) Until the residual CRS search is run, the conclusion is “none found,” not “none exists” as a matter of absolute proof — word it that way.

What Colorado compact law WAS found — gaming and taxation only, not cannabis:

  • CRS Title 44, Article 31 — Tribal-state Gaming Compact. §44-31-101: in accordance with 25 U.S.C. §2710(d)(3)(C), a tribe with jurisdiction over Indian lands where Class III gaming is conducted or to be conducted shall request the Governor to negotiate a tribal-state gaming compact; the Governor shall negotiate in good faith after consultation with the Colorado Limited Gaming Control Commission. Source: CRS §44-31-101 (Verify against the official CRS on leg.colorado.gov; original cited an unofficial reproduction). Gaming only — do not cite as cannabis compact authority.
  • CRS §44-31-103 — Provisions of compact (gaming): may include application of tribal/state criminal and civil laws directly related to licensing/regulation, allocation of criminal/civil jurisdiction, state assessment to defray regulation costs, tribal taxation comparable to state taxation for comparable activities, remedies for breach, standards for operation/maintenance including licensing, and any other subjects directly related to gaming activities. Source: CRS §44-31-103 (Verify against official CRS). Gaming only.
  • BIA Gaming Compacts (Colorado filter): Ute Mountain Ute Tribal-State Gaming Compact approved 10 July 1992; Southern Ute Tribal-State Gaming Compact approved 8 October 1992 and 21 August 1995 (amended). Gaming compacts only. Source: BIA gaming compacts page (Verify — not opened in this audit).
  • CRS Title 24, Article 61 — Taxation Compact Between the Southern Ute Indian Tribe, La Plata County, and the State of Colorado. §24-61-102 approves the Taxation Compact dated 18 March 1996, signed by Governor Roy Romer, Southern Ute Chairman Leonard C. Burch, La Plata County Commission Chairman Fred W. Klatt III, Assessor Craig Larson, and Treasurer Ed Murray, settling a dispute over state/county authority to tax tribal real/personal property within the Southern Ute Reservation; §24-61-103 requires ratification by each signatory's legislative body and approval by the Secretary of the Interior if required. Source: CRS §24-61-102 (Verify against official CRS). Taxation compact only, 1996, La Plata County — not a cannabis compact, not a statewide cannabis IGA.
  • CRS §25-7-1306 (Title 25, Article 7, Part 13 — reservation air programme): state agencies may provide technical assistance/training/consultation to the tribe to carry out an intergovernmental agreement and that part. Air programme IGA context only, not cannabis (Verify against official CRS).

Residual check: run a direct CRS / leg.colorado.gov search for “cannabis” + “tribe” / “compact” before finalising, to confirm or refute the “no Colorado cannabis compact statute” conclusion. Until that search is run, the conclusion is “none found,” not “none exists” as a matter of absolute proof — word it that way. No MED tribal licence list was located (Run 1, Part 5, unchanged). MED lists do not cover tribal licences. Tribal records for either tribe: Unavailable beyond the instruments cited in §§10.2–10.3.

10.5 Tribal Schedule III “state-licensed” question — REMAINS Verify (with full reasoning)

Verdict: Verify — not resolved. No official tribal or state source located in Run 2 shows either Colorado tribe operating a medical marijuana programme, or shows whether any such programme would count as “state-licensed” for the 28 April 2026 Schedule III rule. Keep the flag and print the reasoning, not a resolution by inference.

The fixed baseline rule, as given, is “state-licensed.” State-licensed medical marijuana and FDA-approved products moved to Schedule III effective 28 April 2026 (91 FR 22714); adult-use remains Schedule I. A tribal licence is not, on its face, a state licence.

Neither tribe has a medical programme to which the question could attach. Southern Ute law criminalises marijuana possession so long as it remains illegal under federal law (§10.2) and no Southern Ute medical programme was found. Ute Mountain Ute's Cannabis Control Act expressly does not authorise marijuana licences or marijuana activity on Tribal Lands (§10.3). There is therefore no tribal medical marijuana activity in Colorado that could even be tested against the “state-licensed” definition.

A USDA-approved tribal hemp plan does not answer the question. The Ute Mountain Ute AMS-approved plan is a hemp plan under the 2018 Farm Bill (7 U.S.C. §1639p framework; 7 CFR Part 990). Hemp is, by definition, cannabis at or below 0.3% delta-9 THC dry weight (pre-11 December 2026 federal definition; total-THC definition after 11 December 2026 per the fixed baseline) — it is not “medical marijuana,” and a hemp licence is not a medical marijuana licence, state or tribal. Do not let the hemp plan do work in the Schedule III analysis that it cannot do.

The compact route that could have created functional equivalence does not exist in Colorado. In a state with a cannabis compact statute, a tribe operating under a compact that expressly adopts state licensing could argue functional equivalence with “state-licensed.” No such Colorado cannabis compact or statute was found (§10.4), so that argument has no Colorado footing. (This is a structural point, not a claim about what a future compact could do.)

No guidance was located. No IRS, DEA, or Colorado guidance (MED, DOR, CDPHE, AG, Governor) answering the tribal “state-licensed” question was located in Run 2. MED Bulletin 26:05 (“Attorney General Rescheduling Order,” 4 May 2026) was not opened in full (§9.1) — it might touch the question, which is a further reason to open it before closing this item, but its title alone does not resolve it.

The Southern Ute wording cuts the other way for any future claim. Because §5-7-102 ties unlawfulness to federal illegality, even a future tribal medical programme would need to confront both the tribal code and the federal controlled-substance status of the specific product/activity — Schedule III does not make medical marijuana federally “legal” in the sense of unregulated possession; it makes it a Schedule III controlled substance, lawful only through lawful channels. That distinction must be preserved in any future update.

What would resolve it: (a) a DEA/IRS rule, guidance, or FAQ expressly addressing tribal medical programmes and the “state-licensed” / “qualifying state-issued medical marijuana license” language; (b) a Colorado–tribe cannabis compact expressly adopting state licensing (none found); or (c) a tribal medical programme actually operating under one of those authorities. None was found. Until one appears, the answer is Verify.

Related federal-registration note (secondary, do not overstate): secondary summaries of the federal rescheduling action describe an expedited DEA registration pathway (21 CFR Part 1301) for entities holding a state medical marijuana licence, with the state licence as conclusive evidence of state-law authorisation, and three registration types (manufacturer, distributor, dispenser), with registrations expressly not authorising non-medical use. Source: CRB Monitor CSA Schedule III summary (PDF, secondary commentary on a federal order — Verify against the Federal Register text). If that pathway is as described, it reinforces the “state licence” framing and gives a tribal programme no obvious entry point — but that is a secondary-summary inference, not a holding, and must be labelled as such.

10.6 Interstate — no reciprocity, transport, through-transport, federal land, mail/shipping, import/export

10.6.1 No reciprocity (Run 1, unchanged)

Colorado does not recognise other states' medical cards. Out-of-state patients may not buy medical marijuana in Colorado, but may buy retail if 21+ with valid ID (Run 1, Part 1). No change was located in Run 2. Verify against current MED/CDPHE rules before advising an out-of-state patient.

10.6.2 Transport across state lines — unlawful for marijuana; hemp through-transport is the contested middle

Transporting marijuana across a state line is a federal offence regardless of the laws of the origin and destination states, and Colorado state law does not authorise export (charging statute Verify — cite 21 U.S.C. provisions from the statute, not from secondary summaries). Retail/medical licences authorise activity within Colorado only (Title 44, Article 10 framework, Run 1). Do not describe any Colorado licence as an export licence for marijuana. Hemp through-transport — Serna / Green Room (see §9.4.4 for full holdings): the 2018 Farm Bill “generally preclude[s] states from interfering with the interstate transportation of hemp” (Serna, 58 F.4th at 1168, as quoted in Green Room), but the Tenth Circuit holds that provision does not create an individual federal right enforceable under 42 U.S.C. §1983 (Serna 2023; Green Room 2025). Practical consequence for a Colorado reader: a hemp shipper stopped in transit cannot rely on Serna/Green Room for a personal §1983 damages/injunction claim against the stopping officers; whether the stopping state's restriction is itself pre-empted would need a suit by a proper plaintiff (e.g. the United States) or a different cause of action. Through-transport therefore remains unresolved in the sense that matters to a shipper — lawful in principle under the Farm Bill's text, without an individual enforcement remedy in the Tenth Circuit. Sources: Serna (above); Green Room (govinfo PDF). Ute Mountain Ute through-transport carve-out (tribal, not interstate): the Tribe's Hemp Program Plan does not regulate transport of hemp through Tribal Lands so long as the product is not unloaded onto Tribal Lands; a Hemp Transport Licence is not required for such through-transport (see §10.3). That is a tribal-lands rule, not a Colorado–neighbouring-state rule — do not generalise it. Colorado-internal hemp transport beyond the tribal and federal cases above was not re-researched in Part 10; Part 7 carries the current CDA/CDPHE transport position.

10.6.3 Federal land in Colorado — state law stops at the boundary

National parks — the rule: 36 CFR §2.35(b)(2) makes it an offence to possess a controlled substance anywhere in a park area; 36 CFR §1.4 defines “controlled substance” as anything on Schedules I–V of the federal act. Possession is excepted only when the substance “was obtained by the possessor directly, or pursuant to a valid prescription or order, from a practitioner acting in the course of professional practice or otherwise allowed by Federal or State law” — an exception about provenance, not packaging (Verify against eCFR before quoting verbatim — the original cited this text via secondary citation). Adult-use marijuana remains Schedule I federally, so Colorado-legal adult-use possession becomes a federal offence on park land. Sources (regulation text via secondary citation, Verify against eCFR before quoting verbatim): Puzzle Group; LegalClarity (both secondary). Rocky Mountain National Park (Colorado's own park — the example to use, not Yellowstone/Grand Teton): “Although the use of recreational marijuana is legal in the state of Colorado, it is not legal within Rocky Mountain National Park. If you have marijuana in your possession, dispose of it before you visit, since both possession and use are a federal offense in the park.” Source: Rocky Mountain National Park regulations page (secondary park-information site — Verify against the NPS compendium for Rocky Mountain National Park before printing as an NPS statement). Collateral forfeiture schedule (official federal court document): the U.S. District Court for the District of Colorado approved (January 2023) a National Park Service collateral forfeiture schedule listing 36 CFR 2.35(b)(2) possession of a controlled substance (including marijuana ≥1 oz / 28.35 g, and marijuana-only <1 oz as a separate line) among citable offences. Source: U.S. District Court, District of Colorado — NPS collateral forfeiture schedule (PDF). Jurisdiction nuance (do not flatten): not all parks operate under exclusive federal jurisdiction; many operate under concurrent or partial jurisdiction, where both state and federal law can apply — but federal officers enforce federal law, and possession remains a federal offence regardless of what the surrounding state permits. The Assimilative Crimes Act (18 U.S.C. §13) does not help a possessor here because Congress has directly addressed marijuana possession through the Controlled Substances Act. Source: LegalClarity (secondary — Verify the jurisdiction classification for Rocky Mountain National Park specifically before stating it). National forests / BLM land: no Colorado-specific USFS or BLM marijuana rule text was opened in Run 2. The general principle (federal law governs federal land; adult-use marijuana is federally Schedule I) applies, but specific forest/BLM orders, closures, or penalties are Verify — do not assert a forest-specific rule from the park rule. The same applies to Mesa Verde National Park (which borders the Ute Mountain Ute Reservation — §10.1): it is a national park, so the §2.35 analysis applies in principle, but no Mesa Verde-specific compendium was opened — Verify. Schedule III does not change the park answer for adult-use: Schedule III substances still require a lawful (prescription/registration) channel to possess legally; adult-use marijuana stays Schedule I in any event. Even for state-licensed medical marijuana, the §2.35(b)(2) exception turns on how the substance was obtained and whether federal law allows it — Verify before advising any medical patient that park possession is lawful. Do not advise it on this report alone. Federal facilities generally: federal buildings, military installations, airports' federal areas, and other federal facilities apply federal law; a Colorado medical card or retail purchase does not authorise possession there. Specific facility rules (e.g. Denver International Airport's own policy, which featured in Serna's facts) were not verified as current policy in Run 2 — Verify before printing any airport-specific rule. Serna's facts (Denver police allegedly preventing transport of hemp clones at DIA, March 2021) are litigation facts, not a statement of DIA's current policy.

10.6.4 Mail and shipping — marijuana no, hemp yes-with-conditions (and narrowing after December 2026)

Marijuana by mail is a federal crime regardless of whether it is legal in the sending or receiving state, including within a single legal state, because USPS is a federal agency and every package travels through federal infrastructure; the main charging statute cited in secondary summaries is 21 U.S.C. §841 (distribution) (Verify against USPS Publication 52 and 21 U.S.C. §§841/843 before quoting penalties). Private carriers (FedEx, UPS) follow federal law by policy for marijuana. Sources (secondary summaries of federal law): LegalClarity. Hemp by USPS (domestic only): USPS allows domestic mailing of compliant hemp and CBD products under Publication 52, §453.37, but only when the mailer complies with all federal, state and local laws and retains compliance records (lab results, licences) — secondary summaries differ on the retention period (two years vs three years — Verify against the current Publication 52 text; do not print either period as settled). International mailing of hemp/CBD products is prohibited entirely, including to military APO/FPO/DPO addresses. A Certificate of Analysis from an accredited third-party lab confirming THC below the legal threshold should accompany shipments; USPS can request a “mailability packet” at any time. Vape cartridges — separate federal bar: the Prevent All Cigarette Trafficking (PACT) Act prohibits USPS from shipping any electronic vaping device at all, whether it contains THC, nicotine, CBD, or nothing — so no legal pathway exists for an individual to mail a vape cartridge of any kind through standard USPS shipping, even a hemp-derived one. Source: LegalClarity (secondary — Verify against the PACT Act / Publication 52). Interaction with the fixed federal hemp dates (flag, do not overstate): after 11 December 2026, the federal hemp definition counts total THC and caps products at 0.4 mg total THC per container (fixed baseline). A hemp product that is mailable as “hemp” before that date may cease to be hemp after it — mailers must re-test against the new definition. No USPS guidance updating Publication 52 for the post-11 December 2026 definition was located in Run 2 — Verify before advising any shipper on post-December mailability. Colorado-internal delivery is not “shipping”: regulated marijuana delivery in Colorado is a permit attached to a store/transporter licence, to private residences only, only where the locality opts in (Run 1, Part 1) — it is not mail, not interstate commerce, and not an export channel.

10.6.5 Import / export of hemp products — including Safe Harbor (export-only)

Safe Harbor = export only, registered with CDPHE, may not be sold in Colorado as a hemp product (Run 1, Parts 1/4 — unchanged; see §7.8). No separate “intoxicating hemp licence” outside the MED system was confirmed in Run 1 — Part 7 resolves it: none exists in §44-10-401 (see §7.9; Part 7's verification governs). Potentially intoxicating products may only be produced/distributed/sold by a MED licensee, except the low-dose hemp exception and Safe Harbor exports (SB 23-271 framework, Run 1). International import/export generally: hemp products that meet the federal hemp definition may move in domestic commerce; international movement is governed by destination-country law and, for mail, by the USPS international prohibition above. No Colorado-specific hemp export licence or export volume figure was located — Unavailable. Do not substitute national hemp-trade figures for Colorado exports. Tribal export note: Ute Mountain Ute hemp licences include Hemp Import and Hemp Distribution licences for movement onto/from Tribal Lands (§10.3), but those are tribal licences under a tribal hemp plan, not Colorado export licences, and they do not authorise marijuana movement. Southern Ute has no equivalent instrument located.

10.6.6 Nebraska and Oklahoma's 2014 suit against Colorado — ADDED (absent from the original Part 10)

In December 2014, Nebraska and Oklahoma moved for leave to file a bill of complaint against Colorado in the U.S. Supreme Court under its original jurisdiction over controversies between states, arguing that Colorado's Amendment 64 was pre-empted by the federal Controlled Substances Act and that Colorado's regulated market increased trafficking and law-enforcement, judicial and penal costs in their states. They sought a declaration that the CSA pre-empted Amendment 64's licensing, regulation and taxation provisions and an injunction blocking Colorado from implementing them. On 21 March 2016, the Court denied the motion for leave to file the bill of complaint, without opinion or explanation (6–2; Justice Thomas dissenting, joined by Justice Alito, arguing the Constitution and 28 U.S.C. §1251(a) gave the Court original and exclusive jurisdiction over controversies between states and did not leave it discretion to decline). Effect, stated plainly: the challenge ended at the pleading stage. The denial is not a ruling that Colorado's law was valid, and it did not decide the pre-emption question; nor does it bar later challenges in federal district court. Docket number and U.S. Reports citation Verify against the Supreme Court journal / order list for 21 March 2016 before citing (case name: Nebraska v. Colorado, filed December 2014, denied 21 March 2016, as reported).

No official out-of-state buyer count was retrieved for any Colorado border town (Run 1, Part 3, unchanged).
