Every fact keeps a source link where a source was opened; items still unresolved keep a Verify flag and no figure, date or URL has been invented for them. “Retail” = adult-use. “Medical” = medical marijuana. MED = Marijuana Enforcement Division, Colorado Department of Revenue.

Corrected Federal baseline paragraph

Split scheduling: state-licensed medical marijuana and FDA-approved products are in Schedule III effective 28 April 2026 (91 FR 22714). All adult-use marijuana remains Schedule I. The broader 2024 rescheduling proposal is not final. IRS §280E: Treasury has said rescheduling generally removes §280E as a bar for businesses no longer dealing in Schedule I/II substances, guidance forthcoming. That relief applies to medical-licence activity only; all retail activity remains fully subject to §280E, even from the same premises or company. Colorado licenses medical and retail marijuana separately under one consolidated code, Title 44, Article 10, and many businesses hold both licences. A dual holder must therefore split its activity: medical sales, inventory, books and tax treatment on one side; retail on the other. Verify — no Colorado guidance document opened prescribes the exact federal accounting split for dual holders; check IRS and MED guidance before any filing position. Hemp: Public Law 119-37 §781 takes legal effect 12 November 2026, but Public Law 119-103 §2019 limits it until 11 December 2026 to only the provisions excluding cannabinoids that are not naturally produced or are synthesised. The full total-THC definition and the 0.4 mg total THC per container cap apply after 11 December 2026. USDA enforcement of the DEA-registered-laboratory hemp testing requirement is delayed until 31 December 2026. The federal medical-marijuana appropriations rider is in force through 11 December 2026. No federal cannabis banking law has been enacted. If any tribe operates a medical programme, whether it counts as “state-licensed” for Schedule III is Verify — no tribal medical programme source was located, and MED Bulletin 26:05 (4 May 2026) was not opened. Sourcing rule: official government sources were prioritised. Where a fact rests only on a secondary source, search extract, or a reproduction (Cornell LII / Justia / colorado.public.law / Innodata) rather than the official page itself, that is stated. Anything uncertain, conflicting or unavailable is marked Verify or Unavailable. No proposed bill is presented as current law. Personal phone numbers and emails of individuals are not reproduced; published office contacts are.

PART 11 — OPERATIONS RULES

Rule-version note (read first). The current Colorado Marijuana Rules are 1 CCR 212-3, version effective 5 January 2026 — Colorado Secretary of State adoption order, 1 CCR 212-3. Cornell LII reproductions of individual rules may lag that version. A material renumbering must be carried into this file: Rule 4-115 is the sampling/testing programme rule, while contaminant-testing limits are now in Rule 4-215 (formerly Rules 4-115, 4-120 and 4-121). Health & Safety Advisories therefore correctly cite Rule 4-215, not 4-115. Full current rule book: Colorado Secretary of State — 1 CCR 212-3 (PDF) — Verify verbatim against that official text before court or filing use, wherever this Part cites a Cornell reproduction.

11.1 Premises security and surveillance

Rule 3-225 — video surveillance, general duty: an applicant must install a fully operational video surveillance and camera recording system before exercising the privileges of a Regulated Marijuana Business — Cornell LII — Rule 3-225 (reproduction). Equipment: at minimum digital or network video recorders, cameras capable of meeting the rule's recording requirements, and a minimum of one on-premises video monitor. Rule 3-225(C) — areas that must be recorded: point-of-sale areas; areas where shipping and receiving of Regulated Marijuana occurs; areas where Test Batches are collected; areas where Regulated Marijuana waste is destroyed; and points of ingress and egress to the exterior of the Licensed Premises. All entrances and exits must be recorded from both indoor and outdoor vantage points, and outdoor cultivation is treated the same as indoor Limited Access Areas for coverage purposes. Rule 3-225(E)(1) — continuous recording: all camera views of all Limited Access Areas must be continuously recorded 24 hours a day; motion detection is authorised only when the licensee can demonstrate that monitored activities are adequately recorded. Rule 3-225(E)(2) — retention, VERIFIED in the reproduction: all surveillance recordings must be kept for a minimum of 30 days and be in a format that can be easily accessed for viewing, archived in a format that ensures authentication and guarantees no alteration of the recorded image. Rule 3-225(A)(3) — access and remote viewing: licensees must make video surveillance records and recordings available for viewing at the Licensed Premises on request of the Division, the relevant Local Licensing Authority or Local Jurisdiction, or any other state or local law enforcement agency for a purpose authorised by the Marijuana Code or for any other state or local law enforcement purpose; a licensee may access records remotely to meet the rule. Rule 3-225(E)(6) — preservation on notice: surveillance video recordings may not be destroyed if the licensee knows or should have known of a pending criminal, civil or administrative investigation, or any other proceeding for which the recording may contain relevant information. Source for (E)(6): secondary summary of Rule 3-225 — Verify verbatim against the 5 January 2026 rule text before final reliance.

Related security rules, cited but not re-opened in full: Rule 3-205 (Limited Access Areas) and Rule 3-220 (alarm systems and lock standards) are part of the 3-series security package. Their detailed alarm, lock and access-control specifications are Verify against the 5 January 2026 text — do not copy any local-jurisdiction summary (for example a Silverthorne local code excerpt citing 40-day preservation, or a local plan stating a DVR “holds up to 40 days”) into the state rule. The state minimum is 30 days.

Hours — state rule, not to be conflated with local rules: state stores shall not sell or serve from 12:00 a.m. to 8:00 a.m. Mountain Time; hospitality and hospitality-and-sales businesses shall not sell or permit consumption from 2:00 a.m. to 7:00 a.m. A local excerpt citing state hours of 8 a.m.–2 a.m. with no retail sales 2–7 a.m. was not adopted as the state rule. Source: Rule 3-245, via the Secretary of State rule book; full Rule 3-245 text Verify.

11.2 Inventory control and Metrc

Metrc as system of record: Colorado rules require Metrc as the primary inventory system of record; licensees must measure and record weight/count at key transition points, reconcile weight/count of all on-premises and in-transit inventory at close of business each day, and identify, weigh and track all waste until transfer or disposal. Licensees and employees are responsible for accuracy, and misstatements or omissions may be a licence violation. Source: Colorado State Auditor, August 2019 evaluation of MED/Metrc — direct auditor link not confirmed; do not cite a guessed URL. Rule 3-810 — tracking scope: tracking runs from propagation through transfer to another business, transporter taking control, delivery, point of sale, and disposal; the licensee must be able to reconcile transported and on-hand inventory with the system and with transaction history and transport receipts; a decontamination method must be input into the system. Source: Rule 3-810, Cornell LII (reproduction); full 5 January 2026 text Verify. Transfer manifests — operational content: a Metrc manifest documents product transfers, including weight and description, driver name and vehicle licence plate. Source: DOR presentation summary (secondary); full manifest field list Verify against Rule 3-805/3-810.

Monthly-report deadline — UNRESOLVED, do not publish as settled: secondary guides (IndicaOnline 2025 guide, NACAT, GrowerIQ) claim monthly reports are due by the 15th and monthly reconciliation is required. Run 1 already flagged the 15th deadline as Verify against MED Rule 3-series / Metrc guidance, and Run 2 did not locate an MED confirmation. The daily close-of-business reconciliation above is the verified rule; any monthly deadline remains Verify.

Waste: waste must be tracked in Metrc until transfer or disposal, and destroyed under Rule 3-230 (see §11.7 recall handling). The detailed waste-rendering method (e.g. ≥50% non-cannabis mix) was stated for Utah in other work and must not be imported into Colorado — the Colorado waste-rendering standard is Verify against Rule 3-230.

11.3 Testing — licensed facilities, required tests, sampling, failed tests

Rule 4-115 — programme scope: Rule 4-115 establishes the Division's mandatory testing and sampling programme applicable to Regulated Marijuana Businesses, specifically Medical and Retail Marijuana Testing Facilities; the Marijuana Code requires the State Licensing Authority to establish acceptable contaminant limits and a ±15% potency variance, both included in this rule — Cornell LII — Rule 4-115 (reproduction). Rule 4-115 — Division direction and adulteration hold: the Division may require that a Test Batch be submitted to a specific Regulated Marijuana Testing Facility to verify compliance, perform investigations, compile data or address a public-health concern. Effective 1 July 2023, if a testing facility suspects or has reason to suspect a Sample Increment or Test Batch has been adulterated, it must notify the Division and quarantine the Sample Increment or Test Batch for a minimum of 48 hours from notification before proceeding with any testing. Rule 4-115/4-215 — failure standard: if Regulated Marijuana is found to have a contaminant above the permissible level, it has failed contaminant testing; the Division also reserves the right, on good cause and reasonable grounds, to determine that a particular Test Batch presents a risk to public health or safety and therefore has failed a contaminant test. Verify all of the above verbatim against the 5 January 2026 SOS text.

Rule 4-215(A) — no transfer or processing before passing: a Regulated Marijuana Business shall not transfer or process Regulated Marijuana, Pre-Rolled Marijuana, Infused Pre-Rolled Marijuana, Concentrate or Product unless Test Batches from each Harvest Batch or Production Batch from which it was derived have been tested by a Regulated Marijuana Testing Facility for contaminants and passed all required contaminant tests, except as permitted in Rule 5-205(C), 6-205(C), or where a Reduced Testing Allowance has been achieved — Cornell LII — Rule 4-215 (reproduction).

Rule 4-215 — mandatory test families (not voluntary): microbial contamination, pesticides, mycotoxins, elemental impurities/heavy metals, residual solvents, and THC/cannabinoid potency, plus water activity where specified, are part of the mandatory programme. Microbial testing covers Harvest Batches of flower, shake and trim, re-testing after decontamination, Production Batches of Physical Separation-, Heat/Pressure- or Food-Based Concentrate, Solvent-Based Concentrate produced through Remediation, Products, Pre-Rolled and Infused Pre-Rolled Marijuana, Hemp Products, Pressurized Metered Dose Inhalers, Vaporizer Delivery Devices, and Audited Product, at the frequency in Rules 4-215(A) and 4-230(B).

Rule 4-215 — residual-solvent panel and limits (selected, as reproduced; re-attributed from Rule 4-115 to Rule 4-215 under current numbering; Verify against the SOS text): the residual-solvent test must include, but need not be limited to, acetone, butane, ethanol, heptanes, isopropyl alcohol, propane, benzene, toluene, pentane, hexane, methanol, ethyl acetate and total xylenes (not approved for use; tested because they may be present in approved solvents). Limits: acetone, butanes, ethanol, heptanes, isopropyl alcohol, propane, pentane and ethyl acetate each <1,000 ppm; benzene <2 ppm; toluene <180 ppm; hexane <60 ppm; total xylenes <430 ppm; methanol <600 ppm; any other non-permitted solvent: none detected.

Rule 4-215 — other limits (selected, as reproduced; re-attributed from Rule 4-115 to Rule 4-215; Verify against the SOS text): Shiga toxin-producing E. coli (STEC): absent in 1 g for flower/shake/trim (other than wet whole plant allocated for extraction), products other than Audited Product, pre-rolls and related categories. Aflatoxins (B1+B2+G1+G2): <20 ppb total for specified solvent-based concentrates. Full pesticide/microbial/mycotoxin tables Verify against the 5 January 2026 Rule 4-215 text.

Expanded solvent panel, September 2026 (secondary, operationally important): MED's expanded residual-solvent panel took effect 28 September 2026, adding 17 more solvents for concentrates, many of which — including methylene chloride — must be non-detectable to pass; triethylamine enforcement was to follow after at least 72 hours' notice. The panel had been scheduled for 1 July 2026 but was delayed because no labs were yet certified to run the new tests. Source: Simplifya advisory, 2026 (secondary); Verify the panel list against MED's September 2026 notice before final reliance.

Failed-test handling — secondary summary, Verify against rule text: a failed result is added to the inventory-tracking package; flower/trim failing contamination (except microbials/pesticides) must be destroyed or decontaminated, with two new test batches to the same or two new facilities — if either fails, the failed batches and the entire harvest batch are destroyed and destruction documented; a manufacturer may process a failed sample/pre-roll batch into solvent-based concentrate producing two new test batches, destroyed if they fail required contaminant/potency tests. Source: secondary summary of Rule 4-115 (as formerly numbered); Verify full remediation/retest procedure against Rules 4-215/4-230.

CDPHE certification categories (secondary summary): elemental impurities, microbials, mycotoxins, pesticides, residual solvents, THC/cannabinoid potency and water activity are listed as CDPHE certification categories. Required-vs-voluntary status for any test not in Rule 4-215 is Verify.

11.4 Manufacturing — extraction, solvents, food safety

Rule 6-315 — permitted concentrate categories (retail; Rule 6-815 is the accelerator equivalent): a Retail Marijuana Products Manufacturer may produce Physical Separation-Based, Food-Based and Heat/Pressure-Based Retail Marijuana Concentrate — Cornell LII — Rule 6-315 (reproduction). Rule 6-315 — permitted solvents ONLY: Solvent-Based Retail Marijuana Concentrate may use only butane, propane, CO2, ethanol, isopropanol, acetone, heptane, ethyl acetate and pentane. Any other solvent is expressly prohibited unless approved by the Division; a manufacturer may submit a request for Division consideration of a non-permitted solvent at the next formal rulemaking. Rule 6-315 — solvent purity and documentation: all solvents used in extraction must be food-grade or at least 99% pure; the manufacturer must obtain a safety data sheet for each solvent used or stored on the Licensed Premises, and must maintain the safety data sheet and purchase receipt for each solvent. Denatured alcohol is prohibited unless the denaturant is an approved solvent and all other requirements are met. Rule 6-315 — closed-loop and premises controls: a professional-grade closed-loop system capable of recovering solvent is required except for ethanol/isopropanol-only production; extraction must occur in a fully enclosed room designated on the premises diagram; applicable sanitary rules (3-300 series) must be followed; standard operating procedures must cover step-by-step safety checks, preparation, extraction, purging, cleaning and waste disposal per Rule 3-230; flammable solvents, chemicals and waste must be stored per applicable laws, and never more flammable solvent may be on premises than the maximum established for that premises (maximum amount truncated in prior research — Verify).

Accelerator manufacturers: Rule 6-815 mirrors Rule 6-315 for Accelerator Manufacturers — same three non-solvent categories and the same nine-solvent list, with the same prohibition on any other solvent unless Division-approved. Source: Cornell LII — Rule 6-815 (reproduction); Verify against the SOS text.

Food safety for edibles — scope limit: beyond the 3-300 series sanitary-rules reference in Rule 6-315, detailed edible-kitchen requirements (licensing, food-handler, commissary, or CDPHE food-code provisions) were not re-verified from an opened official source in Run 2 and are marked Verify — do not import another state's food rules. Local overlay, not state law: Aurora local rules (March 2024) additionally require certified industrial hygienist + fire protection engineer verification for metals/butane/propane/other flammable-vapour processes under NFPA 1 Chapter 38. That is a local requirement, not a state requirement.

11.5 Packaging, labelling and advertising — operational detail

Label identity — from advisories (not a cited rule text): all Regulated Marijuana must have a label on the container that reflects the licence number of the business that manufactured the product and the Production Batch number. Consumers use exactly those two fields to check an advisory. Source: Colorado Cannabis Times — Health & Safety Advisory, Colorado Medical Processing LLC dba Colorado's Best Dabs (secondary reproduction).

Retail sale limits that labelling must reflect (Run 1, carried): retail sale 1 oz flower equivalent per transaction (Rule 6-110 reproduction: = 8 g concentrate = 800 mg THC edibles, plus up to 6 seeds); retail edibles 10 mg/serving, 100 mg/package; no general potency cap in Colorado. Medical daily limits: 2 oz flower, 8 g concentrate 21+ / 2 g 18–20 (Rule 5-125), 20,000 mg products. Source: Cornell LII — Rule 5-125 (reproduction; medical figures Verify against the current Rule 5-125 text, particularly SB 23-081 implementation; Rule 6-110 via Run 1 and the reproduction above).

Advertising audience and penalty — partially verified: a secondary summary states advertising violations are classified Level I, up to $100,000 per incident plus possible revocation, with an audience rule of ≥71.6% reasonably expected to be 21+. The $100,000 fine-in-lieu figure for Level I generally is corroborated by Rule 8-235 (see §11.7), but the advertising-specific Level I classification and the 71.6% audience figure remain Verify against the full Rule 8-235 list and the advertising rules (3-1000 series). Do not publish the 71.6% figure as a verified rule. Source: Cornell LII — Rule 8-235 (reproduction); audience figure: secondary LegalClarity summary.

Child-resistant standards, Universal Symbol placement, serving marking, exit packaging — NOT re-verified in Run 2: the detailed 3-1000 series requirements for child-resistant packaging, Universal Symbol size/placement, per-serving demarcation and exit packaging were not opened in full in Run 2. They are marked Verify; no standard, dimension or placement rule is asserted here. Source: 1 CCR 212-3, 3-1000 series, via the Secretary of State rule book.

11.6 Recordkeeping

Run 1 recordkeeping anchor, scope Verify: Run 1 stated recordkeeping of current + 3 prior tax years under §44-10-1001. Run 2 did not re-open §44-10-1001 in full; the scope of that retention duty (which records, which licensee types, whether the 3-year period runs from filing, tax year-end or licence year-end) is Verify against the current statute text before final reliance. Do not expand it in this file to “all business records forever” or narrow it to tax returns only without that check. Source: Run 1. Recall records: Rule 3-905 requires stores to keep recall records; advisories direct licensees to save the advisory, the recall notice and every related email and call log. Source: Simplifya advisory summary of Rule 3-905 (secondary); Verify verbatim. Video records: see §11.1 — minimum 30 days, plus preservation where an investigation/proceeding is known or should be known (Verify on the preservation paragraph, §11.1).

11.7 Inspections and discipline

Rule 8-235 — penalty framework: the State Licensing Authority need not prove harm from any alleged violation type. Penalty determinations are based on severity categories in the rule — Cornell LII — Rule 8-235 (reproduction). Rule 8-235 — Level I (most severe), VERIFIED in substance in the reproduction: Level I may include deliberate and wilful violations or violations that harm or have the potential to harm public health, safety or welfare. Penalties may include licence suspension, a fine per individual violation, a fine in lieu of suspension of up to $100,000, and/or licence revocation, depending on mitigating and aggravating circumstances; sanctions may also include restrictions on the licence. Level I examples include: retail sales to persons under 21; medical sales to non-patients; any conduct constituting an unlawful act under §44-10-701; any disqualifying event under §44-10-307; violations of medical/retail sales limits under Rules 5-125 and 6-110(C); permitting diversion outside the regulated distribution system; possessing marijuana from outside the regulated system or an unauthorised source; and knowingly adulterating or altering (or attempting to) any Sample Increment or Test Batch.

Rule 8-235 — “Other Violations”: suspension, fine up to $25,000 per individual violation, fine in lieu of suspension, and/or revocation, plus restrictions. The full current penalty schedule, mitigating-factor list (including no prior written warning/assurance/disciplinary action in the preceding 24 months) and aggravating factors (including transferring unsafe or potentially unsafe product, and prior summary suspension) were truncated in prior research and are Verify against the 5 January 2026 Rule 8-235 text.

Summary suspension and appeals — Verify: the existence of summary-suspension authority under §§44-10-901(1)–(2) is referenced in Rule 1-105, but the full summary-suspension procedure, hearing timeline and appeal route were not re-verified in Run 2 and are Verify. Source: Cornell LII — Rule 1-105 (reproduction). MED 2025 enforcement context (Run 1, carried; Verify against the MED 2025 report PDF itself): 2,829 licences investigated, 846 subject to administrative action, ~$1.08m in fines, 17 Health & Safety Advisories, 469 underage checks at 99% pass. Inspection powers — Verify in detail: general Division inspection authority under the Marijuana Code was not re-opened section-by-section in Run 2; do not assert warrant, entry-hours or sampling powers beyond what Rules 3-225(A)(3) (video on request) and 4-115 (Division-directed testing) establish.

11.8 Transport between licensees

Transporter licence term: a transporter licence is valid for 2 years. Source: CRS §§44-10-505/601/605 (statute text via Justia/FindLaw reproductions; insert leg.colorado.gov link in any republication and Verify against current statute text). Transporter responsibility and premises: a transporter is responsible once it takes control of product; it may contract with multiple businesses; it may maintain licensed premises for temporary storage / centralised distribution in a jurisdiction permitting medical/retail stores, meeting cultivation-facility security requirements; it must use the seed-to-sale system to create shipping manifests. No mixed consumer-delivery vehicle: a transporter shall NOT make consumer deliveries while also transporting between licensed premises in the same vehicle. Manifest fields (delivery context, see §11.9): transport manifests document, among other fields, time of delivery and the name and ID number of valid acceptable identification (full field list truncated in prior research — Verify).

11.9 Delivery operations

Rule 3-615 — delivery permits: a delivery permit is held by a store or transporter; the permit expiration date is aligned with the business licence on renewal, which may result in a reduced permit term. Source: Rule 3-615 reproduction (Innodata) — Rule 3-615 reproduction; Verify against 5 January 2026 text. Rule 3-615 — delivery vehicle: the delivery motor vehicle must be owned or leased by the store, transporter or owner licensee, Colorado-registered and insured, with real-time route tracking accessible remotely in real time; it must be equipped with video surveillance that digitally records during all deliveries, covering at least the secured, locked, opaque storage compartment and the front view of the vehicle (e.g. dash camera); that video must be kept for a minimum of 30 days, be capable of being embedded with date and time, be reproducible on request from law enforcement, the Division, a Local Licensing Authority or Local Jurisdiction, and be archived in a format ensuring authentication and no alteration.

Rule 3-615 — vehicle value limits (Verify): enclosed vehicle ≤$10,000 retail value; non-enclosed vehicle ≤$2,000 retail value; the vehicle must not leave Colorado with any regulated marijuana in it; only persons licensed by the State Licensing Authority and identified on the transport manifest may occupy the vehicle during deliveries. Source: Rule 3-615 (prior research); Verify. Delivery recipients and residence-only rule (Verify against Rule 3-615): delivery orders may go to patients ≥21, parents/guardians of patients under 18, or consumers ≥21 at a private residence. Delivery orders to patients 18–20 are NOT permitted. Delivery is only to the individual who placed the order, who must be ≥21 with acceptable ID, no more than once per day to the same individual/residence, and only to a private residence (defined as private premises where a person lives, e.g. a private dwelling/place of habitation, specifically excluding premises at a school — full definition truncated, Verify).

$1 delivery surcharge — statute claim, current practice Verify: a retail store charges a $1 surcharge per delivery, remitted monthly to the municipality where the store is located, under the statutory text. This resolves Run 1's surcharge question as current statutory text only in the reproduction sense, but whether it is still collected in practice under the current rule is Verify. Source: CRS §§44-10-505/601/605 (reproductions; Verify against leg.colorado.gov).

Delivery hours — Verify delivery-specific hours: the task brief states delivery hours 8 a.m.–midnight. The verified state store no-sale window is 12:00 a.m.–8:00 a.m. (Rule 3-245, §11.1), which is consistent with an 8 a.m. start but does not by itself prove a midnight delivery cut-off in Rule 3-615. A local example (Northglenn) accepts orders 24 hours/day but prohibits deliveries 10 p.m.–8 a.m. Delivery-specific hours are therefore Verify against Rule 3-615, and local opt-in hours must be checked jurisdiction by jurisdiction. Local opt-in is required for delivery — a store may not deliver into a jurisdiction that has not permitted it. Local delivery conditions (Northglenn example, local only): delivery only to 21+ at a private residence; under-21 medical only to a registered caregiver/parent/guardian ≥21; no delivery to a college campus, public place or business; product pre-packaged at licensed premises and locked in the vehicle; only badged employees/owners on the manifest may occupy the vehicle.

11.10 Hospitality operations

Two hospitality types (Run 1, carried; types confirmed): §44-10-609 consumption-only hospitality (may be mobile); §44-10-610 hospitality-and-sales (not mobile) — CRS §44-10-701, stating the §§44-10-609/610 exception; HB 19-1230 material confirming the mobile / non-mobile definitions. State restrictions (advocacy/secondary summary of statute and testimony — Verify against §§44-10-609/610/701): hospitality businesses must prohibit alcohol, cannot sell/distribute marijuana on-site under the consumption-only type, must restrict entry to 21+, and must ensure consumption is not visible from outside; §44-10-701 makes on-premises consumption unlawful except in licensed hospitality spaces — CRS §44-10-701 (the §44-10-701 exception itself is confirmed statute text; the alcohol/21+/visibility details are not confirmed from that text alone). Source for the details: HB 26-1117 testimony, March 2026, leg.colorado.gov (secondary/advocacy) — HB 26-1117 is a dead bill and must never be cited as law. Mobile hospitality — ventilation and driver separation (Run 1 rule; Verify against current text): the mobile consumption area must exclude the driver/front-seat passenger seating area (Rule 6-940(B)); ventilation must be such that smoke/vape air is not circulated into the driver's area (Rule 6-940(E)). A secondary guide adds: driver's area must have separate ventilation, consumption area must be isolated, facilities not licensed to prepare food may serve hot beverages, pastries and pre-packaged foods, and alcohol cannot be sold or consumed on-site. Source: Rule 6-940 via Run 1; Catalyst guide (secondary).

Local opt-in and Clean Indoor Air Act — Verify: Colorado localities opt in to hospitality; localities may allow smoking including indoors. A secondary claim that the Clean Indoor Air Act does not apply inside licensed lounges is Verify — do not publish it as a verified exemption. Food service in a hospitality business requires health-department permits (secondary guide) — Verify against local health rules. Hospitality hours: hospitality and hospitality-and-sales businesses shall not sell or permit consumption from 2:00 a.m. to 7:00 a.m. (see §11.1; full Rule 3-245 text Verify).

11.11 Hemp operations (cross-reference to Part 7 — no fee-table duplication)

Division of regulation (Run 1, carried; Part 7 governs): CDA regulates hemp cultivation only; CDPHE regulates manufacturing, packaging, warehousing and distribution once the crop leaves the farm. CDPHE hemp registrations: under 6 CCR 1010-24 (adopted 15 November 2023, effective 14 January 2024). Correction to the Part 11 research report's former “Verify” on CDPHE amounts: Part 7 resolves this — $100 non-refundable application fee + $1,500 registration fee = $1,600 per facility per year (see §7.7); the secondary $60/$300 figures are repealed pre-2023 tiers and must not be used. CDA hemp definition and sampling frame: CDA hemp is Cannabis sativa L. at ≤0.3% delta-9 THC dry weight, tested for total THC via post-decarboxylation (see §7.6 for full sampling/remediation detail). CDA sampling, CDPHE manufacturing inspections and hemp-product testing detail beyond that frame were not re-verified from opened official sources in Part 11 and are Verify against current CDA/CDPHE procedures — do not import the marijuana Metrc/testing rules into hemp operations. Hemp in marijuana testing: Rule 4-215 microbial testing expressly includes Hemp Products, and Rule 4-215 residual-solvent limits expressly include Hemp Product (if a solvent was used) — Rule 4-215 reproduction (solvent attribution corrected from Rule 4-115 to Rule 4-215 under current numbering). No standalone MED intoxicating-hemp licence: Part 7 resolves this — none exists in §44-10-401 (see §7.9); Part 11 asserts none. Federal hemp collision (Run 1, carried, corrected to the baseline qualifier): Colorado's 1.75 mg/serving hemp rule collides with the federal 0.4 mg/container cap after 11 December 2026 (until 11 December 2026, PL 119-103 §2019 limits the federal provision to the non-naturally-produced/synthesised exclusion); no Colorado agency response to the 2026 federal hemp dates was located in Run 1 — Verify/Unavailable, re-check after 11 December 2026. A typical 1.75 mg can exceeds the federal 0.4 mg/container cap by more than 4× (1.75 ÷ 0.4 = 4.375×).

11.12 Worker safety and occupational licensing / badges

Occupational licensing in operations: only persons licensed by the State Licensing Authority and identified on the transport manifest may occupy a delivery vehicle during deliveries (see §11.9); the same badged-employee principle appears in local delivery conditions. Badges / digital credentials post-5 January 2026 — UNRESOLVED: Run 1 flagged the post-5 January 2026 badge/digital-credential position as Verify, and Run 2 did not locate an MED notice confirming a digital-credential replacement for physical badges in the opened sources. The position remains Verify — do not state that physical badges have been abolished, nor that a specific digital credential is now mandatory, without an MED source. Worker safety — scope limit: no Colorado marijuana-specific worker-safety rule (OSHA-state-plan provision, PPE, ergonomics, or chemical-exposure standard beyond the Rule 6-315 SOP/safety-check and closed-loop requirements in §11.4) was re-verified from an opened official source in Run 2. General occupational-safety duties are Verify against current Colorado Division of Labor and Standards / federal OSHA material — do not invent a cannabis-specific safety standard. Criminal-activity reporting (operational duty, secondary local plan summary): a local security-plan summary cites Rule 3-905(B)(24)(b) as requiring employees to notify MED, the town clerk and the county sheriff within one business day of discovery of unauthorised entry, theft of cannabis/products/paraphernalia/equipment/money, or any plan or action to steal them. Source: Verts Grand Lake security plan (local filing, secondary); Verify verbatim against Rule 3-905.

PART 12 — CONSUMER AND SOCIAL RULES

12.1 Consumer rights and protections

No general return/refund right located: no Colorado rule granting a general consumer right to return any marijuana product for a refund was located in Run 2. Advisories direct return for proper disposal, not for refund; any refund is a store policy, not a stated rule. A general refund right is therefore marked Verify/Unavailable — do not promise refunds in this file. Complaint route — MED Reporting Form (Verify on the MED site): consumers who experience adverse health effects after consuming an affected product should seek medical attention immediately and report the event to MED by submitting an MED Reporting Form. The MED Health & Safety Advisory page lists all HSAs issued in recent years. Source: Cannabis Law Report — Karing Kind advisory (secondary reproduction).

Recall / Health & Safety Advisory process — how it works (advisory-derived, secondary reproductions; Verify on the MED/DOR advisory page): DOR, in conjunction with CDPHE, issues a Health & Safety Advisory when marijuana is found to contain contaminants above the acceptable limits in Rule 4-215; the advisory is deemed a threat to public health and safety, identifies the manufacturer, licence number and Production (or Harvest) Batch numbers, lists affected stores and sale dates, and states that the manufacturer collaborated with MED to initiate a voluntary recall where applicable. Sources: Cannabis Law Report — Karing Kind advisory; Colorado Cannabis Times — Colorado's Best Dabs advisory (both secondary reproductions).

What to do with recalled product (consumer steps, repeated verbatim across 2026 advisories as reproduced): (1) Check the product label (manufacturer licence number + Production Batch number) against the advisory; (2) stop use immediately; (3) seek medical attention for adverse effects; (4) report adverse effects via the MED Reporting Form; (5) destroy the affected product or return it to the store purchased from for proper disposal; (6) do not give it away or resell it (secondary explainer addition — the give-away/resale prohibition itself is Verify as a rule, though it follows from the disposal instruction). One retailer-facing summary adds: do not destroy affected product at the retail level until disposition instructions arrive from the manufacturer or MED, then destroy under Rule 3-230 and record in Metrc — that retailer instruction differs from the consumer instruction and must not be confused with it.

2026 recall examples (secondary reporting of official advisories — use as examples, not as a complete recall list; none is confirmed on the MED advisory page in this audit):

  • StayCon LLC dba Craft (Staycon/Craft), advisory 25 September 2026: vaporizer delivery devices made with an ingredient containing methylene chloride, an industrial solvent Colorado does not allow in marijuana manufacturing; conflicting counts — do not harmonise: 87 production batches across 11 product lines in the Simplifya summary (49 products in the voluntary recall notice of 18 September 2026); 21 Craft vaporizer flavours in the MED advisory instruction; sold at 405 stores 27 March–25 September 2026; by 9 October 2026 CDPHE had received 38 adverse-health-effect reports, most involving headaches and respiratory discomfort (via Westword/CDPHE spokesperson). A further Craft notice 13 October 2026 covered chlorfenapyr, sold 26 September 2025–11 July 2026 at 226 stores; a separate geraniol/Floraplex issue was reported 2 October 2026. Sources: MJBizDaily, 2 October 2026 (secondary); Simplifya advisory (secondary).
  • Colorado Medical Processing LLC dba Colorado's Best Dabs, advisory 23 October 2026: methyl ethyl ketone above Rule 4-215 limits; manufacturer licence 404R-00345, Production Batch 4635R; sold at 33 stores 2 August–17 October 2026; one adverse-health-event report received. Source: Colorado Cannabis Times advisory (secondary reproduction).
  • Karing Kind, LLC, additional advisory (following 26 November 2025 advisory): pesticides chlorfenapyr and paclobutrazol above Rule 4-215 limits; product sold 9 November 2024–8 December 2025 at six dispensaries; voluntary recall with MED; investigation ongoing and additional batches may be added. Source: Cannabis Law Report advisory (secondary).
  • CC Brands LLC dba Stash House CO: butane above Rule 4-215 limits; sold at 43 stores 13 August–3 September 2026. Source: Cannabis Law Report advisory (secondary).

MED email-alert signup — Verify: a secondary explainer mentions MED email-alert signup for advisories; that route was not confirmed on the MED site in Run 2 and is Verify.

12.2 Patient rights — registry confidentiality, employer, landlord, school, housing, custody

Registry confidentiality — rule text as reproduced (5 CCR 1006-2, Regulation 1; Verify verbatim against the SOS official text): CDPHE shall create and maintain a confidential registry of patients who have applied for and are entitled to receive a registry identification card. All personal medical records and personal identifying information held by the department in compliance with these regulations are confidential information. No person may gain access to registry information about patients, physicians or primary caregivers except authorised department employees in the course of their official duties and authorised state/local law-enforcement employees who have stopped or arrested a person claiming medical use and in possession of a registry identification card (or functional equivalent). The department may confirm card suspension when a patient is no longer diagnosed; it may release specific patient information to that patient with the patient's written authorisation; primary caregivers may authorise inclusion in the voluntary caregiver registry for release to new patients only per Regulation 9(C). A department officer, employee or agent who violates confidentiality is subject to existing statutory penalties. Source: Justia — 5 CCR 1006-2, Regulation 1 (reproduction, current through Register Vol. 48 No. 11, 10 June 2025).

Licensee/applicant data confidentiality (statute, as reproduced; Verify against current CRS text): under §44-10-204, the State Licensing Authority shall maintain confidentiality of licensee/applicant individualised data (sales, leases, organisation, financial, tax returns, credit, cultivation, testing, security plans, customer information); such information is used only for Article 10 purposes and securities/federal/state/local law-enforcement purposes; patient information is medical data under §24-72-204(3)(a)(I), disclosed only to persons directly involved in an active investigation/proceeding; public inspection is limited to final agency actions/orders, aggregated/de-identified testing data, aggregated/de-identified demographic data, and enforcement forms/checklists. Source: CRS §44-10-204 via colorado.public.law (reproduction; insert statute link in any republication).

Employment — Coats, summarised, not contradicted (Run 1): Coats v. Dish Network, LLC, 2015 CO 44, held that “lawful” under CRS §24-34-402.5 means lawful under both state and federal law; off-duty medical use was not protected while marijuana was federal Schedule I. The court held: “the term ‘lawful’ as used in section 24-34-402.5, was not restricted in any way, and we decline to engraft a state law limitation onto the term. Therefore, an activity such as medical marijuana use that is unlawful under the federal law is not a ‘lawful’ activity under section 24-34-402.5” — Coats v. Dish Network, 2015 CO 44, No. 13SC394, decided 15 June 2015. Post-Schedule III application to state-licensed medical use is Verify — no post-28 April 2026 Colorado court decision was located in Run 1. For retail users, Coats reasoning applies unchanged (retail stays Schedule I). No Colorado employment-protection statute overturning Coats was located — Verify via CRS Title 24, Article 34 and 2024–2026 session laws. §16(6)/§44-10-104(5) employer-preservation language is independent of Coats. Source: Run 1.

Housing / landlord — NO patient safe harbour located: archived CDPHE FAQ material states Colorado medical law does not address whether a qualified patient can be evicted because of patient status even with a lawful amount, and that whether to tell a landlord is the patient's decision. Secondary law-firm material adds that a landlord may impose restrictions, that federal illegality means lease “illegal activity” clauses can lead to violation/eviction proceedings, and that medical users are not a protected class under current fair-housing laws — all secondary, Verify against current statute and case law. No Colorado statute granting a housing safe harbour for lawful marijuana use was located.

Schools — Verify: no Colorado statute or rule granting a school safe harbour, or stating a school's duty regarding a registered patient student, was located in Run 2. Position marked Verify/Unavailable — do not assert a school right or a school ban.

Child custody — case law, secondary practitioner assessment only: In re Marriage of Parr & Lyman, 240 P.3d 509, 512 (Colo. App. 2010), is cited for the proposition that just using medical marijuana does not necessarily mean a child is endangered physically or emotionally by time with that parent. Practitioner assessment (secondary, 2023-era) adds: use does not usually affect parenting time if it does not impact ability to parent; the likely outcome is a parenting-plan provision barring use during or for a period before parenting time, and possible drug testing before driving parenting time. No Colorado statute granting a custody safe harbour for lawful marijuana use was located — Verify against current case law.

Historical registry practice — Verify current practice: archived material describes the registry database as on a stand-alone password-protected computer with locked office/files, and law enforcement only calling to verify a specific card. That is historical procedure; current CDPHE practice is Verify.

12.3 Public health

Pregnancy and lactation — official CDPHE guidance, VERIFIED in substance from the CDPHE page opened in Run 2 (direct CDPHE URL not supplied in the original — insert the live CDPHE “Cannabis, You and Your Baby” URL from the CDPHE site in republication; no URL guessed here): CDPHE's “Cannabis, You and Your Baby” page states: all major medical organisations and the CDC strongly recommend against cannabis use during pregnancy and lactation; cannabis components are stored in the body and can pass to the baby during pregnancy and through human milk both while using and weeks later; the effect is unknown; more frequent use (≥once/week) during pregnancy could lead to early delivery and small birth weight, especially with tobacco; use may impact the baby's brain development; more research is needed and effects are hard to separate from tobacco, alcohol, drugs and social factors; pumping and dumping may not be effective because compounds are stored in the body; to lower possible risks, continue breastfeeding while working to stop or reduce use; do not drive while high and do not let a baby ride with a high driver. CDPHE defines cannabis use to include smoking, vaping, eating, drinking, dabbing, and creams/lotions/tinctures/concentrates containing cannabis.

Provider resources: CDPHE publishes printable fact sheets in multiple languages for pregnant/breastfeeding women, parents and youth-serving professionals, and a Cannabis–Pregnancy & Lactation Clinical Guidance document based on a systematic literature review by the Retail Marijuana Public Health Advisory Committee. The Colorado Child Abuse and Neglect Hotline 1-844-CO-4-KIDS (1-844-264-5437) is listed on the CDPHE provider page (official public contact — reproduced here because it is an official public hotline, not a personal number).

Youth prevention: retail use is illegal under 21 (see §12.7). CDPHE's campaign “Responsibility Grows Here” is listed on the provider page; its current content and reach are Verify. Dated survey figures must not be presented as current: CDPHE's 19 July 2018 release reported 2017 Healthy Kids Colorado Survey youth current use at 1 in 5, and adult use 13.6% (2016) → 15.5% (2017) per BRFSS — dated, do not present as a current youth-use rate.

Impaired driving — corrected (upgraded from Verify): Colorado has no per se THC limit. Under §42-4-1301(6)(a)(IV), if a driver's whole blood contains 5 ng/mL or more of delta-9 THC, that fact “gives rise to a permissible inference that the defendant was under the influence” — the jury may draw the inference but is not required to, and the prosecution must still prove impairment. This is distinct from DUI per se for alcohol (0.08 BAC within two hours, §42-4-1301(2)(a)). Source: §42-4-1301(6)(a)(IV) as quoted in People v. Turner, 2025 (Colo. App. No. 23CA0340). Driving while impaired remains unlawful; the CDPHE pregnancy page independently advises “do not drive while high.” Do not call 5 ng a “limit” or a per se offence. CDPHE warnings generally: CDPHE warnings take the form of joint DOR/CDPHE Health & Safety Advisories (see §12.1) and the published fact sheets above. No separate CDPHE consumer-warning regime beyond those routes was located in Run 2.

12.4 Criminal justice and expungement / sealing

Terminology — sealing vs expungement (secondary, March 2025; Verify against CRS §§24-72-701 et seq.): in Colorado, “expungement” (erasing a record as if it never occurred) is available only in very limited circumstances (juvenile offences, some underage alcohol/marijuana charges, arrests without conviction, completed diversion/informal adjustment/deferred judgment); “sealing” removes a record from public view (most employers/landlords/background-check agencies cannot access it) but law enforcement, courts and certain government entities can still see it.

Petition-based sealing waiting periods (secondary — Verify): petty/minor misdemeanours 1 year; most misdemeanours 3 years; Level 3/4 drug felonies 3–5 years; some nonviolent felonies 5 years. These periods are Verify against current CRS §§24-72-701 et seq. and must not be published as verified statute without that check.

Clean Slate Act — SB 22-099 (2022), official bill text: SB 22-099 concerns the procedure for sealing criminal records for nonviolent offences. It created an automatic-conviction-sealing mechanism under §13-3-117, under which the State Court Administrator compiles lists of eligible convictions (excluding Victims' Rights Act crimes under §24-4.1-302(1)) eligible for sealing under §§24-72-703 and 24-72-706. Source: Session Laws, Chapter 276 — SB 22-099 (PDF).

Clean Slate — automatic timelines (secondary summaries of SB 22-099, consistent across sources; Verify all against current §§13-3-117 and 24-72-701 et seq.): automatic sealing in full effect July 2024 (expanded 2025 per a screening-industry summary — expansion Verify); arrest records without charges automatically sealed after 1 year; non-conviction records (dismissals/acquittals) sealed upon disposition; convictions automatically sealed after 4 years (civil infractions), 7 years (misdemeanours), 10 years (eligible felonies, from release/conclusion plus completion of sentence requirements); exclusions include murder, assault, robbery, sex offences and domestic violence (lists vary by source — Verify); outstanding fines/fees do not affect eligibility (one summary) but restitution is retained; prior-conviction caps stated in one summary: petty offences ≤5 separate convictions, lower misdemeanours ≤4, high misdemeanours/eligible felonies ≤3, with multi-charge cases using the most-serious-offence eligibility for all charges.

Marijuana-specific sealing history (secondary, consistent; Verify): a 2017 law provided for expungement/sealing of prior misdemeanour marijuana convictions; HB 21-1090 first allowed those convicted of class 3 felony marijuana offences before 1 October 2013 to petition to have the conviction record sealed (not eligible for the mandatory/automatic process); a 2020 bill allowed mass pardons for possession up to 2 oz (see pardons below); the 2022 Clean Slate Act made petition-based sealing for many drug misdemeanours/felonies automatic in 2024, with waiting periods of 7 years for misdemeanours and 10 years for felonies. Eligibility is narrowed by restrictions and many with prior arrests are excluded (MPP summary). Source: Collateral Consequences Resource Center — Colorado restoration profile, updated 13 October 2026 (secondary).

“159,000 drug records cleared” — DO NOT publish as an official Colorado total: MPP states “More than 159,000 drug records were cleared, most of which were for cannabis.” The source and date for that count were not verified against an official Colorado source in Run 2. It is marked Verify and must not be presented as an official state total.

Underage marijuana sealing: under §18-13-122(13), as amended by SB 22-099 — Session Laws, Chapter 276 — on dismissal after deferred judgment/diversion or other dismissal, or on completion of court-ordered substance-abuse education and payment of any fine for a first conviction, the court shall immediately order the case sealed under §24-72-704 and provide copies for distribution to law-enforcement agencies in the case. Minor-in-possession offences may be sealed automatically for first offences and by petition after a one-year waiting period for second or subsequent offences (CCRC secondary detail — Verify).

Juvenile rules — Verify in detail: a secondary summary states juvenile records will not be expunged if the person was adjudicated a violent/aggravated offender. The full juvenile expungement/sealing procedure, eligibility and waiting periods were not re-verified from statute in Run 2 and are Verify.

Governor pardons — OFFICIAL CBI source, VERIFIED, single authoritative figure: HB 20-1424 authorised the Governor to pardon a class of defendants convicted of possession of up to 2 oz without district-attorney/judge input. On 1 October 2020, Governor Polis pardoned convictions for possession of 1 oz or less through Executive Order C 2020 004. On 30 December 2021, Governor Polis pardoned a class of defendants convicted of possession of 2 oz or less through Executive Order C 2021 019. To date, 2,732 convictions have been pardoned for possession of 1 oz or less and 1,351 convictions for possession of 2 oz or less — a combined floor of over 4,000 convictions (2,732 + 1,351 = 4,083 convictions, not people), with CBI noting the exact number of people is unclear because one person may have had several eligible convictions, and that CBI will continue to work through data to identify eligible convictions. The pardons apply only to Colorado state-level convictions; convictions from another state are not pardoned by either order. Municipal-conviction, juvenile-adjudication and Denver County Court (General Sessions) exclusions stated in the original are retained with Verify for the juvenile and Denver County Court specifics (not confirmed on the CBI page opened); the state-level / other-state limits are CBI-confirmed. Source: Colorado Bureau of Investigation — marijuana pardons (official).

Pardon effect — not expungement/sealing (Verify on visibility detail and current check route): the 2020 pardon does not expunge or seal records, but removes the conviction from public records/background checks; on a law-enforcement check the conviction still appears flagged as pardoned. Pardons were automatic — eligible persons did not need to apply — and eligibility could be checked via comarijuanapardons.com / CBI (secondary reports of the Governor's office; current check route Verify).

Later individual pardons — secondary, do not merge into the mass-pardon total: a 29-person pardon round was announced Wednesday 26 August 2026 (Marijuana Herald, 28 August 2026, secondary reporting of the Governor's office), several marijuana-related, including a 2005 possession >8 oz, a 1997 guilty plea >8 oz, and a 2000 guilty plea 1–8 oz (Marijuana Moment examples). These are individual pardons, not a new mass pardon, and must not be added to the 4,083 mass-pardon conviction total. A Governor's-office total quoted August 2026 (“4,083 marijuana possession pardons, in addition to 165 individual pardons and 35 sentence commutations”) conflicts with a CPR 30 January 2026 figure of 25 commutations — the commutation total is Verify against the current Governor's office clemency page; do not publish a single commutation total without that check. Applications received before the 3 April 2026 deadline continue to be reviewed during Governor Polis's remaining term (Governor's office via Herald/Moment, August 2026, secondary). No year-end pardons in late 2025 (Longmont Times-Call, secondary) — the June 2025 blanket pardon noted in that article was for state psilocybin possession, not marijuana, and must not be counted toward the marijuana total.

Federal firearms — 18 U.S.C. §922(g)(3), stated as a federal issue: §922(g)(3) prohibits possession of a firearm by a person who is an unlawful user of or addicted to a controlled substance. ATF Form 4473 (August 2023 edition, per secondary summaries) asks about unlawful use/addiction to marijuana or other controlled substances and warns that state legalisation does not change federal law; answering falsely is itself a federal crime (secondary). Source: 18 U.S.C. §922(g)(3) and ATF Form 4473 (secondary summaries); Verify current form edition.

Firearms — 2026 developments, all secondary, current ATF position Verify: ATF narrowed the “unlawful user” definition in January 2026 to someone who regularly uses a controlled substance over an extended period without a lawful prescription; a state medical card is not a prescription (Leafwell, October 2026, secondary). United States v. Hemani, decided 18 June 2026, 9–0 (argued 2 March 2026): a prosecution based solely on regular marijuana use (about every other day) for possessing a gun at home violated the Second Amendment as applied; the ruling is narrow — it does not strike down §922(g)(3), does not resolve restrictions on addicted or currently intoxicated persons, and does not directly decide dealer transfers or Form 4473 completion; ATF was reviewing Hemani with updated guidance pending as of August 2026 secondary reviews. Reese v. ATF, 5th Cir. 30 January 2025, remand judgment W.D. La. 27 January 2026, appeal/cross-appeal pending 5th Cir. No. 26-30154 (secondary docket summary — Verify). McCoy v. ATF, cert. denied 30 June 2026 (secondary). Bottom line: §922(g)(3) remains in force as a statute; Hemani limits as-applied prosecutions on regular use alone; the current ATF position after Hemani is Verify — do not state that state-licensed medical use is now federally lawful for firearms purposes, and do not state that a card alone triggers a lifetime ban.

12.5 Social equity outcomes

Denver programme — OFFICIAL, VERIFIED: Denver's marijuana social equity programme reserves store, transporter, cultivation, manufacturing and hospitality licences for social equity applicants until 1 July 2027; there is no cap on the number of licences available to social equity applicants — Denver — marijuana licences FAQ (official).

Denver eligibility and 51% rule — OFFICIAL: a social equity applicant is a person applying for a new or transferred licence who holds a valid finding of suitability from the state licensing authority as a social equity licensee; Denver's criteria align with SB 24-076 and MED rules. Until the exclusivity period expires (1 July 2027), licences granted to social equity applicants must be majority-owned (at least 51%) by one or more social equity licensees; a social equity licensee may sell some or all ownership interest as long as one or more social equity licensees holds at least 51% — Denver FAQ (official). Statewide eligibility criteria detail (residency, opportunity-zone/disproportionate-impacted-area, marijuana-offence, income, revoked-licence bars) is Verify against MED rules / SB 24-076 text.

Denver delivery — corrected, Verify (do not assert as current): the original statement that only social equity applicants may deliver, holding a transporter licence and Denver delivery permit, is not confirmed on the Denver FAQ opened, and secondary Denver history states the social-equity-transporter partnership requirement ended 1 July 2024, after which stores could apply for their own delivery permits. Current Denver delivery exclusivity is therefore Verify against the current Denver code.

Denver exclusivity expiry — what happens after 1 July 2027 (secondary summary of Denver code — Verify vs DRMC): after 1 July 2027, Denver code states social equity licences may transfer to social equity or non-social-equity applicants on manager approval. The current Denver code provision is described in a secondary report as repealed effective 1 July 2027. Source: secondary summary of DRMC; Verify vs Denver Revised Municipal Code.

Denver 2026 report: on 1 July 2026, Denver's Department of Licensing and Consumer Protection (DLCP) published a report on Denver's marijuana business social equity programme, summarising programme history and next steps as the city approaches expiry of the exclusive licensing period on 1 July 2027, with a stakeholder feedback form. The report's outcome counts were not extracted in Run 2 — do not quote counts from it without opening it.

Older Denver outcome figures — DATED, secondary, do not present as current: a Denver report to January 2023 stated 20 of 1,017 registered Denver marijuana businesses were owned by social equity licensees; white people 90% of owners, Black 4.4% (Marijuana Moment via Cannabis Cultivator News, July 2023); a Denver spokesperson at that time stated 32 social equity qualified applicants approved for various licences, 31 pending, 31 licences issued to social equity applicants.

Statewide social equity counts — Unavailable for late 2026: no official statewide late-2026 count was located. The Run 1 figure of 99 approved as of 1 April 2025 is secondary and Verify; the MED annual legislative report was not located in Run 1. OEDIT outcomes — secondary only, Verify vs OEDIT: Run 1 reported a grant round closed since October 2024 (secondary — Verify vs OEDIT); loan/grant amounts in secondary sources ($1m loan fund initial, max $150,000; grant Growth up to $50,000; pitch prize $100,000) are not published here as official figures. 12.7 Tourism and visitor rules

Visitor purchase (Run 1, carried): a visitor 21+ with valid government ID may buy retail on the same terms as a resident since HB 16-1261 (enrolled text Verify). There is no medical reciprocity — an out-of-state medical card does not authorise a Colorado medical purchase. Public consumption: public consumption is illegal except on private property with the owner's permission or in a licensed hospitality business. Open/public use of ≤2 oz is described in secondary material as a drug petty offence punishable by up to $100 plus up to 24 hours' community service — Verify statute. §44-10-701 makes on-premises consumption unlawful except in licensed hospitality spaces (see §11.10) — CRS §44-10-701. Hotels / Airbnb: no general hotel-consumption right was located; hotels may prohibit use on their property (Run 1). HB 25-1331 (hotel/special-event delivery) failed and is not law — leg.colorado.gov — HB 25-1331 (introduced summary only; no signed act); the original's postponement date of 16 April 2025 is Verify against the bill's action history. No Airbnb-specific consumption rule was located; the private-property-with-permission principle and the host's/property's own prohibition govern, and any broader Airbnb rule is Verify. Federal land: marijuana remains illegal on federal land, including national forests, under federal law. A secondary Four Corners article reported patients cited for smoking on national-forest land in Colorado; current enforcement practice is Verify, but federal illegality on federal land is the baseline. Driving and transport for visitors: visitors are subject to the same impaired-driving position as residents (see §12.3, as corrected: 5 ng permissible inference, not a per se limit) and the same transport rule that a delivery vehicle must not leave Colorado with regulated marijuana in it (see §11.9). Personal transport across state lines is not authorised by Colorado law.

12.10 PART 12 CHECKLIST — What a consumer / patient should check before buying

Drawn ONLY from rules stated in Parts 0–12 above, as corrected. Nothing in this checklist adds a new rule.

  • Am I 21+ (retail) or a registered patient with a valid card (medical)? Retail sales to under-21s and medical sales to non-patients are Level I violations. Source: Rule 8-235 reproduction.
  • Am I within the sale limit for this transaction? Retail: 1 oz flower equivalent (= 8 g concentrate = 800 mg THC edibles, plus up to 6 seeds). Medical daily: 2 oz flower, 8 g concentrate 21+ / 2 g 18–20, 20,000 mg products (Verify medical figures against current Rule 5-125). Retail edibles: 10 mg/serving, 100 mg/package. Source: Run 1; Rule 5-125 reproduction.
  • Does the container label show the manufacturer's licence number and Production Batch number? Those are the two fields an advisory uses to identify recalled product — check them against any current MED Health & Safety Advisory before use.
  • Is this product on a current Health & Safety Advisory? If it matches an advisory, stop use immediately, seek medical attention for adverse effects, report via the MED Reporting Form, and destroy it or return it to the store purchased from for proper disposal. Do not assume a refund — no general refund rule was located.
  • Where will I consume it? Only on private property with the owner's permission, or in a licensed hospitality business (21+, no alcohol on-site in hospitality — hospitality details Verify per §11.10). Public consumption is unlawful except in those settings.
  • Am I driving, or will a baby ride with me? Do not drive while high, and do not let a baby ride with a high driver (CDPHE). Note: 5 ng/mL is a permissible inference under §42-4-1301(6)(a)(IV), not a per se limit.
  • Am I pregnant, breastfeeding, or buying for someone who is? CDPHE and the CDC strongly recommend against cannabis use during pregnancy and lactation; compounds can pass during pregnancy and through human milk weeks after use.
  • Am I a patient who needs confidentiality? CDPHE registry information is confidential and is released only to authorised department employees, to law enforcement that has stopped/arrested a cardholder claiming medical use, or to the patient with written authorisation (5 CCR 1006-2 Reg. 1 as reproduced; Verify verbatim against SOS text).
  • Am I a visitor? Bring valid government ID and be 21+ for retail; do not rely on an out-of-state medical card in Colorado (no reciprocity); do not take product out of Colorado.
  • Am I relying on a job, housing or custody protection that Colorado law does not grant? Coats (2015 CO 44) remains the employment baseline, its post-Schedule III application is Verify, no housing safe harbour was located, and custody turns on the child's best interests, not on patient status alone (Parr & Lyman, secondary assessment). Check the specific employer, lease or court position before assuming protection.
